summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Investigation after boy assaulted at Cambridgeshire school remains ongoing
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An investigation launched after a student was allegedly assaulted at a Cambridgeshire school is ongoing after more than seven weeks. Police received a report of an assault at Cromwell Community College, in Chatteris, on Wednesday (September 23). The incident was said to have taken place earlier in the day, Cambridgeshire Constabulary confirmed. The victim, a 13-year-old boy, attended hospital for treatment to his injuries and a crime for grievous bodily harm was raised. In a statement, the Active Learning Trust, which runs the school, revealed a Year 9 student was "hurt in an incident" . A spokesperson said staff "responded quickly and appropriately" and gave "care and support to the injured student". They added: "The college’s pastoral team has been supporting students following the incident and will continue to offer reassurance as required. "We will co-operate fully with the police and their investigation into this matter." In an update on Thursday (November 12), Cambridgeshire Police confirmed the investigation remains ongoing. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Families given five weeks' notice of Huntingdonshire disabled day centre closure
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Families of adults with learning disabilities have raised concerns over plans to move a Huntingdonshire day service from St Ives to Huntingdon with just five weeks' notice. Cambridgeshire County Council has told users of the CATS centre in Bull Lane, St Ives, their families, carers and advocates that the service is due to move to Huntingdon Community Centre on December 7. In a November 2 letter, Cambridgeshire head of provider services Mandy Langley told the Singh family that activities and support would move to the Huntingdon centre, around six miles away. The family says the letter was the first it knew about the plans and questions why relatives were not consulted before the announcement. Surj Singh said his brother has Down syndrome, is non-verbal and relies heavily on familiar people and surroundings. He said the family feared moving the service could seriously affect his brother and others who rely on familiar routines. The family has questioned whether the new centre is suitable, citing noise, summer heat, staffing, supervision, privacy, facilities and personal care. The Singh family complained to the council on November 5 and asked it to pause the move until families had been consulted and individual needs and transition plans addressed. Read more Just under half of children in Huntingdon miss out on NHS dentist visits Decision looms on 600-home plan for St Neots amid flood of objections Hunts man accused of distributing indecent images of children named Thief who stole orangutan statue from garden centre pictured New plan to replace ‘potentially unsafe cladding’ agreed Mr Singh said his brother’s needs raised serious questions about whether the new setting and arrangements would suit him and others with different support needs. The family wants to know when the decision was made, what assessment and consultation took place, and how staffing, personal care and individual suitability will be assured. Mr Singh said his brother had been away from the service because of ill health, and the family had spent weeks planning his return with social services and the provider without hearing about the move. The family has also questioned the move’s timing, just weeks before Christmas. The council said the move was planned because fewer people were using CATS St Ives. It said Huntingdon Community Centre already provides day services and has room for St Ives users, allowing it to "make better use of our buildings and resources". The council said familiar staff would continue supporting users and similar activities would be available in Huntingdon. But Mr Singh said the family feared the Huntingdon centre was much larger and noisier than the St Ives site. The council said users would still have access to the St Ives community while being offered opportunities in Huntingdon. The council said users would be offered extra visits to the Huntingdon centre in November to prepare for the move. It said there would be no break in service and that the St Ives centre would operate until the move. The council said it would discuss any changes to care arrangements or transport with those affected. The letter said: "We are committed to supporting everyone through this change and making it as smooth as possible." The family says the council has acknowledged its complaint but has yet to answer its concerns. A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said: "From Monday, December 7, the council will be bringing together the CATS day service in St Ives with services provided at Huntingdon Community Centre for adults with learning disabilities. "Huntingdon Community Centre already provides a wide range of activities and opportunities, including the Blossom and Bloom Café and TAG Bikes. "Bringing the services together will give people attending CATS access to a broader choice of activities, opportunities to build confidence and independence, and the chance to meet and develop relationships with new people. "Our priority is to ensure a smooth transition for everyone affected, and we will continue to work with individuals and their families throughout the process, including reviewing any transport arrangements required. "The move will also bring services together on one site, providing greater operational resilience and making the best use of council resources. “We can confirm this complaint is being investigated and we have contacted the family to explain the complaints process."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Doctor Who stars Peter Davison and Paul McGann to visit Peterborough exhibition
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Doctor Who stars are set to bring a touch of time travel to Peterborough. Peter Davison and Paul McGann, who played the Fifth and Eighth Doctors, will visit Queensgate Shopping Centre on Saturday, November 21, from 12pm to 3pm as part of the centre’s Christmas lights switch-on. Their appearance comes just days before the opening of the Whoseum, an unofficial Doctor Who exhibition celebrating 63 years of the iconic sci-fi series. Derek Handley, exhibition curator, said: "After last year, people kept asking me how we could top what we had achieved at the museum. I think we've found a way to do it." The Whoseum will officially open on Monday, November 23, and will feature monsters, costumes, original props and recreated sets from the long-running series. Located in Unit 79 at Queensgate, the exhibition is created by Rapido Trains in association with Peterborough Museum and Art Gallery. It promises to take visitors on a journey through time and space, exploring the creativity behind some of Doctor Who’s most memorable creatures. Jason Shron, president of Rapido Trains, said: "For over 50 years, Doctor Who exhibitions have been a way for the fan community to engage with the original props and costumes of their favourite television programme. "I'm delighted that Rapido Trains has helped bring the Whoseum to life, including some of my own costumes made by the talented Rob Allsopp, who was a bona fide monster maker for Doctor Who. "I hope that Whovians all over the UK and around the world will make the trip to Peterborough to take a walk through Doctor Who history." The exhibition will reveal how these monsters were designed and built, offering insight into their cultural impact. Sarah Wilson, heritage manager at Peterborough Museum, said: "I'm delighted that the monsters are coming back in force, thanks to our team from last year and Rapido Trains, and in such a spectacular way, with the inside of the TARDIS and a Dalek spaceship being brought back to life from long-lost Doctor Who episodes from 60 years ago. "Only this time, you can see them for real." From January 2027, the Whoseum will double in size, expanding to fill the entire unit and showcase even more monsters, props and sets. A spokesperson said it will offer fans another chance to experience something new in the new year, with further supporting exhibitions planned throughout 2027.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Herts and Cambs residents urged to get winter-ready with three simple steps
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: People in Hertfordshire and Cambridgeshire are urged to take simple steps now to protect their health and prepare for winter. The advice comes from NHS Central East’s Get Winter Ready campaign, which helps people “protect, prepare and stay well” through the colder months. The campaign covers Bedfordshire, Luton, Milton Keynes, Cambridgeshire, Peterborough and Hertfordshire. Dr Fiona Head, medical director at NHS Central East Integrated Care Board, said: "There are simple things we can all do to help ourselves and those around us stay well this winter. "One of the most important is getting vaccinated if you’re eligible, to help protect yourself and those around you. "Flu and COVID-19 can cause serious illness, particularly for those who are more vulnerable, and vaccination can help reduce your risk of becoming seriously unwell. "It's also important to be prepared. Make sure you have the medicines you need at home and order repeat prescriptions in good time. "If you do become unwell, knowing where to go can help you get the right advice and support, whether that’s from your local pharmacy or NHS 111." The campaign urges people to protect themselves, prepare for winter and stay well. 'Protect' focuses on getting eligible flu and COVID-19 vaccinations, practising good hygiene, and taking care around others when unwell to help prevent the spread of illness. 'Prepare' is about keeping everyday medicines at home, ordering repeat prescriptions early, and using the NHS App to order repeat prescriptions. 'Stay well' encourages people to look after both their physical and mental health, and to use the right services when they need support, such as Pharmacy First for many common conditions or NHS 111 when they need urgent medical help but are unsure what to do. Dr Head said: "Winter is a challenging time for health services, and we’re working closely with our NHS providers and partners across the region to prepare for the months ahead. "We want people to stay safe and well, but we also want everyone to know that the NHS is here when they need it." More information and practical advice are available on the Get Winter Ready: Protect, Prepare, Stay Well webpage.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP disability benefit increase from 2027 for people who need care or mobility help
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The DWP revealed that a million Brits could receive more Disability Living Allowance money from April next year. The Department for Work and Pensions updated their website on November 11 with proposals to increase the weekly payments. The current rates only cover the tax year between April 6 2026 and April 5 2027 so from April 6 next year new rates will apply. These increases are labelled as 'provisional' but the Government website's update history shows the previous provisional figures reflected the final figures to the penny. Disability Living Allowance, which helps cover the costs of extra personal care or mobility, has two components - care and mobility. Both of these are split from highest to lowest rates of payment depending on how severe the need for support is. People are eligible for the care component if they need help with things like washing, eating, cooking, communicating needs, dressing or using the toilet. They may also need supervision to 'avoid putting yourself or others in danger' or to have dialysis. The highest rate is paid to those who need 'help or supervision throughout both day and night, or if a medical professional has said they're nearing the end of their life'. This payment is proposed to rise from the £114.60 per week being paid during the current tax year to £118.60 per week for the 2027-28 tax year. The middle rate is described as being suitable for those who need 'frequent help or constant supervision during the day, supervision at night or someone to help you while on dialysis'. The lowest rate is for those who 'need help for some of the day or with preparing cooked meals' and this rate is proposed to increase from £30.30 per week to £31.35. The mobility component is for people who either cannot walk, can only walk 'short distances without severe discomfort' or who could become 'very ill if they try to walk'. People may also get this if they have no feet or legs, are 100% blind or you were between ages 3-64 on April 11 2011 and have been certified as 'severely sight impaired'. Recommended reading: Other criteria include those at least 80% deaf, those who need someone with them when outdoors or those who are 'severely mentally impaired' with behavioural problems. The lower rate of payment is for those who need 'guidance or supervision outdoors' and this would rise from £30.30 per week to £31.35 in the 2027-28 tax year. The higher rate is for those who have 'any other, more severe, walking difficulty' than covered in the lower rate and this would increase from £80 to £82.80 under the proposed new rates. Payments are usually sent directly to claimants bank accounts every four weeks and if their circumstances change they are told to contact the Disability Service Centre.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: MoneySavingExpert warns Virgin customers to check for 'sneaky' paid add-on
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Virgin Experience Days shoppers are being urged to check whether they were signed up to a paid membership without realising. MoneySavingExpert said its team found the £9.99-a-year Memory Makers+ subscription was being added to orders through a pre-ticked box at checkout. The consumer website said it spotted the issue when it visited the company's website on October 30 and reported it to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA). MoneySavingExpert said Virgin Experience Days changed its website after the issue was raised, so the membership box was no longer selected by default. The membership offers discounts on purchases, free greeting cards and other benefits, and renews automatically each year. CMA guidance says businesses must obtain a customer's express consent before charging for optional extras. It says a pre-ticked box does not provide that consent when a customer must take action to avoid an extra charge. The regulator also says customers who did not expressly agree to an additional charge are legally entitled to claim a refund. MoneySavingExpert recommends searching email inboxes, including junk and spam folders, for an account activation message to check whether the membership was added. It advises customers who want to cancel or request a refund to contact memorymakers@virginexperiencedays.co.uk. A Virgin Experience Days spokesperson said: "Memory Makers+ remains a relatively new addition to our business, and we continually review and refine the programme based on performance data, customer feedback and regulatory developments." The company said most customers saved more than the cost of membership on their first purchase and that it received positive feedback about the scheme. The spokesperson added: "In the small number of cases where a customer wishes to cancel, we operate a seven day a week support operation where queries are handled within 24 hours."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Air ambulance teams safely trial hospital treatment for prolonged cardiac arrests
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: East Anglian Air Ambulance has successfully trialled a hospital treatment for patients in prolonged cardiac arrest at emergency scenes. EAAA teams used the treatment on patients in prolonged cardiac arrest outside hospital as part of the ERICA-ARREST feasibility study. The study tested whether helicopter emergency medical service clinicians could safely use resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) to improve blood flow to the heart and brain during resuscitation. Resuscitative Endovascular Balloon Occlusion of the Aorta (REBOA) is a minimally invasive procedure that involves inserting and inflating a balloon within the aorta to temporarily control blood flow. (Image: East Anglian Air Ambulance) Dr James Price, consultant emergency physician at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust and HEMS consultant and consultant lead for research and development at EAAA, said: "Patients who remain in cardiac arrest despite prolonged resuscitation efforts currently have very limited treatment options and face extremely poor outcomes. "Our study has shown that REBOA can be delivered safely by pre-hospital critical care teams and can improve blood pressure during cardiac arrest, helping to direct blood flow to the organs that matter most. "While this study was not designed to determine whether REBOA improves survival, these findings provide a strong foundation for further research and represent an important step forward in exploring new treatment options for this group of patients." Hospitals typically use REBOA to control severe internal bleeding. Doctors insert a small balloon through a groin artery and inflate it inside the aorta, the body’s main artery. Inflating the balloon temporarily blocks blood flow to the lower body and redirects it to the heart and brain. The study tested whether the technique could help patients whose hearts would not restart after prolonged, high-quality resuscitation. Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest remains a major cause of death, and survival rates for patients experiencing prolonged cardiac arrest have not improved in 50 years. The study included 39 patients, aged 58.7 on average, who suffered non-traumatic cardiac arrests outside hospital and did not respond to advanced resuscitation. Doctors attempted REBOA a median of 51 minutes after cardiac arrest, at a very advanced stage of resuscitation. Researchers found HEMS clinicians could perform the procedure safely, with no related complications reported. After inflation, diastolic blood pressure rose by an average of 59 per cent, directing more pressure towards the heart and brain. Of the 33 patients in whom aortic blockage was confirmed, 24.2 per cent achieved a sustained return of spontaneous circulation, and 6.1 per cent survived to hospital discharge. However, researchers emphasised that the study was not intended to determine whether REBOA improves survival, as it did not include a control group. It instead tested whether the procedure was safe outside hospital and improved circulation as expected. Dr Price said the study followed years of work building the clinical skills, safeguards and research systems needed for such a complex treatment before hospital. The research was carried out by EAAA’s research, audit, innovation, and development (RAID) group. He said: "East Anglian Air Ambulance is first and foremost a regional charity looking after critically ill and injured patients across Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire, Norfolk and Suffolk, but alongside that clinical work we have built a research programme led by clinicians who look after these patients every day and want to find better ways of treating them, and ultimately save more lives." He added that the programme had improved EAAA’s overall care, beyond the ERICA-ARREST study. EAAA regularly responds to cardiac arrests across its region, which account for up to 30 per cent of the charity’s medical call-outs. Its teams deliver advanced critical care normally available only in hospital. Researchers say the findings justify further study of whether the treatment improves survival.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdonshire council seeks consent to fly three flags at Pathfinder House
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A council wants permission to fly three flags outside its main offices. Huntingdonshire District Council is seeking permission from its own planning officers to fly the Emergency Services, Remembrance Day and LGBTQ+ Progress Pride flags each year at Pathfinder House in St Mary’s Street, Huntingdon. Caroline Wilson, who submitted the application on behalf of the council, said: "We have been flying all flags annually before realising we needed consent." Reform UK councillors criticised the council for flying the Progress Pride Flag during Pride Month in June. Read more How global Microsoft outage is impacting Cambridgeshire - live updates Air ambulance teams safely trial hospital treatment for prolonged cardiac arrests Herts and Cambs residents urged to get winter-ready with three simple steps Families given five weeks' notice of Huntingdonshire disabled day centre closure Just under half of children in Huntingdon miss out on NHS dentist visits Reform UK members argued the flag was "divisive" and lacked the necessary planning consent. Cllr Ryan Coogan, Reform group leader, said at the time that councils should not fly "divisive political symbols", particularly where the correct permissions have not been obtained, and stressed that public buildings should represent everyone in the district. The council later admitted it lacked permission to fly the flag, but said it only realised this as the flag was being taken down. A spokesperson for the council said: "The Pride Progress flag is a variant of the original Gilbert Baker Pride flag, adopted widely by members of the LGBTQ+ community and related groups. "In planning terms, the Pride flag benefits from 'deemed consent' under the Town and Country Planning (Control of Advertisements) Regulations 2007 (as amended). "However, the Pride Progress flag is not covered by this provision and therefore requires express consent from the local planning authority." The Progress Pride Flag updates the traditional rainbow design to represent more communities within the LGBTQ+ movement. The council said the flag was taken down to make way for the Armed Forces Day Flag, which was flown in honour of Armed Forces Day on June 27. A hospital redevelopment is moving forward with a fresh environmental impact assessment underway. Plans to rebuild Hinchingbrooke Hospital have reached a new stage after North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust submitted a revised Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Scoping Report to Huntingdonshire District Council (HDC). The report sets out key changes and asks the council for a new EIA Scoping Opinion to inform the Environmental Statement for the planned application. The trust previously secured an EIA Scoping Opinion from HDC in October 2025, based on proposals developed in August 2025. An artist's impression of what the new staff accommodation will look like and what the courtyard area will look like once installed by Zed Pods Ltd. (Image: North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust) Since then, the scheme has undergone further design changes, prompting the need for a revised EIA. The updated plans include a range of modifications to the original development. These include the removal of the lower ground floor from the new hospital building, the addition of an energy centre north of the main building, and the relocation of the ambulance deck to the south-east of the site. Land at Views Common could be used temporarily as a contractor’s compound during construction, which may last up to eight years, subject to a lease agreement with the owner. The northern car park will remain at ground level, with possible solar canopies added. Plans for a multi-storey car park have been scrapped. A separate application is being prepared for car parking on the adjacent Constabulary Land, which has been removed from the main hospital application. The trust plans to submit an outline application covering new hospital buildings, an energy centre, service and administration facilities, parking, cycle storage, landscaping, drainage and improved access from Views Common Road. It will also cover the phased demolition of existing hospital buildings and the removal of some trees protected by Tree Preservation Orders. Approved enabling works include relocating staff accommodation, demolishing former staff blocks and creating a temporary car park. The trust is seeking separate permission for the Constabulary Land car park to maintain parking capacity during construction. A separate application also covers a new main intake substation to provide the hospital with an independent high-voltage electricity supply. The latest EIA Scoping Report confirms that most environmental topics identified in the 2025 assessment remain relevant. However, archaeology has now been scoped in due to the discovery of ridge and furrow earthworks and the high potential for further archaeological remains at Views Common. It also explains how the project will assess air quality, biodiversity, noise and vibration, transport and access, trees, daylight and sunlight, and wind. The trust is working with HDC, statutory consultees and other stakeholders to keep the planning process on track with the project and policy requirements. The site boundary has been redrawn to reflect the latest design, removing areas covered by separate applications and adding land at Views Common. The report says the development is not vulnerable to major accidents or disasters, so those risks will not be assessed further. That conclusion is based on the site’s location, existing safeguards and lack of nearby hazards such as major pipelines. The report also includes an assessment of how climate change could affect the development and how it can withstand those risks. It considers sudden and long-term climate hazards, the vulnerability of key site elements and existing measures to adapt. The assessment will be developed further as the design progresses. The EIA Scoping Report will support the updated hospital planning application and shape its Environmental Statement. HDC is expected to issue a revised Scoping Opinion after consulting statutory bodies and reviewing the report. Hinchingbrooke is one of seven English hospitals being rebuilt through the national New Hospital Programme because of RAAC, with the new facility expected to open by the end of 2032.

The campaign is open to businesses of all sizes and aims to encourage those that have not offered such opportunities before to take their first steps. Charlotte Horobin, chief executive officer of Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce, said: "Businesses across our region are already experiencing the consequences of skills shortages, and the evidence tells us that developing the next generation of talent must be a priority if we are to sustain economic growth. Those making a pledge will be recognised as Future Skills Champions, with their commitments displayed on the Opportunity Pledge Wall and mirrored online through the chamber's website. Participating employers will receive a digital badge and may have opportunities to feature in future campaign activity and case studies. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Former Cambs police officer turned up to work 'smelling strongly of alcohol'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A police officer who turned up to work smelling of alcohol would have been sacked for gross misconduct, a hearing found. Former PC Ciaron Hickey, who served with Cambridgeshire Constabulary, attended a first aid refresher course at force headquarters on September 10, 2025. He arrived late, explaining that this was due to him mistakenly attending a local police station. A member of the Public and Personal Safety Training Team (PPST) detected the smell of alcohol on Mr Hickey’s breath after having a brief conversation with him outside the classroom. The PPST trainer confirmed he smelt of alcohol and reported it to the sergeant present. Mr Hickey was removed from the classroom and later admitted drinking alcohol the night before. A preliminary breath test showed 18 micrograms of alcohol per 100ml of breath. A second test an hour later showed 9 micrograms, and he was taken home. At the time of the incident, he was already under a written warning for a similar offence, having reported for duty on September 11, 2024, with excess alcohol in his system. A police misconduct hearing held at Lysander House in Bedfordshire on October 21 concluded that Mr Hickey’s actions amounted to gross misconduct. The panel found that he breached standards on fitness for duty, orders and instructions, and discreditable conduct by attending training "smelling strongly of alcohol". Mr Hickey resigned from the force on October 19, 2026, did not attend the hearing and was not represented. His federation representative confirmed he did not wish to engage with the proceedings. The panel accepted his early admission and co-operation with the investigation as mitigating factors, but said they did not outweigh the seriousness of his actions. The report stated: "The panel considered that the proven conduct was so serious as to justify dismissal and even more so, when considered together with the live written warning for similar conduct." The panel also considered the "personal difficulties" he was experiencing, but said they did not outweigh the seriousness of his conduct. As Mr Hickey was no longer a serving officer at the time of the hearing, the panel could not impose a formal disciplinary sanction. Instead, it recorded that he would have been dismissed without notice had he still been employed. ACC Vaughan Lukey chaired the misconduct panel, alongside independent members Davide Corbino and Bryan McAlley. David Tyme served as the legally qualified person.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New illegal Fire Stick warning issued as police investigating financial records
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A fresh illegal Fire Stick warning has been issued after police are cracking down on users by tracing payments through sellers’ bank accounts. The alert comes amid growing concerns over the widespread use of modified TV Fire Sticks and so-called “dodgy boxes”. These devices enable users to access premium content from providers such as Sky, TNT Sports, Disney+, and Netflix for free. However, those using the devices have been warned that police are now using financial records to find those culpable. Former detective Rav Wilding issued the warning during an appearance on BBC Morning Live. He explained that police are investigating financial records linked to the sale of modified Fire Sticks, which allow users to access premium TV content for free. Mr Wilding said: "They’re going for the distributors. "They’re going for the sellers. "They are having a lot of success. "But actually, once they’ve got the seller, they’re going through their accounts. "They’re seeing who has been paying the money for these illegal things, and if they’ve been paying them for these sticks then people should possibly expect a conversation or two if the police want to know why they’ve been paying them money for this." The illegal devices typically cost between £30 and £100 and provide unauthorised access to subscription-only TV services, including live football. Although owning a standard Fire Stick is legal, Mr Wilding said using one to stream pirated content is a crime. He said: "It’s a crime. "It’s not allowed. "Owning the stick itself is not a crime, but using it for this purpose is. "They (subscription service providers) are losing money to this, so they have been reaching out and are taking action against those people using them illegally as well. "So I wouldn’t say it’s something you should do. "It is actually a crime and it can have a nasty fine, a huge fine and also a custodial sentence for users and sellers of these things." A post shared by Amazon Fire TV (@amazonfiretv) In the UK, downloading or streaming pirated content can be a crime, but prosecutions of individual viewers remain extremely rare. Despite this, several people have been jailed this year as the clampdown on illegal streaming devices in the UK continues. Recommended reading: Those caught using or selling a 'dodgy' fire stick/box and streaming premium content without paying are in breach of Section 11 of the Fraud Act 2006. It says a person will be in breach if they obtain services "without any payment having been made for or in respect of them or without payment having been made in full". summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Poundland issues major update as UK stores at risk of closure
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Poundland has issued an update today (November 12), following the end of a 10-day period that allowed it to continue to try and secure a potential rescue deal. In recent months, the future of Poundland has been uncertain, with last-ditch efforts hoping to save the struggling retailer. The chain filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the end of October, which expired at midnight last night. Asked if the company was going into administration on Thursday, managing director Barry Williams told reporters: “We’re going to go and have a board meeting now to have those conversations.” Now, Poundland has issued an update, informing customers of its future plans. Poundland customers have been assured that its stores are open as normal for at least the next 10 working days. The Board of Poundland Limited said: “Over the past two weeks, Poundland has been operating under the statutory protection of a Notice of Intention (NOI) to appoint Administrators. “Amid an ongoing sale process, and with funding agreed to enable the business to continue trading during this period, the Board of Poundland has today resolved to make an application for a second NOI with a view to identifying the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and our people. “This extends the current protections over the business for a further 10 working days. “Our stores remain open as usual during this period, and we thank our colleagues, suppliers and customers for their incredible and continued support.” Poundland has roughly 600 shops and 11,000 employees across the UK. Ahead of the announcement, Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice said: “Hopefully the directors will be able to extend the notice of administration period from tonight to allow time for a deal to be done with a new buyer for Poundland. “This will protect many thousands of jobs and keep an important value retailer on the High Street, for hard-pressed consumers worried about rising bills.” After a meeting with MPs on the Commons Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, Mr Williams thanked the chain’s staff, whose jobs are at risk. He told Sky News he was “representing 11,000 colleagues” as well as thousands in the broader supply chain and “maybe even the retail industry” at the meeting. Asked whether he could guarantee the security of jobs and keep the business going in the run-up to Christmas, he said there were “no guarantees at this point”. It is understood that Poundland’s owners, Gordon Brothers, have enabled the release of around £10 million of funding for things such as paying staff, taxes and suppliers of stock. The extension to Wednesday’s deadline could mean the prospect of a deal that would satisfy the company’s creditors remains on the table. Advisers have been in talks with parties interested in buying the brand or parts of the business such as swathes of shops. Recommended reading: It has held talks with potential bidders including Tesco over proposals to buy up to 150 stores, and other chains such as Iceland and Lidl. Investment firm Xyra Holdings emerged as a potential buyer for the whole business, while Irish firm Martin Property Group is believed to remain interested. Gordon Brothers previously rejected a takeover offer from Martin Property Group but management named the firm as the preferred bidder last month. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: HMRC Child Benefit rates to rise in April 2027 - new payment amounts explained
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: HMRC has revealed that millions of families could receive more money in Child Benefit from next April, with new weekly payment rates now appearing on the Government's website. Parents currently receive £27.05 a week for their eldest or only child, with an additional £17.90 paid for each other child. However, these payments are set to increase again for the 2027/28 tax year, according to an update to the Government's Child Benefit information page on November 10. The provisional figures show that the weekly rate for an eldest or only child will rise to £28, while payments for each additional child are expected to increase to £18.55. This would give families an extra £49.40 a year for their eldest or only child, and an additional £33.80 annually for every other child they claim for. The figures are currently marked as 'provisional', meaning they are not yet confirmed as final rates. However, the Government website's update history shows that previous provisional Child Benefit rates have subsequently matched the final amounts announced. The weekly rate of Guardian's Allowance is also expected to increase, rising from £22.95 in 2026/27 to £23.75 in 2027/28. Guardian's Allowance is an additional payment for people bringing up a child whose parents have died. In some circumstances, it can also be claimed where one parent has died and the surviving parent cannot look after the child. Child Benefit is available to parents or guardians responsible for a child under 16, or under 20 if they remain in approved education or training. Only one person can claim Child Benefit for each child, but there is now no limit on the number of children families can receive payments for. This follows the abolition of the two-child limit in April this year. Previously, the restriction meant parents could generally only claim Child Benefit for a maximum of two children. However, some families may face a tax charge if their earnings exceed the High Income Child Benefit Charge threshold. The charge applies if either parent has an individual income of more than £60,000 in tax years from 2024/25 onwards. For tax years up to and including 2023/24, the threshold was £50,000. Child Benefit is usually paid directly into a claimant's bank account every four weeks. Claiming also provides valuable National Insurance credits, which can help protect a parent's entitlement to the State Pension.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: More than one million yellow box fines issued - what are the rules and how to appeal
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than a million yellow box junction penalties have been issued by councils in England and Wales since 2023, research suggests. Used car retailer cinch said 37 councils reported issuing 1,047,472 penalty charge notices between 2023 and 2026, with nearly £58 million in penalty payments also reported. The company sent Freedom of Information requests to 217 authorities across the UK, but the penalty figures reported are not a total for every council or for the whole country. The underlying council responses were not supplied with the release and could not be independently checked. Its figures include 347,614 notices in 2025 and a further 231,458 in 2026 up to July. In Hackney, the number rose from 314 in 2024 to 8,567 in 2025, while Buckinghamshire recorded an increase from 3,618 to 16,120. Liverpool recorded 7,622 notices in 2025, compared with 3,376 the year before, according to the research. At Dennis Road Roundabout in Surrey, the number rose from 1,557 in 2024 to 9,101 in 2025. Cinch said councils had received more than 100,000 challenges since 2023 and accepted over 18,000. Those included 6,954 accepted challenges in Redbridge out of 27,615 received, and 3,582 out of 8,328 in Cardiff. Ben Welham, a motoring expert at cinch, said: "Yellow box junctions help to keep traffic moving, but they can be difficult to navigate, particularly in busy towns and cities where traffic is constantly stopping and starting." Yellow box junctions have criss-cross markings designed to keep traffic from blocking the road. Under rule 174 of the Highway Code, drivers must not enter until their exit road or lane is clear. There is an exception for drivers turning right who are held up only by oncoming traffic or other vehicles waiting to turn right. At a signalled roundabout, drivers must not enter a box unless they can cross it completely without stopping. The Northern Ireland Highway Code sets out the same box-junction rules. Penalty amounts and payment periods depend on the issuing authority, so motorists should check the details on their notice. For example, Newcastle City Council says its yellow box penalty is £70, reduced to £35 if paid within 21 days. In England and Wales, a motorist who believes a council PCN is wrong can make a formal challenge, known as a representation, to the authority that issued it. Cinch says drivers generally have 28 days to challenge a notice and should provide supporting evidence, such as photographs or available camera footage. Check the notice for the applicable deadline and instructions, including how to view any footage. If the authority rejects the formal challenge, GOV.UK says there are 28 days after receiving the rejection notice to appeal to an independent tribunal. The appeal is made to London Tribunals for a PCN issued in London, or the Traffic Penalty Tribunal for one issued elsewhere in England or Wales. Scotland and Northern Ireland have different appeal arrangements, so drivers there should follow the instructions from the issuing body. If an appeal is successful, the PCN is cancelled and the motorist does not have to pay.

The plan details the authority’s strategy for replacing cladding which does not meet fire safety standards on residential buildings of five stories or more. Cllr Sarah Conboy, chair of the committee, said: “This comes from a very difficult place, many of us will remember the heart-wrenching experience that happened at Grenfell. “The horrendous loss of life, but also the impact it had on a whole community as well as everybody involved in responding to that incident.” It was earlier revealed that there are ten high-rise flat buildings of seven stories or more in Cambridgeshire – all in Cambridge – which still need cladding replaced. “This was along with 62 medium-rise flats, of five or six stories, across the county according to the latest report presented to the committee. “It added that a few buildings have come in and out of scope 'during detailed assessment'. The combined authority has previously said they are “confident” in meeting the government’s targets that cladding on high-rises be replaced by the end of 2029 and end of 2031 for medium-rises – deadlines introduced in 2025. The updated plan, replacing the LRAP approved in 2025, addresses “key risks” including “landlord reluctance, contractor capacity and developer disputes”. The report presented to the committee added that “contractor capacity and quality of workmanship is a particular risk given this is a nationwide task”. Sean Hedger, the remediation manager, said that replacing cladding is a “lengthy process” which can take up to two years. He said he was concerned about the term “unsafe buildings” as it could worry residents, reassuring them that they are still safe to live in. He said: “Just because a building requires remediation of the external wall system it does not mean that the building is unsafe to live in. Responsible persons would often put in interim measures such as an upgraded fire alarm system to enable simultaneous evacuation instead of a stay put policy.” He said that in areas of the country where residents have had to move from their flats, this is “generally” due to “a mixture of fire safety and structural issues as well”. Cllr Ros Hathorn said this was “such important work” and they are the growth committee so their remit includes housing and development. She said: “Actually this is one of the most important things we need to do because Grenfell caused massive damage, but also damaged people’s confidence in living in flats. “And actually we need to rebuild that reassurance and until we do that it is going to be very challenging to respond to the housing crisis so this is such an important piece of work.” The committee recommended the plan be approved when it goes to the CPCA board for a final decision later this month.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Funding threat could render world-leading Cambridgeshire telescope defunct
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A world-leading radio telescope could be shut down if its funding is withdrawn. The Cambridge Telescope, at the Mullard Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Cambridgeshire, is one of seven e-MERLIN radio telescopes that work as a single powerful instrument. Its future is uncertain after the Science and Technology Facilities Council and UK Research and Innovation proposed ending all operational funding for e-MERLIN after March 2028. Cllr Bridget Smith, leader of South Cambridgeshire District Council, has written to the Secretary of State urging a review of the decision and warning of its potential impact on UK science. Read more Cyclist seriously injured in van hit and run as police appeal for witnesses Four roads near Ely set to close for marking and surfacing works Tributes pour in remembering beloved Littleport pub landlord Young boy taken to hospital after crash involving bike and car In a November 10 letter, she said ending funding without a replacement plan posed an "existential threat" to e-MERLIN and could leave the Cambridge Telescope "defunct." Cllr Smith said: "This is a world-leading scientific facility, right here on our doorstep, and we are facing the very real prospect of losing it. "Once we lose facilities like this, we can't simply bring them back. "Decades of expertise and scientific achievement could be lost for good. "It's extraordinary that the Government is talking about making Cambridge the engine of Britain's economic growth while allowing the funding to disappear from the very scientific infrastructure that makes this area so special. "The Government needs to put its money where its mouth is. "If Ministers are serious about backing Cambridge and British science, they need to step in and save this telescope." The telescope, owned and operated by the University of Manchester, works alongside six others across England. The network’s 200km spread gives it a 200km baseline and resolution comparable to the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes. It has helped produce more than 1,000 peer-reviewed papers and supports thousands of researchers worldwide. The funding row comes as the Government promotes Greater Cambridge and the Oxford-Cambridge Growth Corridor as engines of economic growth. In her letter, Cllr Smith argued that e-MERLIN supports the wider research and innovation economy by attracting investment and creating highly skilled jobs in science and engineering. She warned that losing the facility could undermine the future success of the growth corridor. South Cambridgeshire MP Pippa Heylings also voiced concerns. Ms Heylings said: "Cambridge is known across the world for its ground-breaking science, and this telescope is part of what makes that possible. "You cannot build a world-leading science economy by dismantling the world-leading science facilities we already have. "Yet that is exactly what these cuts risk doing. "This isn't just about one telescope. "It's about the future of British science, the skilled jobs and expertise we depend on, and whether the Government is genuinely committed to the growth it keeps promising. "We need a proper long-term funding solution, not a decision that could throw away decades of scientific achievement." Cllr Smith has called on the Government to work with UKRI and STFC to find a sustainable long-term funding solution before the existing arrangements expire in March 2028. She also wants any final decision delayed until its scientific, economic and strategic effects are fully assessed. The letter was also sent to Liberal Democrat MPs Pippa Heylings, Ian Sollom and Charlotte Cane, and to the party’s science, innovation and technology spokesperson Victoria Collins. The observatory has also been the subject of concerns over East West Rail, with the University of Cambridge warning that electromagnetic interference and vibration could jeopardise research.

A decision looms on a plan for up to 600 new homes in St Neots, despite a flood of objections from residents. The outline application by Bloor Homes for land at Priory Hill, north of St Neots, is set to be considered by Huntingdonshire District Council's (HDC) development management committee on November 16. The 87-hectare site would create a new neighbourhood between Priory Hill Road, Huntingdon Road, the River Great Ouse, and the East Coast Main Line. An illustrative sketch of the land in St Neots where 600 new homes could be built (Image: Bloor Homes) The scheme seeks permission for up to 600 homes, with 40 per cent designated as affordable housing. Alongside the housing, the plans include a community hub, mobility hub, public open space, allotments, walking and cycling routes, landscaping, and associated infrastructure. Around 64 hectares of the site would be retained as green space, including meadows, parkland, wildlife areas, and sustainable drainage features. Developers say the plans would extend Priory Park northwards, creating a new 'Priory Piece', new pedestrian and cycle links, and providing opportunities for a future footbridge across the River Great Ouse connecting to Paxton Pits Nature Reserve and the Ouse Valley Way. The site sits close to Priory Park (Image: Newsquest) For access to the site, the plans would see two new T-junctions introduced on Priory Hill Road. Road speeds would be reduced to 30mph along Priory Hill Road and Huntingdon Road, with additional traffic-calming measures. In addition, the double-mini roundabout at the B1043 Huntingdon Road, Priory Hill Road and Mill Lane intersection would be changed to a staggered T-junction, as the developers claim it had previously been identified as "a safety concern". The double-mini roundabout at Priory Hill Road (Image: Newsquest) The double-mini roundabout near the site could be changed to a staggered T-junction (Image: Newsquest) Members of the development management committee are expected to make a decision on the application at a meeting at 7pm on November 16. Planning officers are recommending that the scheme be approved subject to conditions, or refused if an S106 agreement has not been reached. St Neots Town Council and Little Paxton Parish Council have both lodged objections to the scheme. The town council said it is concerned that "the development would place additional pressure on local services and infrastructure, particularly secondary school provision" and raised additional concerns over loss of agricultural land, flood risk and drainage. Additionally, HDC has received a total of 92 objections from residents. One neighbour wrote: "It would cause demonstrable harm to infrastructure, landscape, biodiversity, and the wellbeing of existing residents. "I therefore respectfully urge Huntingdonshire District Council to refuse planning permission for this development." What do you think about the plans? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Just under half of children in Huntingdon miss out on NHS dentist visits
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Just under half of young children in Huntingdon are missing out on NHS dental care, which is below the national average. Practice Radar figures show 53 per cent of children in Huntingdon saw an NHS dentist in the year to March 2026. That compares with 58 per cent across England when measured on the same basis. The gap is even wider among younger children, with just 41.3 per cent of those aged between one and five in Huntingdon seeing an NHS dentist during the year. The figures come amid ongoing national concerns about access to NHS dentistry, especially for younger children. Practice Radar analysed NHS Business Services Authority data to estimate child dental attendance in all 543 English constituencies. The analysis found large regional differences, with the proportion of children seen by an NHS dentist ranging from 32.2 per cent in the City of London and Westminster to 74.5 per cent in Sheffield Hallam. In 62 constituencies, fewer than half of children saw an NHS dentist during the year. Read more Decision looms on 600-home plan for St Neots amid flood of objections Hunts man accused of distributing indecent images of children named Thief who stole orangutan statue from garden centre pictured New plan to replace ‘potentially unsafe cladding’ agreed The rare wildlife species that can be found in Cambridgeshire Huntingdon’s 53 per cent rate is five points below the England average, but the area is not among the worst performers. The study also examined tooth decay among five-year-olds, but those figures are reported by council area rather than constituency. In Huntingdonshire, 11.4 per cent of five-year-olds had experienced tooth decay in the 2023/24 survey, compared with 22.4 per cent nationally. Huntingdon is therefore not among the 60 constituencies with below-average NHS dental attendance and significantly higher childhood tooth decay. Practice Radar warned that the two figures cover different geographic areas. The 53 per cent attendance rate covers children living in Huntingdon, while the 11.4 per cent decay rate covers the wider Huntingdonshire council area. The research also examined NHS dental contracts in the area. The analysis included seven NHS general dental contracts in Huntingdon, with a median payment of £34.51 per unit of dental activity (UDA). A UDA is the NHS measure for dental work, with different treatments given different values. Across England, the median constituency had an NHS dentist visit rate of 58.6 per cent for children and 47.5 per cent for one- to five-year-olds. Fewer than 40 per cent of one- to five-year-olds saw an NHS dentist in 111 constituencies. There are signs of improvement across England, with 508 out of 543 constituencies recording a higher proportion of children seen by an NHS dentist compared to two years earlier. However, the researchers emphasised that the figures only cover NHS dental care. Children treated entirely privately are excluded, so the figures do not show how many receive dental care overall. Children are counted by where they live, not where their dentist is based, so some Huntingdon residents may receive care outside the constituency. The analysis used NHS Dental Statistics for England 2025/26, tooth-decay data from the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities and population estimates from the Office for National Statistics. A recent Cambridgeshire MP survey found nearly half of respondents were not registered with an NHS dentist, while about half had paid privately after struggling to access NHS treatment. Local NHS dentists have told an MP that contracts are financially and operationally "unviable", with practices losing money on NHS work and subsidising it through private income.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: David Walliams content removed from iPlayer after sexual misconduct allegations
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The BBC is removing content featuring David Walliams from iPlayer. It follows an investigation into sexual misconduct allegations against the comedian and writer. Multiple women have accused David Walliams of sexually inappropriate behaviour and grooming, including when they were teenagers, according to an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News. Walliams denies all allegations against him. A BBC spokesperson said: "These are serious allegations. "As such, the BBC is looking carefully at all material featuring and written by David Walliams on our platforms. "We are in the process of removing some programmes, including Little Britain, whilst this review is underway." Other affected shows include The Wheel and Would I Lie To You. ITV announced this afternoon that it is set to air a new documentary tonight about the allegations. David Walliams: Power and Silence will air tonight at 10.50pm on ITV1. The hour-long special is available to stream now on YouTube or ITVX. It comes following a three-year joint investigation by ITV News and The Guardian. The investigation alleges Walliams preyed on teenage girls and young women for sexual purposes. David Walliams was today (November 10) named as the celebrity who tried to block publication of his identity amid allegations of “inappropriate sexual activities” with girls and young women. Multiple women accuse Walliams of “grooming” them as teenagers, while another described her alleged encounter with Walliams as “sexual assault”. Walliams is also accused of inappropriate conduct and sexual harassment at his former publisher HarperCollins, and while working on Britain’s Got Talent. Responding to the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams denied all allegations against him. He said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with... I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. “And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did... “I am not a sexual predator... I have not broken the law... I am devastated that some of the women I met ten to twenty years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.” Walliams, 55, brought legal action against Independent Television News (ITN) and Guardian News and Media (GNM), publisher of The Guardian, ahead of the two organisations reporting allegations against him, including of sexual misconduct and potential criminal activity. Lawyers for the media organisations previously told the High Court in London the allegations involved Walliams’ alleged “abuse of power and status” to contact young women and try to engage in “inappropriate and exploitative sexual activities”. Walliams denied the claims and unsuccessfully sought an injunction to prevent these publications because of the risk he would take his own life, after two previous suicide attempts. The author was granted anonymity during the proceedings, which was lifted after his injunction bid was dismissed and GNM and ITN published their investigations on Tuesday. During a two-day trial in October, the court was told by the media organisations’ lawyers that the allegations were gathered after “a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation” and that there was a “strong” public interest in publishing them. Gavin Millar KC said that reporters from the media organisations had spoken to more than 100 people, including more than 30 sources with first-hand accounts as well as Walliams’ friends and colleagues. Walliams’ lawyers said that he had initially attempted suicide after receiving letters from ITN and GNM asking for his reply to the allegations, because of “long-term trauma and the fear of trial by media”. Sara Mansoori KC, representing Walliams, told the court that any publication relating to him about these allegations “would have a potentially fatal impact”. The barrister said: “The only reason they would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life.” Judge Mr Justice Nicklin refused the bid for an injunction, ruling it would be an “exceptionally serious interference” with freedom of expression. In the 52-page judgment, he also said that granting the injunction would not treat the man’s psychiatric condition or eliminate his elevated risk. He continued that hospitals and health staff caring for Walliams, who was detained under the Mental Health Act in October, meant that the state had “assumed responsibility” for his immediate safety and “can provide significant protection”, which “materially reduces the likelihood of suicide”. The former Britain’s Got Talent judge, known for appearing in comedy shows including Come Fly With Me and Little Britain alongside Matt Lucas, has sold more than 60 million copies of his children’s books globally. They include The Boy In The Dress, Fing, and Gangsta Granny, the latter of which was turned into a one-hour BBC special in 2013, followed by a sequel starring Sheridan Smith in 2022. Walliams’ book publisher HarperCollins dropped him in December 2025, after an investigation into allegations he had “harassed” young women, which Walliams strongly denied. Earlier this month, theme park Alton Towers permanently closed its World Of David Walliams attraction, which featured rides inspired by the books. Walliams left Britain’s Got Talent in 2022 after he apologised for making “disrespectful comments” about auditioning contestants during filming breaks in January 2020 at the London Palladium. In 2023, Britain’s Got Talent producer Fremantle apologised and reached an “amicable resolution” with Walliams after the remarks he made while on the show were leaked.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Workers over 21 given £910 cash boost confirms Andy Burnham
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of workers are in line for a pay rise next April, with Andy Burnham's Government confirming a 3.9% increase to the National Living Wage. The increase means people aged 21 and over who work full-time on the minimum rate will see their gross annual earnings rise by £910 from April 1, 2027, according to HM Treasury. The National Living Wage will increase from £12.71 to £13.21 an hour, with around 2.3 million workers across the UK expected to benefit from the changes. Younger workers will also receive a boost, with the National Minimum Wage for those aged 18 to 20 rising by the same percentage. Their hourly rate will increase from £10.85 to £11.27, also from April 1. The 3.9% increase is higher than the latest Consumer Prices Index (CPI) inflation figure, which stood at 3.5% in the 12 months to September 2026. Confirming the changes, HM Treasury said: "To support low-paid workers across the UK, the government is raising the National Living Wage and National Minimum Wages, which is expected to benefit around 2.3 million workers. "On 1 April 2027, the National Living Wage will increase by 3.9% to £13.21 per hour, equivalent to an increase of £910 in the gross annual earnings of a full-time worker on the National Living Wage. The National Minimum Wage for 18- to 20-year-olds will also increase by 3.9% to £11.27 per hour. "By accepting the Low Pay Commission's recommendations in full this year, the government is ensuring workers are rewarded fairly for their work, while protecting jobs, backing businesses, and strengthening the conditions for economic growth." The £910 annual increase applies to someone aged 21 or over working full-time on the National Living Wage. It is a rise in gross earnings, meaning the figure is before Income Tax and National Insurance deductions. The new hourly rate of £13.21 will apply from April 1, 2027. Workers aged 18 to 20 will see their minimum hourly pay increase by 42p, from £10.85 to £11.27. The latest increase also marks a change in the pace of pay rises for younger workers. Since Labour returned to power in 2024, the National Minimum Wage for 18 to 20-year-olds has increased by 26%. The 2027 rise brings their increase into line with the percentage increase for workers aged 21 and over, rather than giving younger workers a larger proportional uplift. The 3.9% increase is above the latest CPI inflation rate of 3.5%, recorded by the Office for National Statistics in the year to September 2026. Recommended reading: The Low Pay Commission (LPC), which advises the Government on minimum wage rates, had previously said the National Living Wage would need to rise by around 3.7% in 2027 to reach £13.18 an hour, keeping pace with its expectations for average pay growth. However, in March, it changed the LPC's remit to give it more scope to consider labour market conditions when setting the minimum wage for 18 to 20-year-olds. The new rates will take effect on April 1, 2027.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Woman with MS delivers 16,000-signature petition calling for fairer PIP assessments
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A woman living with multiple sclerosis (MS) in Huntingdon has delivered a petition signed by over 16,000 people to the UK Government. The petition calls on the government to make Personal Independence Payment (PIP) fairer for people with MS. It was delivered on November 3 by 56-year-old Sharon Docherty, who has secondary progressive MS. She was joined by Janis Winehouse, Amy Winehouse’s mother and also living with MS, and Neil Duncan Jordan MP. Sharon said: "During my assessment, it appeared the assessor had not read any of the medical evidence I'd submitted. "It also felt like the questions they asked did not allow me to explain the full nuances of living with a condition like MS." MP Neil Duncan-Jordan PIP hand in (Image: Sharon Docherty) The petition was organised by the MS Society to coincide with the government’s review into PIP, the Timms Review, which will be published later this month. Sharon worked closely with the charity to develop the campaign. More than 150,000 people in the UK live with MS, including an estimated 1,900 in Cambridgeshire. The neurological condition affects the brain and spinal cord and can cause a wide range of physical and cognitive symptoms that often fluctuate or remain invisible to others. PIP is designed to help disabled people cover the extra costs of living independently, but the assessment process has been widely criticised as "rigid" and not reflective of variable conditions like MS. Sharon said: "At times, the system can feel as though it is designed to discourage people from applying rather than support those who need help." She said receiving PIP has allowed her to engage in activities recommended by her therapist, but she's due to be reassessed in five years' time despite having a progressive condition. The MS Society is calling for a more flexible, person-centred approach to PIP, including lifetime awards for people with long-term, progressive conditions and an end to unnecessary reassessments.

PC Chris Ogden was named Police Officer of the Year. Police Officer of the Year Chris Ogden (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) He disrupted an organised drug network through intelligence-gathering and a determined investigation. The north and south spree offender teams won Team of the Year for managing repeat offenders and reducing harm through proactive partnership work. Unsung Hero Amanda Large (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) Amanda Large was named Unsung Hero after more than 30 years supporting colleagues, volunteers and young people across the force. Grand Prix Employee of the Year Chris Ogden (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) PC Ogden also won the Grand Prix Employee of the Year award, chosen by the chief constable from the winners. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Martin Lewis issues 'awful' energy bill warning as price cap set to jump by £276
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Martin Lewis has warned households struggling with energy bills that costs are likely to get worse before they get better, as millions of people face the 'awful' prospect of a sharp rise in January. On his X account, the Money Saving Expert founder said: "The latest predictions for the January Price Cap - AWFUL, up 28.8%! This is our internal MSE document where we average three forecasts and how its changed over the past few weeks as wholesale rates have continued to rocket." It comes as energy analysts predict the Ofgem price cap could jump by 16 per cent at the start of 2027, adding hundreds of pounds to the annual bill of a typical household. Experts at Cornwall Insight forecast that the cap will rise by £276, taking it from £1,723 to £1,999 a year for a typical dual-fuel household from January 2027. The prospect of another increase will be particularly worrying for families heading into one of the coldest and most expensive periods of the year, when heating demand typically rises and daylight hours are shorter. There are also fears the increase could be even bigger if the conflict involving the US, Iran and Israel continues to disrupt energy markets and push up wholesale gas prices. The latest predictions for the January Price Cap - AWFUL, up 28.8%! This is our internal MSE document where we average three forecasts and how its changed over the past few weeks as wholesale rates have continued to rocket. PS Jan prediction is getting much more locked in as we're 85% through the 19 August to 17 November 2026 assessment period. April & July predictions are much more crystal ballgazing. — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) November 3, 2026 There has been some positive news for households, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham announcing a series of measures intended to ease pressure on energy bills. These include removing VAT from domestic energy bills, which is expected to save the average household around £45 to £50, and a £100 winter energy payment for around 20 million households living in Council Tax bands A to D. The Government has also confirmed plans to scrap gas standing charges, which are fixed daily fees households pay regardless of how much gas they use. Best to keep the heating on low all day? Does foil behind radiators work? Is now the time to fix? Got questions on energy bills, energy efficiency, solar panels & more, that's next week's @ITVMlshow. I'll be joined by specialist heat engineers so pls post questions by reply. — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) November 6, 2026 However, Martin Lewis warned that consumers could have to wait until late 2027 or even January 2028 before the change takes effect. Chancellor John Healey said the Government would ask Ofgem to deliver the removal of the charges in 2027, or as soon as possible afterwards. Speaking about the timetable, Mr Lewis said: "The gas standing charge, on the price cap anyway, is to be scrapped in 2027. What does 2027 mean? Well, as it's part of the price cap, it definitely won't be before the 1st of October." The typical gas standing charge is currently around £108 a year for households paying by direct debit or prepayment meter. Under the planned changes, this fixed cost will be moved into the unit rate – the amount customers pay for each kilowatt-hour of gas they use. That means the reform will not automatically cut everyone's bill. Instead, households that use less gas should benefit, while those who use more could pay more. Mr Lewis said: "This isn't about saving money in totality. This is about a structural change and I've always argued that – for fairness – so that those low users who struggle at the moment to cut their bills because so much of it is about the standing charge, and I get so many messages about this, that won't happen anymore." He estimated that the change could add roughly 0.8p to 0.9p per kilowatt-hour to the gas unit rate, although he stressed this was only a rough calculation and the final figure would depend on energy prices at the time. He added: "What does it mean? Lower users will pay less, higher users will pay more. And actually, because there are quite a lot a low number of very high users and it's done on the mean average, it actually works out 60 per cent of people will pay less, 40 per cent of people will pay more." The Government estimates that around 60 per cent of account-holding households could save an average of £45 a year as a result of the change. In a statement, the Government said: "Tens of millions of households will no longer pay standing charges on their gas bills as the Government gives families more control over what they pay and some more breathing space. "A standing charge is a fixed daily fee added on top of a household gas bill, regardless of how much gas has been used. A household could use no gas at all but still must pay the standing charge. "The Chancellor will announce an end to this unfair and outdated practice. He will ask Ofgem to deliver removal of these charges – which are £108 a year for the typical household on average – in 2027 or as soon as possible after. "Instead, these fixed costs will be paid on the unit rate, which could save 60% of account-holding households around an average of £45 off their annual bill." The Ofgem price cap currently stands at £1,723 a year for a typical dual-fuel household paying by direct debit. This is a 3.6 per cent increase on the previous three-month period. The price cap sets the maximum rates suppliers can charge customers on standard variable tariffs for each unit of gas and electricity, as well as the daily standing charges. It is not a limit on the total amount a household can pay, meaning bills will be higher for those who use more energy. Cornwall Insight expects the cap to rise by 16 per cent in January 2027, reaching £1,999 a year – an increase of £276. The consultancy said: "The price cap is expected to rise by 16% compared to October, reaching £1,999 a year for a typical dual-fuel household in January 2027, an increase of £276 and the largest rise since January 2023." It said the increase was largely being driven by escalating conflict in the Middle East, which continues to disrupt gas supplies in the UK and around the world. The consultancy added that EU gas storage stocks had fallen to their lowest September levels in 15 years, adding to pressure on the market. It also warned that some of the price increases had already been reflected in the calculation for January's cap. Cornwall Insight said: "Ofgem sets the wholesale part of the cap using prices from a fixed period known as the observation window. With that window for the January cap now nearly halfway through, the price rises seen in September are already locked in, making a January increase all but certain."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: School praised for ‘courteous’ pupils and strong attendance by Ofsted inspectors
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire primary school has been praised for its community spirit and pupils’ behaviour after a recent Ofsted inspection. Brington CofE Primary School, in Church Lane, Brington, received the report after inspectors visited on September 29 and 30. Ofsted rated attendance and behaviour as “strong”. Achievement, curriculum, teaching, early years, inclusion, leadership, governance, personal development and wellbeing met the “expected” standard. Kirsty Baish, headteacher, said: "I feel incredibly privileged to lead a school that means so much to me. "I want every child who walks through our doors to be happy, feel safe, be challenged academically and have the confidence to fulfil their potential. "I am incredibly proud of how far we have come, but we are not a school that stands still. "We have high aspirations for our children." The report described pupils as “courteous” and “respectful”. Older children looked after younger pupils and helped everyone feel included. Inspectors said pupils approached learning enthusiastically, helping create a “calm, inclusive and purposeful environment”. Read more Reform councillor complains to Parliament over MP’s response to 199-home plan IN PHOTOS: Hundreds gather in Huntingdon for Remembrance Sunday parade and service Plans go in for up to nine more homes on agricultural land on village outskirts Driver arrested after woman dies in five-vehicle crash near Peterborough Motorist helps police stop swerving lorry on A1 Pupils made good academic progress across a wide range of subjects and developed the knowledge and skills needed for their next stage of education. Ofsted singled out reading as a strength and said it was at the heart of the curriculum. The school’s approach to phonics and early reading was said to help pupils develop both confidence and fluency. The school says its motto, “Build each other up to be the best you can be”, sums up its aim of helping children support one another, believe in themselves and aim high. Children in the early years made a strong start, while pupils with special educational needs and disabilities were included across school life and given tailored support. Ofsted also praised the wider opportunities available to pupils, including sport, music, and leadership activities. Swimming was singled out as a particular strength, with the school’s on-site pool helping children develop water confidence and swimming skills. However, inspectors identified areas for improvement. Some lessons offered effective challenge and adaptations, but this was not consistent across subjects and year groups. Ofsted recommended that leaders improve the consistency of curriculum delivery to ensure all pupils, especially those needing adaptations or capable of greater challenge, could build securely on previous learning. The report also called for stronger leadership to ensure improvement work is properly assessed and changes are consistently embedded. Debra Beachus-Wells, chair of governors, said: "Brington isn't just a school; it's a whole community, one that is inclusive and welcoming to all pupils and parents. "Since Mrs Baish took on the headship in May 2025, she has achieved such positive improvements across the school. "The progress made is clear for everyone to see and is reflected in the recent Ofsted report. "The Governing Board is fully committed to continuing to work closely with Mrs Baish, the staff, pupils and parents to build on this success. "Together, we want to keep moving the school forward, making further improvements and ensuring Brington continues to be the fantastic school and community that we all know it can be. "We are proud of what has been achieved so far and excited about what we can accomplish together in the future." The report said overall absence was 3.9 per cent in 2025/26, compared with 5.1 per cent nationally. Persistent absence was 8.4 per cent, compared with 14.4 per cent nationally. Mrs Baish said: "This is a celebration of our whole school community – our wonderful children, dedicated staff, supportive governors and families. "We are proud of Brington, proud of our journey and excited about our future."
