summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: How Virgin Media 02 customers can keep free emails as service ends
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Virgin Media is closing its free email service, leaving account holders to decide whether to transfer or move elsewhere. Users who want to keep their existing address can switch to Junara, an email provider owned by Atmail. The change affects addresses ending in virginmedia.com, virgin.net, ntlworld.com and blueyonder.co.uk. Virgin Media says it is contacting affected account holders in phases and they will have at least 45 days from the first communication to decide what to do. They can sign up with Junara, download their emails and data before moving to another provider, or close their account. Junara says users whose accounts are suspended after their deadline have another 120 days to sign up and reactivate them. After that period, the account and its data will be permanently deleted and cannot be recovered, the provider says. Virgin Media stopped offering email accounts to new customers in May 2022. Current Virgin Media broadband, landline or TV customers who move to Junara will be offered their first 12 months free, subject to a 99p transfer fee. Customers who have told Virgin Media they need additional support will be offered their first 18 months free. Former Virgin Media customers who no longer have those services will need to sign up to a standard Junara plan to keep their email service. Those who do not want to transfer can download their data and move to another provider, including a free service. Virgin Media says its messages about the change will not include clickable sign-up links, and customers should be cautious of unexpected requests for personal details, passwords or payment information. A Virgin Media spokesperson said: "As we focus and prioritise our investments and resource on ensuring our customers have the best connectivity experience, we've taken the decision to close the remaining Virgin Media email accounts. "We are transferring our email service to Junara, a specialist cloud-based email provider owned by Atmail, giving users a clear route to keep their existing Virgin Media email address if they choose to. "We're writing directly to all impacted customers to clearly explain the changes and will provide a 45-day window to either sign up with Junara, move to an alternative email provider, or close their account. "To support users through this transition, all current Virgin Media customers wishing to move to Junara will receive their first year of service free of charge, with additional support available for those who need it."

The Food Standards Agency (FSA) has warned that the products could pose a health risk to anyone with an allergy to soya. The alert applies to England, Scotland and Wales. The affected products are Waitrose & Partners Sweet, Fluffy, Golden Ring Doughnuts 5's and Waitrose & Partners Jammy, Messy, Squidgy Doughnuts 5's. Tuesday 10 November - Waitrose & Partners recalls various Waitrose & Partners Doughnuts 5’s because of undeclared soya #FoodAllergy https://t.co/daUpmhxwL3 https://t.co/eFbF2SVY8L — Food Standards Agency (@foodgov) November 10, 2026 Both are sold in packs of five, with best-before dates of November 10 and November 11 included in the recall. The FSA advises anyone who has bought the affected doughnuts and has an allergy to soya not to eat them. Instead, they should return the products to the store where they were bought for a full refund. A receipt is not required. Waitrose has contacted allergy support organisations, which will tell their members about the recall, according to the FSA. For more information, please contact: Waitrose Customer Care 0800 188 884, option 4." If there is a problem with a food product that means it should not be sold, then it might be 'withdrawn' (taken off the shelves) or 'recalled' (when customers are asked to return the product). The FSA issues Product Withdrawal Information Notices and Product Recall Information Notices to let consumers and local authorities know about problems associated with food. In some cases, a 'Food Alert for Action' is issued. This provides local authorities with details of specific actions to be taken on behalf of consumers.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP starts bank checks on benefit claimants – what officials can now see
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has confirmed it has issued its first notice requiring banks to check accounts linked to benefit payments, marking the start of a major new crackdown on fraud and incorrect claims. The new powers mean banks and other financial institutions must check certain accounts against information supplied by the DWP to help establish whether people are still entitled to the benefits they receive. The measure could affect people claiming Universal Credit, Pension Credit and New Style Employment and Support Allowance (ESA), with the Government estimating it will save taxpayers £1.2billion over five years. Work and Pensions Minister Lilian Greenwood confirmed the first eligibility verification notice had been issued in a written statement to Parliament on October 26, explaining: "I am informing the House that the Department for Work and Pensions has issued the first eligibility verification notice under powers introduced by the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Act 2025, which amends the Social Security Administration Act 1992." The checks are designed to identify potential problems with benefit entitlement, particularly where someone may have more savings than the rules allow or has spent too long abroad. However, the DWP has stressed that the new powers do not give officials unrestricted access to people's bank accounts. Banks cannot hand over full statements or details of everyday spending, and a flag does not automatically mean someone has committed fraud or will lose their benefits - the full details are clarified here . The Eligibility Verification Measure (EVM) applies to three benefits: Under the system, the DWP sends banks and other financial institutions information known as 'eligibility indicators'. These are based on benefit rules relating to a claimant's capital, such as savings, and the amount of time they have spent abroad. Financial institutions then check the information they hold on accounts receiving specified DWP benefit payments. If an account meets one of the indicators, the bank must share limited information with the department. The checks can also cover linked accounts and joint accounts. The account does not necessarily have to belong to the person claiming the benefit – it could belong to someone else if it is linked to the account receiving the payment. The new powers do not give the DWP direct access to people's online banking or allow officials to monitor accounts in real time. Banks and financial institutions can share limited information if an eligibility indicator is met. This can include: However, banks cannot share full bank statements, details of individual transactions, how someone spends their money or the specific locations where transactions took place. They are also banned from sharing sensitive personal information about a person's background, such as political opinions or religious beliefs. Financial institutions could face fines if they disclose information they are not permitted to share. Today we discussed a new Bill to crack down on fraud. It's fair enough to go after those ripping off public money, but one section of the Bill has become a vehicle for bank spying powers, mandated by the DWP targetting benefit claimants. These new eligibility verification powers allow suspicionless surveillance - not a good precedent - and needs to be challenged, however much taxpayers money we're told mass financial monitoring will recoup. — Claire Fox (@Fox_Claire) May 15, 2025 A bank flag does not automatically mean someone has committed benefit fraud or will lose their payments. The information is intended to act as a prompt for the DWP to carry out further checks, rather than proof that someone has done something wrong. In her statement to Parliament, Ms Greenwood said: "The information received will act only as a prompt for further checks." She added: "Information received through EVM will not, in isolation, imply that a person is guilty of any wrongdoing or that their benefit entitlement will change." If information supplied by a bank suggests someone might be receiving an incorrect benefit payment, the DWP will review their claim. It could find that they are no longer eligible or that the amount they receive is wrong. The department may then contact the claimant to ask questions or request further information to establish whether they are still entitled to the benefit. The minister said: "DWP will have regard to all information relevant to a benefit decision, including information that was not obtained through EVM. Decisions will continue to be made by trained departmental staff through established processes." This means any decision about benefit entitlement or payments will be made by DWP staff, rather than automatically following information received from a bank. The department says it will contact people through their Universal Credit online journal if they have one. Those without an online account may be contacted by phone, letter or text message. Claimants are advised to respond as soon as possible to avoid their payments being delayed or stopped. Anyone who disagrees with a decision can ask the DWP to look at it again through a process known as a mandatory reconsideration. The new guidance also reminds claimants that they must keep the DWP informed if their circumstances change. This is particularly important for people whose benefit entitlement is affected by savings, income or time spent abroad. Changes that should be reported include: The DWP warns that failing to report a change promptly could mean someone receives too much benefit and has to repay the money. People who provide incorrect or incomplete information, or fail to report a change, could also face prosecution or a fine. If a claimant is unsure whether a change affects their payments, they should check the eligibility rules for the benefit they receive or contact the relevant DWP office. In her October 26 statement, Ms Greenwood told MPs that the department had issued its first eligibility verification notice under powers introduced by the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Act 2025. She said: "This marks an important step in the Department’s use of data to assist with identifying and preventing fraud and error, correcting inaccurate benefit payments sooner and helping prevent avoidable debt." Recommended reading: The minister said the measure was expected to save taxpayers £1.2billion over the next five years. She added that it would help ensure people received the support they were entitled to while protecting public money and addressing suspected fraud. The department will initially introduce the system through a controlled test-and-learn phase, allowing it to assess how it works before expanding its use. The Government says safeguards have been built into the legislation and a statutory code of practice, which sets out how the powers can be used and how personal information must be protected. Ms Greenwood told Parliament: "The measure contains a number of clear and vital safeguards."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Drug dealer jailed after police find £24,000 heroin and crack cocaine stash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A drug dealer has been jailed after police stopped him in Cambridgeshire and later found a stash of £24,000 worth of heroin and crack cocaine. Robert St Paul, 27, was intercepted alongside Brooklyn Coburn, 27, after police stopped a grey Subaru on Cromwell Road, Cambridge, on December 10. The force had received intelligence linking the vehicle to drug dealing. Officers searched Coburn, the driver, and found crack cocaine and heroin concealed in his underwear. St Paul, who was a passenger in the vehicle, was found with a mobile phone, while two more phones and cash were discovered in the car. Police then searched both men’s homes as part of the drug investigation. Police found cash at Coburn’s Woking address and heroin and crack cocaine worth £24,000 at St Paul’s flat in Hall Road, Newham. Police found a stash of heroin and crack cocaine worth £24,000 (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) At Cambridge Crown Court on November 9, Coburn, of Beckenham, London, was given a two-year prison sentence suspended for two years. He must also complete 180 hours of unpaid work. St Paul, of no fixed address, was jailed for 40 months on May 5 after pleading guilty to the same offences. Police intercepted St Paul in Cambridge (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Detective Constable Ben Bowen, who investigated, said: "Cambridgeshire is not a soft target for drug dealers. "If you travel into our county to sell drugs, we will use intelligence to identify you, stop you and put you before the courts. "Drug dealing causes misery in our communities and often goes hand-in-hand with violence, exploitation and other crime. "We will continue to target those responsible and disrupt the supply of Class A drugs."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The rare wildlife species that can be found in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire’s fens, wetlands and waterways are home to some very unusual species of wildlife. If you're an avid birdwatcher, an aspiring lepidopterist or simply an animal lover, you'll want to keep a look out for these amazing creatures. So without further ado, here are some of the rare wildlife species that can be found in Cambridgeshire. Otters have made a remarkable comeback in Cambridgeshire after once being driven close to extinction by pollution and habitat loss. They are now regularly spotted along the River Great Ouse, the River Cam and waterways such as Fen Drayton Lakes. Footage from Cambridge City Council shows an otter caught on camera at Logan's Meadow Local Nature Reserve. The UK's biggest and rarest newt is widespread across lowland England, particularly in wetlands. It has spotted flanks, a striking, orange belly, warty skin and is almost black in colour. The great crested newt is common in wetland environments (Image: Peter Hagger) The UK's tallest bird, standing at an impressive four feet, is instantly recognisable but disappeared from Britain for centuries. When a trio of migrating birds were blown off course in 1979, ending up in Norfolk, reintroduction projects began and there are now around 160 in Britain. If you're lucky, you can spot them in the Cambridgeshire Fens. Cambridgeshire’s wetland habitats are important for the bittern, a secretive heron whose distinctive booming call can be heard during spring and summer. Once extinct in the UK as a breeding species, its numbers have recovered through habitat restoration projects. According to the RSPB, the species is now thriving at the Ouse Fen nature reserve. A bittern in open flight (Image: Nigel Sprowell) According to the Essex Wildlife Trust, the East of England is the only place in Britain where water vole populations are increasing. However, they are under serious threat from habitat loss by the American mink. It can be distinguished from the brown rat by its furry tail and rounded nose.

A Reform UK councillor has complained to Parliament about MP Sam Carling over a 199-home development between Ramsey and Bury. Cllr Karan Maheshwari, who represents Ramsey on Huntingdonshire District Council, has submitted a complaint to the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards. It concerns North West Cambridgeshire MP Mr Carling’s response to Cllr Maheshwari’s request for him to intervene in planning application 25/01382/OUT, for 199 homes between Ramsey and Bury. A copy seen by this publication is dated November 2 and marked “DRAFT – NOT SUBMITTED”, but Cllr Maheshwari later confirmed he submitted it on November 3 and received confirmation on November 4. The dispute began after Huntingdonshire District Council’s development management committee said it was minded to reject the scheme. Cllr Maheshwari says he asked Mr Carling to urge the Secretary of State not to “call in” the application. A planning application being called in means the Government takes responsibility for deciding it instead of leaving the final decision with the local authority. Mr Carling replied in social media posts included with the complaint: “Karan, this is misinformation. MPs have no power over planning.” Mr Carling also said intervention with the Secretary of State could trigger a judicial review and give the council another route to overturn its refusal. Cllr Maheshwari disputes the suggestion that his request amounted to misinformation. He argues that, although an MP cannot decide a planning application, an MP can make representations about a planning case. The row continued the next day when Cllr Maheshwari posted a further criticism of Mr Carling and urged him to stand up for residents. The councillor accepts in his complaint that the post contained “direct political criticism”, including a call for Mr Carling to stand down if he would not represent residents’ concerns. Mr Carling replied that there was “absolutely no need for full-on personal nastiness” and said voters wanted politicians to work together. He added: “I am not going to engage. Particularly when most of what you're doing is AI-generated anyway.” The AI reference forms another part of Cllr Maheshwari’s complaint. The Reform councillor argues that using AI to research or draft material should not by itself discredit someone’s arguments. He stresses that he is not accusing Mr Carling of unlawful discrimination and accepts that the comments do not prove a wider policy of refusing to engage with AI users. Instead, Cllr Maheshwari asks whether residents’ or elected representatives’ concerns could be dismissed because they used AI to prepare their arguments. The complaint asks the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards to consider whether the exchanges breached Rule 11 of the House of Commons Code of Conduct. Rule 11 covers conduct serious enough to damage the reputation and integrity of the House of Commons or MPs generally. Cllr Maheshwari accepts that the rule sets a high bar and that an ordinary political disagreement would not normally be enough. The complaint acknowledges that the Commissioner may decide the matter is not serious enough to investigate. If that happens, Cllr Maheshwari has asked the Commissioner to consider whether the concerns should instead be raised with Mr Carling under a separate parliamentary procedure, without a formal investigation. He says the complaint is not intended to stop robust political debate or force Mr Carling to support a particular planning position. Instead, it asks for scrutiny of how elected representatives handle public concerns. The document includes screenshots of the exchanges and copies of Cllr Maheshwari’s posts as evidence. A Facebook post at the centre of the dispute has since been removed, but Cllr Maheshwari says he does not know who deleted it or why and makes no allegation about its removal. Mr Carling has been approached for comment. The application was submitted by David Wilson Homes South Midlands.

Walliams denies all allegations against him. A joint investigation by ITV News and the Guardian alleges Walliams preyed on teenage girls and young women for sexual purposes. Multiple women accuse Walliams of “grooming” them as teenagers, while another described her alleged encounter with Walliams as “sexual assault”. Walliams is also accused of inappropriate conduct and sexual harassment at his former publisher HarperCollins, and while working on Britain’s Got Talent. Responding to the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams denied all allegations against him. He said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with... I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. “And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did... “I am not a sexual predator... I have not broken the law... I am devastated that some of the women I met ten to twenty years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.” Walliams, 55, brought legal action against Independent Television News (ITN) and Guardian News and Media (GNM), publisher of The Guardian, ahead of the two organisations reporting allegations against him, including of sexual misconduct and potential criminal activity. Lawyers for the media organisations previously told the High Court in London the allegations involved Walliams’ alleged “abuse of power and status” to contact young women and try to engage in “inappropriate and exploitative sexual activities”. Walliams denied the claims and unsuccessfully sought an injunction to prevent these publications because of the risk he would take his own life, after two previous suicide attempts. The author was granted anonymity during the proceedings, which was lifted after his injunction bid was dismissed and GNM and ITN published their investigations on Tuesday. During a two-day trial in October, the court was told by the media organisations’ lawyers that the allegations were gathered after “a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation” and that there was a “strong” public interest in publishing them. Sara Mansoori KC, representing Walliams, told the court that any publication relating to him about these allegations “would have a potentially fatal impact”. The barrister said: “The only reason they would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life.” Judge Mr Justice Nicklin refused the bid for an injunction, ruling it would be an “exceptionally serious interference” with freedom of expression. In the 52-page judgment he also said that granting the injunction would not treat the man’s psychiatric condition or eliminate his elevated risk. He continued that hospitals and health staff caring for Walliams, who was detained under the Mental Health Act in October, meant that the state had “assumed responsibility” for his immediate safety and “can provide significant protection”, which “materially reduces the likelihood of suicide”. The former Britain’s Got Talent judge, known for appearing in comedy shows including Come Fly With Me and Little Britain alongside Matt Lucas, has sold more than 60 million copies of his children’s books globally. They include The Boy In The Dress, Fing, and Gangsta Granny, the latter of which was turned into a one-hour BBC special in 2013, followed by a sequel starring Sheridan Smith in 2022. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 5 film and television locations you can visit in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Famous film and TV locations are closer than you might think. Cambridgeshire has quietly become a star of the screen, with its historic streets, rural villages, and grand buildings providing the backdrop to some of cinema and television’s most memorable moments. From Netflix’s The Crown to ITV’s Grantchester, the county has featured in a growing list of productions, attracting fans keen to follow in their favourite characters’ footsteps. Here are some of Cambridgeshire’s best-known filming locations. Wansford Station and the Nene Valley Railway near Peterborough has been used for not one, but two James Bond films. (Image: Nene Valley Railway) Ely Cathedral is one of Cambridgeshire’s most spectacular filming locations. The cathedral stood in for Westminster Abbey in Netflix’s The Crown, including during wedding and coronation scenes. More recently, Bradley Cooper filmed one of Maestro’s most memorable scenes inside the cathedral. Cooper played legendary American composer and conductor Leonard Bernstein, and directed and co-wrote the film. For one of the film's major scenes, Cooper recreated Bernstein's celebrated 1973 performance of Gustav Mahler's Resurrection Symphony at Ely Cathedral. The sequence was filmed inside the cathedral with a live orchestra, choir and extras, and much of it unfolds in a single six-minute take. Visitors to Ely can walk through the cathedral used for one of the Oscar-nominated film’s major musical sequences. The Green Man n Grantchester is used by ITV for its detective drama Granchester starring Robson Green. (Image: Google Street View) Few places in Cambridgeshire are as closely linked to a television programme as Grantchester is to Grantchester. The picturesque village provides the setting for ITV’s detective drama of the same name, which uses several real locations. Fans can explore the village’s buildings and landscapes, which regularly appear on screen alongside Robson Green, Tessa Peake-Jones, Kacey Ainsworth and Al Weaver. One particularly recognisable location is the Church of St Andrew and St Mary, which has appeared in Grantchester as the village church and churchyard. Grantchester Meadows is another location visitors can enjoy for free. The meadows beside the River Cam feature in Grantchester and offer fans a taste of the countryside behind the programme. The meadows are also worth visiting in their own right, especially for fans who want to combine screen tourism with a riverside walk. Fans can stop for a drink at The Green Man pub, frequented by Geordie and his colleagues in the show. It lets visitors step inside a genuine screen location instead of viewing it from the road. Wisbech offers a very different look, with the Fenland town’s historic streets appearing in films and television productions. Peckover House in Wisbech has been used for films including Dean Spanley starring Peter O'Toole. (Image: Image: National Trust Images Jemma Finch) The town is known for its Georgian architecture, particularly North Brink, which overlooks the River Nene and has an impressive row of period properties. The National Trust’s Peckover House, a Georgian merchant’s home dating from 1722, also stands on North Brink. Productions filmed in Wisbech include the 1994 television adaptation of Martin Chuzzlewit, David Copperfield from 1999 to 2000 and the 2008 film Dean Spanley. The 2022 independent film Wild Bones was also filmed in Wisbech. Peter O’Toole filmed Dean Spanley in Wisbech in 2007 alongside Sam Neill, Bryan Brown and Jeremy Northam, with Peckover House and Wisbech Castle among the locations used. Visitors can explore much of the town’s Georgian heritage on foot, especially around North Brink, South Brink and the River Nene. James Bond fans have good reason to visit Peterborough: the area provided locations for two 007 films. The Nene Valley Railway featured in 1983’s Octopussy, starring Roger Moore as James Bond. Wansford Station became the fictional Karl Marx Stadt station, while filming also took place around Orton Mere and Ferry Meadows. The Bond franchise returned to Peterborough for 1995’s GoldenEye, Pierce Brosnan’s first 007 film. The Nene Valley Railway hosted action scenes involving the film’s imposing Russian armoured train. The former British Sugar factory at Woodston also featured in GoldenEye. Part of the site became a Russian rail depot, and Peterborough provided the backdrop for the tank chase’s finale. The former industrial site has been redeveloped, but the Nene Valley Railway remains open, so Bond fans can still visit a location featured in two 007 films. Just outside Cambridgeshire’s modern boundary, Burghley House is one of the wider region’s most impressive filming locations. Burghley House, just over the border near Stamford was used for the 2005 series of Pride and Prejudice among other films and TV series. (Image: Burghley House) Read more 5 Christmas markets and fairs to visit in Cambridgeshire this winter 'A sad loss': Hunts residents react to beloved department store closing 1,700 Cambridgeshire households urged to claim unclaimed Healthy Start support Tom Littler appointed to lead Arts Theatre Cambridge ahead of 90th anniversary Nearly 4,000 Huntingdonshire households could continue paying no council tax The Elizabethan mansion is best known for appearing as Rosings Park, Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s imposing home, in the 2005 adaptation of Pride & Prejudice. The house and grounds are open to visitors during the visitor season, giving film fans a chance to see the grand setting for themselves. From Bradley Cooper conducting inside Ely Cathedral to James Bond racing through Peterborough, Cambridgeshire has made a striking mark on the big and small screens. And with many of the locations open to the public, film and television fans do not have to settle for watching them from the sofa.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A rare 50p coin has fetched more than 400 times its face value after an online auction. The 2009 Kew Gardens piece drew 19 bids on eBay on November 4. A winning bid of £221.36 landed the coin, with an extra £9.55 buyer protection fee included. Released by the Royal Mint in 2009, the Kew Gardens 50p had a circulating mintage of 210,000. It marks the 250th anniversary of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew. Its reverse shows the Great Pagoda encircled by a climbing vine, while the obverse carries a portrait of Queen Elizabeth II. The Royal Mint ranks the 2009 Kew Gardens coin as the second-rarest 50p to enter circulation by mintage, behind the 2023 Atlantic Salmon. It says demand for the 50p denomination was low in 2009, accounting for the unusually small number struck that year. The 50p piece has a seven-sided shape and provides space for commemorative designs. The Kew Gardens 50p measures 27.30mm across. A coin's mintage, design and condition can all influence its value, according to the Royal Mint. An unusually low mintage may mean a coin sells for more than face value on the secondary market. Condition can also matter, with coins closer to mint condition potentially worth more. The Royal Mint advises collectors to research secondary-market listings and consult a coin expert if in doubt. The price paid for this graded Kew Gardens coin does not guarantee the same return for another example. Royal Mint figures list these 50p coins among the rarest to enter circulation, ranked by mintage: The 2023 Atlantic Salmon coin has the lowest mintage of any 50p issued for circulation, according to the Royal Mint. Collectors can check the Royal Mint's published mintage figures to find out how many examples of a circulating design were issued.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Thousands of Vauxhall owners warned 'stop driving' over safety issue
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Thousands of Vauxhall drivers have been told to stop driving over an airbag safety risk. Stellantis UK, Vauxhall's parent company, issued the stop-drive instruction for certain vehicles fitted with Takata airbags, which were already part of a recall. Vauxhall says the airbag inflator can degrade over time in high heat and humidity and may explode with excessive force in a crash, causing serious injury or death. Law firm Bond Turner estimates the recall affects 320,000 vehicles and is investigating potential claims over motorists' losses. The firm's estimate is not a confirmed count of vehicles currently subject to the stop-drive instruction. Vauxhall says drivers who receive a stop-drive warning should stop using the vehicle as soon as it is safe to do so. Its recall page lists the following models under the stop-drive action: Astra Hatch (2005 to 2015), Astra Van (2006 to 2013), Astra Twin Top (2006 to 2015), Vectra (2005 to 2008) and Signum (2005 to 2008). Not every vehicle in those model ranges is necessarily affected, and owners should check their vehicle identification number (VIN) to see whether their car is included and what action is advised. Vauxhall says the only exception to the stop-drive instruction is a direct journey, without stops, to a pre-booked recall repair appointment, provided the vehicle can be driven there lawfully. Other models are subject to the recall but not the stop-drive instruction, and their owners should still take action as soon as possible. These are the Astra J and Astra GTC (2010 to 2018), Meriva B (2010 to 2017), Mokka and Mokka X (2013 to 2018), Cascada (2013 to 2018) and Zafira C (2012 to 2016). Drivers can use Vauxhall's vehicle recall checker to check their VIN and register for a free repair. The 17-character VIN can be found on a V5C registration certificate or in the vehicle. Owners who cannot register online can call Vauxhall's recall helpline on 0800 917 9285. Vauxhall says registered keepers of affected vehicles will be sent a letter and should make sure their contact details are up to date with the DVLA. Bond Turner is looking into whether motorists may be able to recover expenses linked to the recall, including alternative transport, replacement vehicle hire and loss of earnings. Malcolm Lewis, head of group litigation at Bond Turner, said: "For many people, their car is essential to everyday life, whether that is getting to work, taking children to school or fulfilling family and personal commitments." Mr Lewis said: "Our investigations will look at who may be legally responsible for the losses experienced by affected motorists, including the cost of alternative transport and replacement vehicle hire, loss of earnings and other associated expenses." Vauxhall says it has made mobility solutions available for customers affected by the stop-drive action and asks them to discuss any specific needs with their retailer when booking.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP confirms State Pension age change - people with these birthdays face longer wait
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: People approaching State Pension age are being warned they could have to wait several months longer before receiving their first payment as the Government continues its phased increase from 66 to 67. The change is being introduced gradually over two years, with the State Pension age rising by one month at a time for people reaching 66 during the transition. The next stage begins on November 6 and affects people born between November 6 and December 5, 1960. Rather than receiving their State Pension when they turn 66, this group will have to wait until they are 66 years and eight months old before becoming eligible. For someone born on November 6, 1960, that means they will reach State Pension age on July 6, 2027. The delay increases by another month for each subsequent group of birthdays. Those born between December 6, 1960 and January 5, 1961 will have to wait until they are 66 years and nine months old, while the next group will reach State Pension age at 66 years and 10 months. The phased increase will eventually mean people born from March 6, 1961 onwards have to wait until their 67th birthday to claim their State Pension. The State Pension age is currently 66 for men and women, but is rising to 67 between 2026 and 2028. The increase began on April 6, 2026, and affects people born between April 6, 1960 and April 5, 1961. The exact age at which someone can claim depends on their date of birth, with the delay increasing by one month for each successive group. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) timetable is: The latest increase comes amid calls for the State Pension age to be reduced to 65 for everyone. A public petition calling for the change has attracted thousands of signatures, with campaigners arguing that people in their mid-to-late 60s can face poor health, caring responsibilities and limited options to remain in work. Tim Grimsditch, Managing Director of Unbiased, said: “A public petition calling for the State Pension age to be reduced to 65 for everyone has gathered more than 80,000 signatures and is approaching the 100,000 needed for Parliament to consider debating it. Its argument is that many people aged 65 to 67 face poor health, caring pressures, and limited options to keep working - and the evidence that healthy life expectancy varies considerably by income and occupation gives that weight. “The Government has consistently rejected calls to lower the State Pension age, and the Third State Pension Age Review is currently underway to determine what the age should be in future decades. There’s a difficult balance here: the State Pension is one of the largest items of public spending, and allowing people to claim it earlier would mean paying it to more people for longer. Both sides of this are serious arguments. “Either way, the timing matters for planning. The State Pension age is currently rising from 66 to 67, a change that began in April 2026 and completes in March 2028, affecting people born between March 1961 and August 1977. Legislation already exists to take it to 68 after that. “The practical issue for most people isn’t the State Pension age itself - it’s the gap before it. "Private pensions can generally be accessed from 55, rising to 57 in April 2028, while the State Pension now arrives at 67. Someone who stops working at 63 through ill health or caring responsibilities is funding four years entirely from their own provision. That’s the question the petition is really about, and it’s worth planning for regardless of what happens to it." Recommended reading: The increase from 66 to 67 was brought forward under the Pensions Act 2014. The legislation changed the timetable so that the State Pension age for men and women would rise to 67 between 2026 and 2028, rather than over the longer period previously planned. The DWP said: “The Pensions Act 2014 brought the increase in the State Pension age from 66 to 67 forward by eight years. The State Pension age for men and women will now increase to 67 between 2026 and 2028. “The Government also changed the way in which the increase in State Pension age is phased so that rather than reaching State Pension age on a specific date, people born between 6 April 1960 and 5 March 1961 will reach their State Pension age at 66 years and the specified number of months. “For people born after 5 April 1969 but before 6 April 1977, under the Pensions Act 2007, State Pension age was already 67.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Walkers crisps and Rubicon drink recalled from UK supermarket shelves
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A drink and a snack box feature in this week's round-up of product recalls. AG Barr is recalling Rubicon Yuzu & Pink Grapefruit cartons, while PepsiCo is recalling its Walkers Variety Snacks Sharing Box. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) has published allergy alerts for both products, including details of which batches are affected and what customers should do. The FSA says the 1L cartons may contain sulphites not mentioned on the label, posing a possible health risk to people sensitive to sulphur dioxide or sulphites. Four batches are affected: Anyone with a sensitivity to sulphur dioxide or sulphites who has bought an affected carton should not consume it, the FSA advises. They can return it to the shop where it was bought for a full refund, or contact consumercare@agbarr.co.uk for further information. The FSA says notices explaining the recall will be displayed in retail stores selling the product. PepsiCo is recalling the 655g box of six packs because wheat is not declared on the outer packaging, according to the FSA. The problem concerns an 85g pack of Monster Munch Giants Roast Beef inside the box, which contains wheat and gluten. The affected batch code is 107543, with best-before dates of 21 November 2026 or 16 January 2027. The FSA says the product poses a possible health risk to people with an allergy or intolerance to wheat or gluten, or with coeliac disease. Those customers are advised not to eat the affected product and can contact the PepsiCo Consumer Care Line on 0800274777 or visit contact.pepsico.com/walkers for a full refund. The alert applies to England, Scotland and Wales. The FSA explains that a food may be withdrawn from sale when there is a problem that means it should not be sold. A recall is when customers are asked to return the product, rather than it simply being taken off shelves. Food can be withdrawn or recalled because allergy information is missing or incorrect, or because there is another food allergy risk. When there is a food allergy risk, the agency issues an allergy alert.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Russell Brand sentenced to more than 10 years for rape and sexual assaults
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Russell Brand has been sentenced to more than ten years, following convictions of rape and sexual assault. The 51-year-old former actor and comedian was found guilty at Southwark Crown Court of raping a woman in 2009 and sexually assaulting three others, all of whom were female TV and radio workers. The offences took place between 2004 and 2009, during the height of Brand’s fame. Today, November 9, at Southwark Court, Mr Justice Bennathan, sentenced Brand to 10 years and six months. Russell Brand with his wife Laura Gallacher (Image: Maja Smiejkowska/PA) On Monday, Mr Justice Bennathan slammed Brand’s “staggering arrogance” as he sentenced him to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and three counts of sexual assault. Sentencing judge Mr Justice Bennathan told rapist comedian Russell Brand he had become a “sexual predator” as he was starting to become famous. Beginning his sentencing remarks, he told the defendant: “About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous. “You were clever – and in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. “You had also become a sexual predator.” Mr Justice Bennathan told the court: “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and demand justice in the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Mr Brand, act without their consent.” The judge told Brand “imprisonment will deprive your children of the presence of their father, that sad loss to them however is caused by your serious offending.” The judge said factors in mitigation for Brand included his lack of previous convictions and that “17 years had passed” since his final offence, and how Brand had lived his life subsequently including helping those “wrestling with addictions”. Brand showed no emotion as he was jailed for 10 years and six months, but told his wife “we’ll be OK” as he was taken downstairs by the dock officers. The couple shared a brief conversation before the shamed comedian was taken downstairs. Ahead of the sentencing, victim statements were shared in the courtroom, with Brand's rape victim sharing: "When I eventually reported what had happened, it was not simply because of the media documentary. "By that stage I had become aware of the police investigation and felt that I was finally in a stronger position mentally to disclose my experience. "Reporting what happened was something I had hoped I would eventually be able to do, but it took a long time to reach that point." The sentencing follows a four-week trial that revealed how Brand used his celebrity status to exploit and abuse women. During the trial, Brand described his life as “promiscuous” and "full of idiocy," but claimed all sexual encounters were consensual and denied any criminal wrongdoing. Victims, however, painted a starkly different picture of a powerful man who kissed and groped women moments after meeting them, pursued sexual encounters aggressively, and later dismissed or ridiculed them for objecting to his behaviour. Brand was found guilty of raping a 21-year-old fan in 2009, whom he met after a stand-up show at the Hammersmith Apollo. Russell Brand leaves Southwark Crown Court, London, (Image: PA) The woman, who told jurors she was a huge Brand fan, told jurors she had consensually participated in a threesome with the comedian backstage that night, despite having a boyfriend. She later visited Brand’s Hampstead home for sex, but said the encounter turned violent when he forcibly raped her. Brand was also convicted of sexually assaulting a woman at a Nordic bar in Soho in 2004, groping her breasts just seconds after being introduced to her. Another victim described how Brand kissed and groped her during a 2005 visit to Capital Radio’s London studios, and said she looked to his entourage for help but no one intervened. Brand was also convicted of putting his head into the groin of a female Channel 4 worker, after she had been forced to give him a massage in 2009. The woman told the court how Brand had refused to continue a recording session unless she massaged him, and members of his entourage encouraged it instead of protecting her. During the trial, Brand’s 2007 memoir, My Booky Wook, was cited as evidence, including his claim that he would not stop pursuing sex until achieving his "birthright orgasm." Russell Brand and his wife Laura Gallacher outside Southwark Crown Court. (Image: PA) Brand was cleared of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault. Following his convictions, the Metropolitan Police confirmed Brand is under investigation for two additional rape allegations. Sir Mark Rowley, Metropolitan Police Commissioner, warned that more victims may come forward.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 1,700 Cambridgeshire households urged to claim unclaimed Healthy Start support
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Families in Cambridgeshire are being encouraged to apply for the NHS Healthy Start scheme through a new outreach campaign. Cambridgeshire County Council, in partnership with district and city councils, is targeting around 1,700 low-income households identified via its Low-Income Family Tracker (LIFT) platform. The campaign will run throughout November and aims to raise awareness of unclaimed financial support for healthy food and milk. Councillor Alison Whelan, chair of the Communities, Social Mobility and Inclusion Committee, said: "We know that many families across Cambridgeshire continue to face significant cost-of-living pressures, and Healthy Start can provide valuable support at a time when every pound counts. "Through this targeted campaign, we're helping families access money that they are entitled to, putting additional income into household budgets while supporting healthy eating and giving children the best possible start in life." Healthy Start is a national scheme offering pregnant women and families with young children weekly payments of £4.65 per child under the age of four, rising to £9.30 for infants under one. The funds are loaded onto a payment card and can be used in most supermarkets to buy items such as cow’s milk, fresh fruit, and vegetables. The campaign is part of the council’s wider anti-poverty programme, which includes income maximisation services, targeted outreach, and crisis payments. Just 62 per cent of eligible Cambridgeshire families currently claim Healthy Start, meaning more than £431,000 could be going unclaimed each year. Households that have been identified will be contacted by letter, email, phone call, or text message. Those who do not receive a notification are still encouraged to check their eligibility through the NHS Healthy Start website. Residents are reminded that if they are ever in doubt about the authenticity of a letter, email, text message or phone call, they can contact their district or city council directly for verification. Information on scam awareness is available on the Cambridgeshire County Council website.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: WATCH: Drunk e-scooter rider banned from driving after crash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A man has been banned from driving after riding a rental e-scooter while drunk. CCTV showed Neil McGovern, 43, staggering along Cambridge’s St Andrew’s Street shortly after midnight on June 21 before riding away on an e-scooter. About 10 minutes later, ambulance crews alerted police after finding a man unconscious with a serious head injury following an e-scooter crash. McGovern, of River Lane, Cambridge, was taken to Addenbrooke’s Hospital for treatment, where a blood sample revealed he had 204 milligrams of alcohol per 100 millilitres of blood—more than twice the legal limit of 80 milligrams. After recovering, he attended a voluntary police interview but gave no comment when shown CCTV footage of himself riding the e-scooter. He pleaded guilty to drink driving and was disqualified from driving for 20 months at Cambridge Magistrates’ Court on November 5. PC Jack Brown said: "Some people may not realise that e-scooters are classed as motor vehicles and the same drink driving laws apply as they do to cars." McGovern was also ordered to pay more than £1,000 in fines and costs. Private e-scooters remain banned on UK public roads and pavements, although authorised rental schemes operate in trial areas.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'A sad loss': Hunts residents react to beloved department store closing
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A beloved Huntingdonshire department store has announced it will be closing, sparking sadness among residents. Family-run department store Townrow, which opened in 1871, said it had not taken the “difficult” decision to close its St Ives store lightly. The independent chain sells clothing, shoes and kitchenware, with stores in Maldon and Frinton-on-Sea, Essex. Managing Director Edward Townrow said: "Like many independent retailers, we have faced increasingly challenging trading conditions, rising operating costs and changes in shopping habits. "Despite exploring a number of alternatives, we have regrettably been unable to establish a financially sustainable future for the store in its current form." Residents were asked to share their thoughts on the closure. Judith Brass said: "It's a sad loss for the town. "It's pretty much the only place worth shopping at for ladies. "We have such great eating places in St Ives nowadays, I was hoping the town was on the up so this is a blow." Ms Natalie Flack praised Townrow for stocking “concession brands like Vera Moda, Mango, Radley, Barbour” and said the staff are wonderful. She added: "I hope they get given another chance." Anne Dellar said: “Personally I am very sorry to see Townrow closing...this will be an enormous loss to St Ives. "More importantly my thoughts are with the staff of Townrow and sincerely hope that other local businesses who may be looking for staff can contact the Townrow staff for vacancies they may be looking to fill before looking further afield." Diane Langley said: "It's sad. The store had character unlike the national chains." However, other residents said they hoped popular chains such as M&S Food took over the premises. Miriam Rogers said: "Maybe we could have a Home Bargains in that space for St Ives." Alison Smith added: "B&M or Home Bargains would be good in its place." The store will hold a closing-down sale in the coming weeks.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Convicted sex offender jailed after creating secret social media account
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A convicted Cambridgeshire sex offender has been jailed for breaching a court order after creating a secret social media account. Harry Yeardsley, 20, admitted two breaches of a Sexual Harm Prevention Order (SHPO). The order was imposed earlier this year after Yeardsley pleaded guilty to sexual communication with a child. Specialist officers from the Management of Sexual Offenders and Violent Offenders (MOSOVO) unit visited Yeardsley’s home in Wheelers, Great Shelford, on November 5 as part of routine checks. During the visit, officers discovered that Yeardsley had created, used, and deleted an account on Kik, an anonymous messaging app, earlier that week, in direct violation of his SHPO. Yeardsley was arrested and later admitted two SHPO breaches. He was jailed for six months at Cambridge Magistrates’ Court on Friday, November 6. Detective Sergeant Andy Harding said: "Sexual harm prevention orders are there to manage risk and safeguard the public. "Breaching them is a serious offence, and we will take robust action against anyone who fails to comply. "I would encourage anyone with concerns about someone’s behaviour, particularly where children may be at risk, to report it to us."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Romesh Ranganathan tackles online outrage and family life in sharp Cambs comedy show
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridge welcomed Romesh Ranganathan as part of his sell-out 'Romesh Will Change Your Life' tour, with the evening proving to be anything but a conventional comedy show. A live DJ, a sell-out audience and a comedian with absolutely no intention of playing it safe, the TV star delivered an evening of sharp wit, awkward truths and wonderfully self-deprecating humour. Before the, a live DJ set was accompanied by various clips from Romesh's television appearances, including Rob & Romesh and his recent winning moment on Celebrity Traitors. It was an unconventional opening, but one that immediately established the atmosphere of the evening. From family life and relationships to racism, immigration and wider social issues, no subject was entirely off limits. Romesh moved effortlessly between everyday observations and contentious topics, delivering his trademark dry humour with a healthy dose of self-deprecation. Romesh Ranganathan on the Cambridge Corn Exchange stage (Image: Angela Smith) He also addressed the recent controversy surrounding his BBC TV advert "What has the BBC ever done for me", which attracted online criticism and abuse directed at both him and his wife. Rather than shy away from the subject, he used it as another opportunity to expose the absurdities of online outrage and the world of keyboard warriors. However, some of the evening's biggest laughs came when Romesh turned his attention closer to home. Joking about being fed up with seeing himself on television, he launched into imagined stand-up performances by his wife and son. His ability to impersonate his own family, while simultaneously making himself the butt of the joke, proved a particular highlight, generating some of the most raucous laughter of the night. He weaved jokes about his childhood trauma and his womanising dad into a therapy-themed narrative, which made it feel as though he was baring his soul on stage under the guise of comedy. It is this willingness to ridicule himself, alongside his sharp observations and unapologetic approach to difficult subjects, that makes Romesh such an engaging performer. 'Will Change Your Life' may be a bold promise, but if the measure is an evening of laughter, uncomfortable truths and refreshingly honest humour, Cambridge certainly got its money's worth.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Motorist helps police stop swerving lorry on A1

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A driver has been arrested after a woman died in a five-vehicle crash on a busy road near the Cambridgeshire border. The collision took place on the A605 between Warmington and Elton, near Peterborough, at around 1.30am on Sunday, November 8. The driver of a BMW 2 travelling towards Thrapston was involved in a crash with the driver of a BMW X6 heading in the opposite direction towards Peterborough. Two HGV drivers travelling towards Peterborough stopped at the scene to help, at which point a Kia Ceed collided with the stationary BMW 2. The driver of the BMW X6, a woman in her 40s, sadly died as a result of the injuries she sustained in the collision. The driver of the BMW 2, a man in his 20s, sustained serious injuries and has been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving. Both HGV drivers were injured in the collision involving the Kia Ceed and the BMW 2, with one sustaining serious injuries. A passenger in the Kia Ceed suffered minor injuries. The A605 was closed after the crash but has since reopened. Detectives from the Serious Collision Investigation Unit are appealing for witnesses or anyone with dashcam footage of the incident to come forward. Anyone with information is asked to email Northamptonshire Police, call the Drivewatch Hotline on 0800 174615, or contact the force on 101. Callers should quote incident number 26000690175 when providing any information.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: IN PHOTOS: Hundreds gather in Huntingdon for Remembrance Sunday parade and service
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Hundreds of residents, veterans, serving personnel, cadets and community organisations gathered in Huntingdon on Sunday November 8 to honour those who have lost their lives in military conflicts, whilst serving their country. The annual Remembrance Sunday Parade and Service, organised by Huntingdon Town Council in partnership with the Royal British Legion Huntingdon Branch and RAF Wyton, saw the RAF Wyton Area Voluntary Band lead the parade of RAF Wyton serving personnel, and local cadet groups from all three armed branches. The parade marched from Princes Street to Huntingdon’s Market Square for a moving Service of Remembrance at the Thinking Soldier War Memorial. Wreaths were laid by a wide range of representatives, including Dr Jaspal Singh DL on behalf of the Lord-Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire, Amanda Norton for the Royal British Legion’s Huntingdon Branch, and the Mayor of Huntingdon, Councillor Patrick Kadewere, together with senior representatives from local authorities, RAF Wyton and RAF Alconbury. Many community groups, charities, cadet organisations and local associations laid wreaths during the ceremony. Following the service, the parade reformed and marched through Huntingdon town centre, with the Mayor of Huntingdon and Deputy Lieutenant receiving the salute from participants as they passed along the High Street. The Mayor of Huntingdon, Councillor Patrick Kadewere, said: "It was wonderful to see so many people come together to pay their respects and reflect on the sacrifices made by generations of servicemen and women. "On behalf of Huntingdon Town Council, I would like to thank everyone who took part in the parade, attended the service, laid a wreath, volunteered, or simply stood in silence with us. "Your presence helps ensure that remembrance remains at the heart of our community." The mayor and Huntingdon Town Council has since thanked all those who contributed to the success of the commemorations. A spokesperson for the council said: "In particular, thanks are extended to Royal Air Force Wyton, The Royal British Legion (Huntingdon Branch), The Military Wives Choir of Wyton and Brampton, the RAF Wyton Area Voluntary Band, and Reverend Jan Smith, Chaplain working with Deaf and Deafblind people in Ely Diocese, ensuring the day was both meaningful and accessible for all those attending." Armistice Day service Huntingdon's commemorations continue with the annual Armistice Day Service at the War Memorial in Market Square on Wednesday November 11. The service will commence at 10:55am, ahead of the National Two-Minute Silence at 11:00am, and will include prayers, readings and wreath laying. All are welcome to attend as the community once again comes together in remembrance.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Here is some of Huntingdonshire's most unusual bridges and where to find them
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From a medieval bridge with its own chapel to a 55-arch causeway, Huntingdonshire is packed with unusual crossings. The district’s rivers, floodplains and Fenland waterways have shaped travel for centuries, leaving medieval crossings and Fen drainage bridges behind. Here are some of Huntingdonshire’s most striking bridges and where to find them. St Ives Bridge One of the county’s most extraordinary bridges spans the River Great Ouse at St Ives. The town’s first bridge was built of wood in 1107, before work began on a stone replacement in the early 15th century. The stone crossing was completed in 1425, and a chapel was added the following year. It is one of only three bridges in England with a chapel. The bridge also still bears the scars of the English Civil War. Parliamentary troops destroyed part of it to hinder Royalist forces, so a temporary drawbridge was installed. When the damaged section was rebuilt in 1716, it was given rounded arches instead of matching the pointed medieval ones, leaving a visible difference today. The chapel has also served as a toll house, inn and private home. The bridge is also a scheduled monument. Huntingdon Old Bridge Another remarkable medieval bridge links Huntingdon and Godmanchester across the River Great Ouse. Grade I-listed Huntingdon Bridge dates from around 1330 and has six pointed stone arches. Historic England says a band of trefoil decoration above two arches probably marks the bridge’s oldest surviving section. Its third arch was replaced by a drawbridge during the English Civil War. The bridge also has a slight kink. Historical accounts say builders started on both riverbanks, but the two sections failed to meet in a straight line. Historic England calls it a "fine and famous example of a medieval bridge". The Nuns' Bridge, Huntingdon The lesser-known Nuns’ Bridge stands on Brampton Road in Huntingdon. Grade II-listed Nuns’ Bridge dates from the 15th or 16th century, was repaired in the 17th and largely rebuilt in the 18th. The stone-and-brick bridge has five arches and brick parapet walls. Unlike many historic bridges, it has avoided modern traffic because the main road now bypasses it. It is both a Grade II-listed building and a scheduled monument. The New Bridges, St Ives Despite their name, St Ives’s New Bridges are more than 200 years old. The extraordinary brick causeway runs about 220 yards across the Great Ouse flood plain and opened in 1822 after being built by the Bury to Stratton Turnpike Trust. Its astonishing number of arches makes the causeway stand out. It has 55 arches, keeping the route across the flood meadows open when the surrounding land flooded. About 1.2 million bricks were reportedly used to build it. One brick carries its own piece of history. One brick bears the date 1822 and the signature of John Turner, who oversaw the work and apparently signed the wet clay before it was fired. The New Bridges are Grade II* listed. Bridge over the River Great Ouse, Godmanchester Godmanchester has another historic crossing a short distance from the famous medieval Huntingdon Bridge. The bridge over the River Great Ouse at The Avenue is separately Grade II listed. It makes a useful stop on a riverside walk, where visitors can see several generations of crossings around Huntingdon and Godmanchester. Forty Foot Bridge, Ramsey Forty Foot For a bridge in a very different landscape, head into the Fens around Ramsey Forty Foot. Forty Foot Bridge carries the road over the Forty Foot River, part of the Middle Level Navigations. The unusual name refers to the waterway, not the bridge’s length. The Forty Foot Drain, also known as Vermuyden’s Drain, is part of the historic network built to drain the Fens. The name traditionally refers to the width of the original drainage channel between the bank tops. The surrounding settlement also took its name from the waterway and bridge, making them defining features of the Huntingdonshire Fen landscape.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Nearly 4,000 Huntingdonshire households could continue paying no council tax
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Thousands of households could continue receiving full council tax support if a key scheme is renewed. Nearly 4,000 of the most financially vulnerable homes in Huntingdonshire currently receive up to 100 per cent support through the district council’s council tax scheme, which is now under review for 2027/28. The scheme cleared its first approval stage after the Overview and Scrutiny (Environment, Communities and Partnerships) Panel met on November 5. Councillor Nathan Hunt, executive councillor for resident services and corporate performance, said: "HDC's up-to 100% Council Tax Support Scheme is one of the most important things we do to keep people out of crisis and build a fairer Huntingdonshire. "It puts money back in the pockets of those who need it most, takes a fair and compassionate approach, and helps make processing the scheme much more efficient." Some 3,997 households currently receive the maximum support, accounting for 4.69 per cent of all households in the district. That is 56 more households than in August 2025 and 104 more than in August 2024. By August 2026, 5,035 households were receiving council tax support, about 5.92 per cent of households in the district. Read more Here is some of Huntingdonshire's most unusual bridges and where to find them Paralympic champion Lauren Steadman to open inclusive community gym in Hunts Cambridgeshire PC praised after cutting deliberate fires at landfill by 81 per cent Beloved African lion Ghana dies aged 16 after declining health at Cambs zoo Four EV charging bays approved at Hunts shopping centre despite parking concerns The scheme, which is means-tested, is designed to reduce council tax bills for working-age residents on low incomes. Central government sets support for pension-age claimants. For 2024/25, Huntingdonshire District Council raised the maximum support under the scheme from 80 per cent to 100 per cent for many claimants. The council also introduced income bands linked to Universal Credit allowances and scrapped the need for claimants to submit a separate application. The council says the change has helped more residents claim support they might otherwise have missed. Under the banded scheme, the highest category gets a full discount, while lower bands offer 75, 50 or 25 per cent support. Eligibility thresholds are updated each year to reflect changes to Universal Credit. The scheme also encourages people to work by ignoring up to £50 a week of their earnings in assessments. The assessment excludes some benefits, including disability payments, Carer's Allowance, child benefit, child maintenance and parts of Universal Credit. The council says the revised scheme has made administration more efficient. Between April and August 2026, 71.44 per cent of changes in circumstances were processed automatically, up from 69.84 per cent in 2025 and 62.52 per cent in 2024. The number of processed changes also rose by 5,400. The average processing time for changes rose slightly to 3.02 days, from 2.86 days in 2025, but remained below 3.42 days in 2024. New claims took an average of 20.79 days to process—up from 18.8 days the previous year but down from 22.7 days in 2024. The council says scheme changes meant 452 fewer council tax bills were issued despite more updates being processed. The council also reported further falls in non-payment reminders and summonses. The scheme reduces the council’s tax base because it is classed as a discount, not a benefit. All authorities that collect council tax in the district share the cost. Officers recommend keeping the scheme’s core principles for 2027/28, while raising income thresholds in line with Universal Credit. The proposals go to the council’s cabinet on November 17, with full council expected to make the final decision on December 16.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Here's some of the historic buildings are at risk in Huntingdonshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Six historic churches have been named on Historic England’s 2025 Heritage at Risk Register. Located across Huntingdonshire, the churches are among nearly 1,000 places of worship in England on the register. Historic England’s annual register highlights buildings and sites most at risk from neglect, decay and other threats. All six Huntingdonshire entries are churches, including Grade I-listed buildings in Huntingdon, Abbots Ripton and Bythorn and Keyston. Four of the six currently have no agreed plan in place to address their condition. Here is a closer look at each site on the register. PARISH CHURCH OF ST JOHN THE BAPTIST, BYTHORN AND KEYSTON The Grade I-listed church is in “poor” condition and has medium vulnerability. The building is in slow decline, and no solution has yet been agreed to address the issues. It faces an immediate risk of rapid deterioration or loss of fabric, with no agreed solution. CHURCH OF ALL SAINTS, OFFORD CLUNY The Grade II*-listed church on High Street faces the same threat. It is in poor condition, has high vulnerability and carries a priority rating of B, meaning it faces an immediate risk of rapid deterioration. A solution had been agreed but was not in place when the site was assessed. CHURCH OF ST MARY, HUNTINGDON The Grade I-listed Church of St Mary on Huntingdon High Street is one of the district’s most prominent buildings at risk. It is in poor condition, has high vulnerability and carries a priority rating of C, indicating slow decay. No solution had been agreed at the time of the assessment. CHURCH OF ST ANDREW, ABBOTS RIPTON The Grade I-listed church on the High Street is in poor condition and has medium vulnerability. Like St Mary’s, it has a priority rating of C, and no repair solution had been agreed. PARISH CHURCH OF ALL SAINTS, BROUGHTON The final entry is Broughton’s Grade II-listed Parish Church of All Saints on Causeway Road. It is in poor condition, has high vulnerability and faces an immediate risk of rapid deterioration or loss of historic fabric. No solution had been agreed when it was assessed. A place on the Heritage at Risk Register does not mean a building will be lost, but it signals that urgent action is needed. The register helps Historic England direct support and resources to the most vulnerable heritage sites. Sites can leave the register after repairs or once a sustainable plan is in place. The 2025 register includes 1,460 buildings and structures across England, along with 986 places of worship, 1,864 archaeological sites, 105 parks and gardens, three battlefields, four protected wreck sites, and 469 conservation areas. This year, 138 sites were added to the register and 129 removed after conservation work. The register underlines the need for investment, community support and long-term planning to protect the region’s heritage.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Tom Littler appointed to lead Arts Theatre Cambridge ahead of 90th anniversary
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A theatre director has been appointed to lead The Arts Theatre Cambridge as it prepares to mark its 90th anniversary. Tom Littler, currently artistic director and joint chief executive of the Orange Tree Theatre in Richmond, will take up the post of chief executive and artistic director in June 2027. He will succeed interim joint chief executives Victoria Beechey and Rachel Tackley. Ms Tackley will step down upon his arrival, while Ms Beechey will continue as executive director. Mr Littler said: "I am excited to lead The Arts Theatre Cambridge into its tenth decade. "The recent refurbishment of its beautiful main house, and the plans for a new 200-seat studio, make this a pivotal moment. "I have loved The Arts for many years, have directed there many times, and seeing shows there most weeks was one of the joys of my years as a Cambridge resident. "The Arts is a much-loved and storied theatre close to the hearts of audiences and theatre people alike, and it is also an institution of unique potential. "I am delighted that Victoria Beechey will remain as Executive Director and look forward to working together to steer The Arts into new waters as a presenting and producing theatre of international renown." Nigel Hugill, chair of the Arts Theatre, said: "In Tom Littler, we have found exactly that calibre of visionary leader able to advocate and demonstrate the value of humanities in a tech-driven environment. "His exceptional track record is one of creative innovation, deep communal engagement and performing house vitality." Mr Hugill also paid tribute to the theatre’s current interim leaders. He said: "Rachel Tackley and Victoria Beechey have together provided exceptional interim leadership in stewarding a remarkable two years of transformation and renewal at The Arts. "Rachel will step away next summer with our love and unending gratitude."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: BBC licence fee could change as Government makes major announcement on future plans
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A petition calling for the BBC licence fee not to be extended to subscribers of rival streaming services has received a Government response, amid growing questions over how the broadcaster will be funded in future. The petition, which has attracted 18,418 signatures, warns that households could face extra costs if ministers decide to extend the licence fee to people who subscribe to streaming platforms not owned or operated by the BBC. Campaigner Alec Burns, who created the petition, argues the move would be "wholly unacceptable", particularly during the cost-of-living crisis. The petition, which can still be signed, states: "Amid a cost-of-living crisis, we believe the Government should be finding ways to save the public money, not expanding their means of taxation." It also claims the BBC already has a "tarnished reputation" and warns that extending the charge could further damage public confidence in the broadcaster. The Government has now responded, confirming it is considering a range of options for the BBC's future funding but stressing that no final decisions have been taken. In its response, published on November 2, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport said ministers were considering feedback from a public consultation on the BBC Charter Review Green Paper. It said: "The Government is keeping an open mind on the future funding of the BBC and no decisions have been taken at this stage." The response added that ongoing policy development was looking at the potential impact of different funding arrangements on households, consumers, investment and the wider creative economy. Ministers said the BBC remained a "vital national institution" which informs, educates and entertains audiences across the UK. The Government also highlighted the broadcaster's contribution to the UK's creative industries, saying it supports jobs and growth across the nations and regions. It pointed to research from the Reuters Institute, which found that 59% of UK respondents trusted BBC News in 2026, making it one of the country's most trusted news brands. However, ministers acknowledged that viewing habits have changed significantly as more people turn to streaming services and other ways of watching television. The Government said: "The changing media market and audience viewing habits mean the Charter Review needs to consider whether the current funding model remains suitable for the future." It also revealed that the total number of TV licences in force has fallen by three million since 2017/18. The Government confirmed it is looking at several options to ensure the BBC has sustainable funding in the years ahead. These include making the broadcaster operate more efficiently, generating more commercial revenue and potentially reforming the licence fee itself. Ministers also acknowledged concerns about the cost of the charge for households already struggling with their finances. The response said: "We understand that ensuring the licence fee is affordable is important." It added that the Government wanted to keep costs as low as possible for households while ensuring the BBC had the resources it needed to continue providing its services. The response did not confirm whether people subscribing to non-BBC streaming platforms could eventually be required to pay the licence fee. Instead, ministers stressed that they were still considering consultation responses and engaging with stakeholders. A White Paper setting out the Government's plans for the BBC's future is expected before the end of 2026. Recommended reading: The Government also highlighted existing support for households struggling to pay the annual licence fee. Since February 2025, more households have been eligible for the Simple Payment Plan, allowing them to spread the cost through weekly, fortnightly or monthly instalments. Other support includes: Ministers said the Charter Review was also considering whether further concessions or alternative payment schedules could better reflect different household circumstances.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Shoppers at Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda, Lidl and more risking £100 parking fines
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Drivers could face a £100 charge for parking outside a supermarket's opening hours. Some supermarket car parks restrict when vehicles can be left there, even if the car park is empty. Select Car Leasing highlighted the issue. Graham Conway, managing director of Select Car Leasing, urged drivers to read signs before deciding whether to park. He said: “Check the signage as you enter the car park carefully before making a decision about whether to stay or not. “Not all store car parks punish after or before-hours parking, but many do, and it’s an issue that’s causing real confusion among motorists.” Mr Conway said the company had seen cases where people were charged after leaving a vehicle for a matter of minutes. Supermarket car parks can be managed by private operators, which issue Parking Charge Notices when they believe conditions have been broken. Some use automatic number plate recognition cameras, with notices sent by post. Other conditions can include limits on the length of a stay, parking within marked bays and restrictions on who can use disabled or parent and child spaces. A private Parking Charge Notice is different from a penalty charge notice issued by a council. In England and Wales, Citizens Advice says drivers should check whether the parking company belongs to an accredited trade association when considering an appeal. It advises that if a non-member puts a ticket on a vehicle, the driver should not contact the company unless it writes to them first. In Scotland, Citizens Advice says someone who wants to challenge a private ticket should first contact the operator, explain their reasons and ask for it to be withdrawn. It says they could also approach the landowner, such as the supermarket, and provide the operator with evidence including photographs of unclear signs. In Northern Ireland, the Consumer Council says a driver who believes a private notice was issued incorrectly may be able to appeal, using evidence such as photographs of damaged signs. It says registered keepers in Northern Ireland cannot automatically be held liable for private parking charges, unlike in England and Wales, and that the driver is liable. An independent appeal may be possible if an operator rejects a challenge, depending on the company and the relevant appeal service.
