BT's new home phone service is called Digital Voice and switching over is described as being "simple". Over 99% of home phones are compatible with the new service. Customers are set to be contacted about the changes at least four weeks before the digital switch to make sure they are ready. Customers that might need some extra support when changing their landline service can book a free in-home engineer visit. Huntingdonshire District Council planning officers recommended approval despite strong objections from Godmanchester Town Council. Application 26/01647/FUL revised an earlier scheme, cutting the proposed charging spaces from six to four. Plans to install four electric vehicle charging stations at a Godmanchester shopping centre have been approved despite concerns over parking and safety near a school. (Image: Google Maps / Street View) Six existing parking bays will be replaced by four EV charging spaces. Planning officers said the scheme would improve access to rapid EV charging and encourage greener transport. They concluded that it would provide sufficient parking and vehicle movement and would not cause significant harm to neighbours, highway safety or biodiversity. However, Godmanchester Town Council strongly recommended the plans be refused, arguing that dedicating four spaces to EV charging had not been adequately justified given demand for parking at the site. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Officers seize huge stash of illegal fireworks from Peterborough shop
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A large stash of illegal fireworks has been seized from a shop in Peterborough. Officers found unlicensed fireworks at a Lincoln Road shop on November 6 during a joint operation involving Peterborough City Council’s trading standards team, Cambridgeshire Constabulary and Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service. The inspection followed intelligence that fireworks were being sold there without a licence. Councillor Zameer Ali, cabinet member for communities and public safety, said: "In the lead up to Bonfire Night, the community in this area has been disturbed by several firework-related incidents, which have been widely reported on. "While we don't know if these are linked, I am relieved that this sizeable quantity of fireworks has been removed from this address, as it was clearly presenting a hazard to those who lived nearby. "There are obvious serious safety risks in buying, storing, and selling fireworks in an unlicensed premises. "Fireworks are explosives and those sold by unlicensed sellers may not meet safety standards. "They could be improperly stored, incorrectly labelled, damaged and unsafe to use, increasing the risk of injury, property damage and fire." During the visit, officers found more than 21kg of fireworks with net explosive content (NEC). NEC is the total mass of explosive substances, excluding packaging, outer casings, containers, or inert components. These fireworks were subsequently seized. Sam Tucker, Peterborough neighbourhoods inspector, said: "Our officers joined partners in visiting this premises as part of our ongoing efforts to tackle issues involving inappropriate use of fireworks in the city. "Additional patrols will take place in the area tonight and this weekend, and we would strongly urge anyone with any concerns to report this to us, so we can build an accurate picture of anti-social behaviour in the area and work to combat this." Anyone who believes fireworks are being sold illegally can contact the Citizens Advice Consumer Service on 0808 223 1133. If someone is in immediate danger always call 999.

The 34-year-old, who has represented Britain in both swimming and triathlon at the Paralympics, winning a hat-trick of medals, and has also seen success at the World and European championships, is excited about the new project, which she hopes will see elite Olympians training alongside regular gym-goers. The gym will open from 6am to 8pm Monday to Saturday and close on Sundays. The gym will be inclusive of all ages and abilities. (Image: Lauren Steadman) Members can sign up for gym memberships or use a pay-as-you-go option. Lauren is studying for her Level One boxing qualification and will be able to lead some junior and beginner classes. "I have never boxed before; that is Bradley's area of expertise, but I am enjoying learning. Boxing is a great way to exercise, and it teaches discipline and helps young people control their emotions and harness their energy," said Lauren. Lauren Steadman and her partner Bradley Chapman cannot wait for the gym to officially open on Monday. (Image: Lauren Steadman) The gym includes an outside wellness area complete with ice baths. (Image: Lauren Steadman) Lauren hopes the gym will see the community getting behind it as she intends to get involved with local projects with The Engine Room. (Image: Lauren Steadman) She said: "It is great that we are able to open such a facility in a village like Sawtry, and we hope the community will get behind us; we are really excited for Monday's opening." Bradley was previously selected as captain of the Royal Navy boxing team, whose squad included Great Britain and England team boxers.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Wetherspoon set to open up to 25 more pubs as sales jump higher
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Up to 25 more Wetherspoon pubs could open this financial year. JD Wetherspoon estimates it could open a further five to 10 managed pubs and 10 to 15 franchised sites in the year ending August 1, 2027. That would be in addition to the six managed pubs and two franchises it has already opened this financial year. The expansion plans came as the pub group reported an 8.2 per cent rise in like-for-like sales in the 14 weeks to November 1, covering its first quarter and a further week. Chairman Tim Martin said: “The company has had a good start to the financial year. “There are still three quarters to go and profit forecasts are very dependent on the level of sales growth.” The six managed pubs opened so far are at Manchester Airport and Heathrow Airport, and in Crewe in Cheshire, Ferndown in Dorset, Dibden Purlieu in Hampshire and Kempston in Bedfordshire. Wetherspoon said it had sold one pub during the period and now had 797 trading managed pubs, alongside 25 franchises. Bar sales rose by 9.4 per cent over the 14 weeks, while food sales increased by 6.8 per cent. Like-for-like growth slowed to 7.5 per cent in the most recent five weeks, compared with 8.6 per cent in the first nine weeks of the quarter. Martin said the company was “comfortable” with market expectations once adjusted for the 53-week financial year. The company put the consensus profit estimate, compiled from seven analysts, at £76.4 million. In the previous 52-week financial year, pre-tax profit fell 28 per cent to £58.6 million as staff and other costs offset higher sales. The company also argued that labour cost increases affect pubs more heavily than supermarkets, estimating the labour cost of a pub pint at £1.68 compared with about 15p for a supermarket pint. Its calculation used an AI-derived estimate of the price of a supermarket pint and wage costs as a percentage of sales. The group argued that the effect had widened the price gap between pub and supermarket pints and reduced employment. Its next trading update is expected on January 20, 2027.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Thousands could unlock £2,600 savings after major government rule change
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Thousands of young people who lack the mental capacity to manage their finances could find it easier to access money held in their Child Trust Funds under new Government plans. The proposed changes aim to remove a complicated legal hurdle that has left many disabled young adults and their families facing lengthy and costly court processes to release savings that belong to them. Under the reforms, parents and carers will be able to approach Child Trust Fund providers directly to access the money on behalf of young people who lack the mental capacity to make financial decisions. The Government said the changes could help between 63,000 and 126,000 young adults who have so far faced difficulties accessing their accounts. Child Trust Funds are long-term, tax-free savings accounts introduced for children born between September 1, 2002 and January 2, 2011. The accounts were designed to give young people a financial asset when they reached adulthood, with money becoming accessible at the age of 18. Justice minister Jake Richards said: “Young people who lack the mental capacity to make financial decisions should be able to access their savings as easily as possible – especially when this money was put aside by loved ones to help them take their first steps into adulthood. “This is simply an injustice that we’re finally putting right and as campaigners have argued for years, change is long overdue. “This legislation will ensure this group of young adults no longer face difficulty from accessing money that is rightfully theirs.” Economic secretary to the Treasury Lucy Rigby said the reforms would help tens of thousands more young people access their accounts. She said: “The changes that we’re introducing will help tens of thousands more young people to connect with their child trust funds - worth on average £2,600 each.” Recommended reading: The Government said it would work with others to develop the new process, including deciding who will be able to access the money, what evidence will be needed and what safeguards should be put in place to protect young people who lack mental capacity. Speaking in the Commons, Ms Rigby said: “The last Labour government introduced child trust funds with the intention that every child in this country could access a financial asset as they enter adulthood, and almost three million young people have already accessed their funds, currently containing an average of £2,600 each.” She added: “I am going to be bringing forward an amendment to the Financial Services Bill. The second reading of which is next week, which will enable the Ministry of Justice to make regulations to put this in action.” Anna Bird, chief executive of Contact, said families had faced unnecessary difficulties when trying to access the money. She said: “For too long, tens of thousands of young disabled people and their families have faced a complicated and costly process to access money that rightfully belongs to them.” The Court of Protection will remain available as an alternative route for protecting the financial interests of adults who cannot make financial decisions for themselves.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Channel 4 axes major series after 11 years amid 'serious allegations of wrongdoing'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Channel 4 has cancelled Married At First Sight UK. The decision follows an external review prompted by "serious allegations of wrongdoing" involving the show. Earlier this year, two female participants alleged rape and a third claimed sexual misconduct by their on-screen husbands in a BBC Panorama documentary aired in May. In June, a cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape. All three men have denied the allegations. Chief executive of Channel 4, Priya Dogra, said: "Welfare across all our programmes is a primary concern. "Whilst the review praised the welfare protocols in place and made no findings that Channel 4 breached the Ofcom Code or that the format is inherently unsafe, I have to consider when is the right time for Channel 4 to move on from a format. "The recommendations are eminently sensible and feasible, but considering their wholesale implementation provoked fundamental questions about the editorial proposition of a show that, I believe, has now run its course over 10 years." She also addressed the women who made the allegations. Ms Dogra said: "I am very sorry for the distress those women have clearly felt. "I hope our actions – in swiftly commissioning the review and taking clear, decisive steps – demonstrate our commitment to the wellbeing of all contributors and our desire to relentlessly strengthen industry standards." The sixth season of Married at First Sight UK, filmed earlier this year, will not be aired. A planned spin-off series, featuring contestants from the UK and Australian versions, was also halted during the review. The external review was commissioned by Ms Dogra after the allegations surfaced. It was split into two parts: Channel 4 said the reviews did not attempt to judge the allegations, which remain a matter for the relevant authorities. Clyde & Co reviewed more than 31,000 documents and 20 hours of footage. Their findings concluded that Channel 4 and production company CPL had complied with the Ofcom Broadcasting Code and had not breached any regulations in handling the issues raised. However, the review identified isolated incidents where the welfare framework was not fully followed. One example involved participants breaking the code of conduct regarding "prohibited substances." They received a first and final warning instead of being removed from the show. Ms Heggessey’s review also found that some aspects of the programme could "implicitly put pressure on contributors to be intimate" and that participants could "become dependent on production and lose touch with reality," impacting their ability to make decisions. A post shared by Shona Manderson 🪐✨🌸 (@shoniemandy) The review recommended improvements, including reducing the frequency of questions about couples’ physical relationships and discontinuing Intimacy Week and Partner Swap Week. It also suggested changing the show’s "leave or stay" mechanism. Currently, if one person in a couple chooses to leave but the other wants to stay, both must remain for another week. The review proposed allowing a participant to leave if they wish. Despite these concerns, the review described the welfare protocols as "extensive, extremely thorough and of a high standard." Ms Dogra said implementing the recommendations would require a "materially greater level of intervention, monitoring and supervision that would fundamentally alter the format and editorial proposition of the programme." She concluded that, given the maturity of the show and the required changes, ending the series was the right decision. Channel 4 said the budget for Married At First Sight UK will be redirected toward "bold, innovative new programmes from the UK independent production community." A spokesperson said: "CPL has always put contributor welfare at the heart of its programme making and will continue to do so. "CPL have worked closely with Channel 4 for many years and throughout the review process, and we look forward to working with them again in the future." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Minister responds to claims smoky bacon crisps could be banned in UK in new EU deal
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cabinet minister told an interviewer to “get a life” over a question about smoky bacon crisps. Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle was asked whether closer alignment with the European Union could lead to restrictions on the crisps' labels. Speaking to Times Radio host Stig Abell, she compared the issue to the debate about EU rules on bananas during the Brexit referendum. She said: “Oh, Stig. I mean, really, we’ve had EU straight bananas, and now we’re talking about banning smoky bacon crisps, I think you should get a life.” (Image: Peter Byrne/PA) Dame Angela added: “If you want to obsess about smoky bacon crisps, I suppose that’s your choice.” The concerns relate to whether rules on the use of meat names for products without meat could affect flavour descriptions, rather than ban the crisps themselves. FoodNavigator reported that the European Snacks Association had raised the possibility that flavours such as smoky bacon could be caught by the rules. It also reported that an amendment had been proposed to exempt products including snacks from restrictions on flavour descriptions. The question comes ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on November 20, where Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to seek agreements on food and farming, emissions trading and youth mobility. The proposed food deal is expected to align the UK with EU plant, animal and food trade standards to remove post-Brexit checks on exports. Dame Angela argued that reducing barriers would make it easier for farmers and food producers to trade with Europe. She said: “We’ve got huge potential growth in our economy if we allow our farmers and food producers to be able to export into Europe again without all the huge uncertainty and the costs and frictions that Brexit brought us.” “This will be a deal that improves that situation and it will enable this economy to grow and for us to have higher levels of prosperity than we’ve had before.” The minister declined to commit to giving farmers more time to adapt to the new trading arrangements, saying that removing barriers quickly would bring “huge economic benefits”. Asked on BBC Radio 4's Today programme about the Government's rejection of farmers' calls for a 24-month transition, she said ministers were listening to their concerns. She said: “The transition is a balance between getting and accessing those benefits as quickly as possible, but dealing with some of the transitional issues that you have to deal with whenever you’re moving from one system to another.” Mr Burnham has said the deals could raise GDP by 0.4%, compared with a previous estimate of 0.3%. Meanwhile, former EU Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier suggested the UK could negotiate to rejoin the bloc without being obliged to adopt the euro, but would have to accept freedom of movement and single market membership. He told Sky News: “If it is the choice of the UK to ask for a new negotiation to rejoin, it’s perfectly possible to begin such a negotiation without any kind of obligation to take part in the euro.” On the single market, Mr Barnier said: “There is no … possible negotiation on any kind of cherry-picking or the single market ‘a la carte’.” Mr Burnham has said the Government will “explore options” for a different long-term relationship with the EU after the summit. He has insisted voters would be “the boss” of any changes, amid questions about EU membership and freedom of movement.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Blue Badge drivers could face unexpected fines despite having a permit
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: UK Blue Badge holders heading to Italy have been issued a warning over a little-known driving rule that could land them with a fine of up to €335. British disabled drivers have been given a boost after the Department for Transport confirmed that UK Blue Badges will now be recognised in Italy. But motorists have been warned that being able to use their badge does not mean they can simply park or drive wherever they would be allowed to in Britain. Italy has its own regional parking restrictions and traffic rules, with one particular trap involving historic city centres potentially catching holidaymakers out. Letitia Smith, Head of Communications at AllClear Travel Insurance, said the change was welcome news but urged drivers to check local requirements before setting off. She said: “This is brilliant news for disabled drivers heading to Italy, but ‘recognised’ doesn’t mean the rules are the same as at home. Concessions vary from region to region, so don’t assume the parking rules will be the same as you’re used to in the UK. “The biggest thing to watch out for is Italy’s restricted traffic zones, or ZTLs, which cover many of the historic city centres. Your badge may give you access but check whether you need to register your number plate with local authorities first. Cameras log all car entries, and driving in without correct authorisation can mean a fine of between €84 and €335.” The warning is not limited to Italy. Disabled drivers planning to visit several countries should check the rules separately for each destination. Ms Smith said: “If you’re planning a wider European road trip, check each country's Blue Badge rules separately. Denmark and Switzerland require parking discs if you use time concessions, and in Spain recognition is decided by local authorities, so it can be different from one town to the next.” The Government has published guidance on using a UK Blue Badge in the European Union, including information for motorists planning trips abroad. UK Blue Badges are recognised in many European countries, but rules and concessions vary. Drivers should check local requirements before travelling. UK Blue Badges are recognised in: Countries with additional conditions or restrictions: Two important rules to remember: Italy's restricted traffic zones, known as ZTLs, operate in many historic city centres and limit which vehicles can enter. Blue Badge recognition may allow disabled motorists to access certain areas, but drivers could still need to register their number plate with the local authority before entering. Cameras monitor vehicles going into these zones, so motorists who drive in without the correct authorisation risk being fined between €84 and €335. The rules can vary between regions and towns, making it important to check the requirements for the specific destination rather than assume the same concessions apply everywhere. Recommended reading: AllClear has highlighted three things disabled drivers should consider before travelling to Italy. Check the local parking rules Look up the rules for the exact area you are visiting, including whether you need to register your vehicle or display a local notice alongside your UK Blue Badge. Take supporting documents Carry a translation of your Blue Badge and any relevant supporting paperwork, such as a doctor's letter. This may be requested in countries with stricter parking requirements. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Which? warning over common mistake that is making homes colder and bills higher
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Drying clothes on radiators could leave homes colder and bills higher, Which? has warned. In a TikTok video, the consumer organisation advises households to stop putting wet washing directly on radiators and suggests using an airer instead. It says damp clothes can act as a barrier to heat, potentially leaving a room taking longer to warm up and increasing energy use. Which? also raises the risk of mould when moisture from drying clothes ends up in the air inside a home. Which? suggests putting washing on an airer near a radiator rather than covering it, allowing air to circulate around the room. For people who need another option, it suggests a heated airer for smaller loads or a tumble dryer. However, a heated airer does not make the moisture disappear, so the room still needs ventilation. In separate tests of indoor drying methods, Which? found that the cheapest option depends partly on the amount of washing. It says an unheated airer uses no electricity, while its tested heated airers took around four to five hours to dry a small cotton load. The organisation found a heated airer could save money compared with vented or condenser tumble dryers when a small load fits on it in one go. For larger loads that need several rounds on an airer, Which? says a tumble dryer is likely to be cheaper to run. Heat pump dryers have lower running costs than vented and condenser models, according to its comparison, although they can cost more to buy. Ventilation matters whichever indoor drying method is used: South Kesteven District Council advises drying washing outside if possible. If that is not possible, it recommends a heated, well-ventilated room, such as a bathroom with the door closed, and says not to put clothes on radiators. The council advises opening windows wider or using extractor fans where fitted when drying clothes, and keeping permanent vents clear. Energy Saving Trust says condensation forms when moisture in the air meets a cold surface, such as a window. Its advice notes that damp can have other causes too, including leaks, damaged guttering and faults that allow groundwater into walls. Signs of a problem can include persistent condensation, a musty smell, peeling wallpaper or mould, according to the trust. It says the underlying cause needs to be addressed, and leaks or signs of rising damp should be dealt with quickly.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: British man with Ebola in DRC to be flown to UK for treatment
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A British man has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo. He is expected to be flown back to the UK for treatment following the diagnosis. A Government spokesperson said: "A British citizen currently in the DRC has tested positive for Ebola. "The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated." The patient, identified by Reuters as a healthcare worker, is expected to be medically evacuated to the UK, though the timing of the flight remains unclear. Only four cases of Ebola have ever been confirmed in the UK, including three involving health workers who responded to the outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015. Dr Damien Tully, associate professor at the Medical Research Council/Uganda Virus Research Institute and London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine Uganda Research Unit, said: "This case is a stark reminder of the risks faced by those responding to the outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in the DRC. "However, it does not suggest that the virus has become more transmissible or that the threat to the UK has increased." Dr Tully described the infection as "deeply concerning, but it is not entirely unexpected." He said: "Healthcare workers are on the front line of these outbreaks, often treating severely ill patients under extremely challenging conditions. "Even with rigorous protective measures, accidental exposures can occur." Read More He stressed that the risk to the British public "from this planned medical evacuation is extremely low" because Ebola is "transmitted primarily through direct contact with infected bodily fluids, and people are not generally infectious until they develop symptoms." The UK has two high-level isolation units equipped to handle such cases – at the Royal Free Hospital in London and the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle. Dr Tully said: "These facilities are equipped with specialist isolation systems and staffed by highly trained infectious disease teams."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. Concerns have been raised as average ticket prices could double following a major Cambridge venue’s refurbishment. The Corn Exchange is set to be redeveloped as part of the wider £95.7m Civic Quarter scheme to revitalise the city centre. The venue, considered the largest performance venue in the East of England, would see upgrades to the main auditorium, improvements to foyers and bar areas, improved seating, acoustics, sound quality and lighting. The wider plans also include work on refurbishing the Guildhall, Market Square and public spaces in-between. A report to Cambridge City Council ’s performance, assets and strategy overview and scrutiny committee said a revived Corn Exchange would act “as the catalyst for a renewed arts and culture scene in Cambridge drawing on its roots which saw it at the forefront of the changing trends in the UK’s music scene.” Sam Scharf, the council’s director of communities, said: “It’s already failed – I mean, last year it rained a bit and we had to cancel Tim Peake. “We then put a short-term remedy in with a bit of leading on top and that is not going to hold up – it’s not got any longevity.” Council officers said income from the venue will help fund the rest of the Civic Quarter scheme and project it will increase by a large amount after the refurbishment. Performances are estimated to increase from 180 a year to 340 and average ticket prices for council-run events from £24 plus VAT currently to £50 plus VAT in year five of the new venue’s opening. Officers said this only applies for events they self-promote and a larger amount of their income comes from hiring the venue out, when they don’t have control of ticket prices. Cllr Beth Gardiner-Smith said: “The business case also notes that the projection of event income is high compared to the benchmark venues. “I think it’s projecting a 43 per cent increase in attendance in year five and similar increases in performances. That feels big to me so I just want to make sure that we think that is robust. “What I don’t think we want to see, but maybe others would disagree, is that people across Cambridge are priced out of going to events on a regular basis at the Corn Exchange. “It’s a public venue for a purpose and it’s all part of this idea that we are creating a public realm and a civic space for our community and therefore we want tickets and events to remain affordable wherever possible.” Council officers said that the higher end of tickets is “growing exponentially” compared to lower-priced tickets which has driven up the average. Chair of the committee, Cllr Karen Young, said: “I’m hearing a lot of concern about the public not being priced out so we will pass that message onto cabinet.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire knifeman has been jailed after stabbing his ex-girlfriend’s new partner during a confrontation at her home. Matthew Beckett, 32, of Damson Crescent, St Neots, admitted wounding or inflicting grievous bodily harm without intent and possessing a knife in public. The attack took place less than two weeks after Beckett was ordered not to visit his former partner’s home as part of his bail conditions, after pleading guilty to harassing her in June this year. Beckett arrived at the property on June 29, argued with the woman’s new partner and left. He later returned, banging on the door while armed with a knife. When the man opened the door, Beckett lunged at him with the knife. The victim backed away as Beckett fled down the stairwell. The man chased him, but Beckett stabbed him in the chest through the stair railings and pinned him against a wall. Matthew Beckett previously pleaded guilty to harassing his ex-girlfriend (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) The victim was taken to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries, while Beckett was arrested. He was sentenced to two years and three months in prison at Huntingdon Law Courts on Tuesday, November 3. Detective Constable Luke Currie said: "Beckett had been given clear bail conditions to stay away from his former partner’s home, but chose to ignore them. "Not only did he turn up at the address, but he also returned armed with a knife and this incident could easily have resulted in an even more serious outcome. "I hope this sentence provides some reassurance to the victim and others affected by Beckett’s actions."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The Cambridge Oven bakery opens in St Ives to queues out the door
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire food reviewer Lucy Melton shares her thoughts following a recent visit to The Cambridge Oven in St Ives I had my eye on The Cambridge Oven ever since I heard it was coming to St Ives, so I made sure I headed there as soon as I could. I went on the first Saturday it was open and, unsurprisingly, there were people queuing out the door. It moved quickly though, and although a few things had already sold out, there was still a really good variety to choose from. Spinach and ricotta croissant (Image: Lucy Melton) The Cambridge Oven has been open in Cambridge since 2018 and has always been a must-stop when visiting, so I was really pleased to hear it was opening closer to home. I couldn't decide between sweet and savoury, so naturally I went for both. Starting with the spinach and ricotta croissant, I absolutely loved this. There was plenty of filling, the flavours worked really well together and the highlight was definitely the cheesy pastry, which added so much flavour. I then had the banana Danish, and the pastry was crispy, flaky and soft all at once. There was a lovely sugary coating which made it extra yummy, and I absolutely loved the banana crème in the centre. Banana Danish (Image: Lucy Melton) It had such a lovely flavour and went really well with the dried banana. I did wish there was a little more of the filling, but the pastry around it was tasty enough to make up for it. My brother-in-law went for the apple and almond Danish and really enjoyed it too. He particularly liked how light the pastry was and thought the filling was great. Overall, I was really pleased with everything I tried and will definitely be back to work my way through more of the menu. I love a visit to St Ives, so The Cambridge Oven will certainly be top of my list each time!

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Enormous sadness' as beloved Hunts department store to close
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A beloved Huntingdonshire department store has announced with "enormous sadness" that it is set to close its doors for good. Townrow, a family department store business which opened in 1871, insisted the "difficult" decision to close its St Ives store was not taken lightly. Retailer Eaden Lilley went into administration in February 2009 and their 10,000 square foot St Ives store on Bridge Street was purchased by Townrow. The historic independent chain sells clothing, shoes, and kitchenware and also has stores in Maldon and Frinton-on-Sea in Essex. Managing Director Edward Townrow said: "Like many independent retailers, we have faced increasingly challenging trading conditions, rising operating costs and changes in shopping habits. "Despite exploring a number of alternatives, we have regrettably been unable to establish a financially sustainable future for the store in its current form. "What makes this decision particularly difficult is the extraordinary relationship we have with the people of St Ives. "Our customers have been nothing short of wonderful. "Over the years, we have been privileged to welcome generations of families through our doors. "We have shared in their everyday lives, celebrated special occasions with them and formed friendships that extend far beyond the shop floor. "Their kindness, warmth and loyalty have meant more to us than I can possibly express. "I want every customer to know how genuinely grateful we are for their support." Mr Townrow also paid tribute to the "remarkable" team at the St Ives store. He said: "They are the heart and soul of the store, and I could not be prouder of them. "Their dedication, professionalism and genuine care for our customers have made Townrow a very special place." The store will hold a closing-down sale in the coming weeks. Mr Townrow added: "Although this marks the end of a chapter for our existing St Ives store, we remain committed to our other stores and to the values that have defined Townrow for more than 150 years. "Finally, to our customers, our colleagues and the entire St Ives community: thank you, from the bottom of my heart. "It has been an absolute privilege to be part of your town."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Calls to cut state pension age to 65 and free up jobs for younger workers grow
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A petition calling for the state pension age to be cut to 65 for everyone has passed 112,000 signatures, with the campaign now set to be considered for a debate in Parliament. The petition, created by Michelle Gill, argues that lowering the retirement age would allow people to retire with dignity, avoid hardship and potentially free up jobs for younger workers entering the labour market. It has attracted 112,304 signatures and remains open until March 16, 2027. The campaign comes as the state pension age is gradually increasing from 66 to 67, with the change having started in April 2026 and due to be completed by March 2028. However, the Government has already rejected the call to bring the pension age back down to 65, saying it has no plans to make the change. The petition says: "Reduce the state pension age to 65. We believe this could mean people can retire with dignity and avoid hardship. We also think it could free up jobs for younger workers. "Many aged 65–67 face poor health, caring pressures, and limited work options, which we think is unfair." The campaign passed the 100,000-signature threshold, meaning the Petitions Committee will consider it for debate in Parliament. An update published on October 24 confirmed that the petition would be considered for debate. It does not mean a debate has been scheduled or that the Government has agreed to change the rules. In its response, published on October 13, the Government said: "The Government has no plans to lower the State Pension age. "There are no plans to reduce State Pension age to 65." Ministers pointed to rising life expectancy and said pension age policy takes account of the fact that people are living longer and society is ageing. The Government cited Office for National Statistics projections showing that men aged 66 in the UK could expect to live a further 19.3 years on average in 2026, while women of the same age could expect to live another 21.9 years. By 2046, those figures are projected to increase by a further 1.6 years. The response also said increases to the state pension age had been in legislation since the Pensions Act 1995 and were intended to maintain fairness between generations and protect public finances. The Government confirmed that its Third State Pension Age Review is underway. The review will consider what state pension age is appropriate for future decades, taking into account a range of evidence, including life expectancy projections, findings from the Government Actuary, independent reports from Dr Suzy Morrissey and the Pensions Commission, and lessons from previous increases. The Government also acknowledged that people aged 50 and over can face barriers to staying in work or finding a new job. These include ill health, disability, caring responsibilities, menopause and outdated skills or qualifications. Ministers said support for older workers includes dedicated 50PLUS Champions, additional time with work coaches for new Universal Credit claimants aged over 50, and Midlife MOTs delivered in Jobcentres. The petition, which can still be signed here, argues that lowering the state pension age could free up jobs for younger people. In its response, the Government said it was investing an additional £2.5 billion by 2029 into the Youth Guarantee and Growth and Skills Levy. It said the investment would support almost one million young people and create up to 500,000 opportunities to earn and learn. The measures include expanded Youth Hubs, additional work experience and training, a £3,000 Youth Jobs Grant and a £2,000 apprenticeship hiring payment for employers. The Government also said it would provide a fully funded six-month job for long-term unemployed people aged 18 to 24. The petition remains open for signatures until March 16, 2027.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire firefighters tackle smoke-filled soft play rescue exercise

New firefighters at Ely practised safely pitching a large ladder, a task that requires a four-person team. At Thorney, crews tackled a mock incident involving hazardous materials and heavy smoke, wearing breathing apparatus to search for casualties and extinguish a simulated fire. "Thank you to Play2Day Wisbech for hosting us." Training doesn’t always take place at stations, however. Thorney firefighters recently completed a confined space exercise at Play2Day Wisbech, a children’s soft play centre. Wearing full breathing apparatus and with vision deliberately obscured to simulate smoke, firefighters navigated the play structure to find and rescue training casualties. Paul Oliver, group commander and head of on-call for the service, said: "Being an on-call firefighter is a very exciting role. "Our crews take part in all kinds of training to help maintain their skills to keep them ready to respond to emergencies, whether its station based drills or larger exercises with other stations involving more complex scenarios. "It’s a great way to learn new skills and take on a challenge. "We are always looking to recruit more local people that can join stations as on-call firefighters. "We’d urge anyone living close to one of our on-call stations and can respond to emergencies around other commitments to visit our website to find out more about joining." More information is available on the Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service website.

The visitors began the afternoon second in the table, but neither side looked capable of imposing itself during a largely uneventful first half. Chances were scarce, although Zane Campbell cut inside from the left and forced a good save from Knowle goalkeeper Matt Horton. Just before the interval, referee Michael Dunkley dismissed the away side’s appeal for a penalty after a challenge involving Hayden Purves. The match changed shortly before the hour when Rovers full-back Alfie-Ray Turner stayed down following a challenge. Both benches called for play to be stopped, but the referee allowed the game to continue until the ball eventually went out. Matty Allan then received a ten-minute sin-bin punishment after voicing the home side’s frustration at the decision. Rather than pushing the visitors back, Rovers attempted to manage the game from deep and invited increasing pressure. Jack Mason produced an excellent save to keep the hosts level, but Knowle continued to threaten before taking the lead after 70 minutes. Captain Jack Duggan’s effort appeared to be heading wide, only for two deflections to send the ball looping over Mason and into the opposite corner. Rovers’ task became harder five minutes later when Tim Momodu, recently cautioned, committed another rash challenge and was shown a second yellow card. Seb Hayes introduced Declan Rogers and Micael Goncalves in a desperate attempt to rescue the contest, but Knowle saw out the remaining minutes as the fog thickened. Rovers now face successive away games against Lutterworth and Highgate United before hosting fellow strugglers FC Stratford on November 21.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Memorial appeal for heroic World War II 'Ghost Patrol' soldiers
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The families of men who served in one of the Second World War’s most remarkable special forces units are launching a £150,000 appeal to create a permanent memorial to their courage and achievements. The Long Range Desert Group (LRDG), nicknamed ‘Ghost Patrol’ by opposing Italian forces, was formed in Cairo in 1940 and often operated in secret behind enemy lines. The appeal follows the death in August of Jack Mann, the last surviving veteran of the LRDG, at the age of 100. Born Zacharia Zuckerman in Cairo in 1925, he altered his age to enlist while still a teenager and was recruited by the LRDG as a radio operator. A talented linguist and wireless operator, he was recruited into the LRDG and subsequently served with other wartime special forces units.  He later served with 21 SAS. The LDRG were founded after explorer and British Army officer Major Ralph Bagnold proposed the creation of a small, fast-moving reconnaissance force capable of travelling vast distances behind enemy lines in the deserts of Egypt and Libya. The unit became renowned for its ability to navigate across apparently featureless desert and operate hundreds of miles from conventional forces, gathering vital intelligence on enemy movements and carrying out raids and other operations. Its expertise also made the LRDG an important partner to the newly formed SAS, transporting and guiding its men across the desert on some of their early operations. After the North African campaign, the LRDG continued to operate across the Aegean, Adriatic, Albania, Italy, Greece and Yugoslavia. The cost was considerable. Fifty-one LRDG men are known to have died during the war and at least 182 were captured. The LRDG Memorial Fund, a registered charity established by people with family connections to members of the unit, plans to erect a spectacular 5.8-metre-high sculpture of a scorpion — the LRDG’s emblem — at the Royal British Legion National Remembrance Gardens in Staffordshire. While many Second World War units are represented at the Gardens, the Long Range Desert Group is not currently among them. The memorial has been designed by internationally recognised British sculptor James Doran-Webb, renowned for his monumental animal sculptures.  At its centre will be a giant driftwood scorpion, surrounded by a three-metre stainless-steel ring with compass-style markings reflecting the LRDG’s navigational skills. The sculpture will stand on a plinth designed to trace the unit’s wartime journey from North Africa to the Aegean, Italy and the Balkans. The LRDG Memorial Fund is seeking donations from the public, military community and organisations towards its £150,000 fundraising target. Donations can be made at www.lrdgmemorialfund.org where there is a link to JustGiving. Meg Kennedy Shaw, daughter of Bill Kennedy Shaw, the LRDG’s intelligence officer, said: “Jack Mann's death this summer marked the passing of the last surviving member of the Long Range Desert Group. "With him, the final living link to this extraordinary group of men has gone. For those of us whose fathers and grandfathers served with the LRDG, it makes it all the more important that their story is not lost with their generation. “These men operated for almost five years across deserts, islands, mountains and coastlines, frequently deep behind enemy lines and in extraordinarily difficult conditions. "They showed exceptional courage, ingenuity and resourcefulness, yet their story remains relatively little known. “We believe the time has come to give the LRDG the permanent public recognition it deserves. The scorpion memorial will be a striking and lasting tribute to them, and a place where their families and future generations can remember what they did.” Sculptor James Doran-Webb added: “The scorpion gave us a powerful starting point because it comes directly from the LRDG’s own insignia. "I wanted the memorial to reflect the incredible ingenuity, endurance and navigational skill of the men who served, while creating something dramatic enough to stop people in their tracks and make them curious to discover who the LRDG were and what they achieved.”

Ambitious ideas to transform St Ives with new riverside moorings, pedestrianised streets, an enhanced market area and a regenerated bus station have been unveiled. The St Ives Town Team has published an updated 'A Vision of St Ives', setting out ideas to boost the town while protecting its historic character. Town Team spokesman John Souter said the document is a starting point for discussion, with businesses, organisations and other interested parties due to meet next month. MP Ben Obese-Jecty (centre) with John Souter and Sheila Stones of the St Ives Town Team, which has created an updated Vision for St Ives document. (Image: Ben Obese-Jecty) The meeting will be closed to the public, but people will have a chance to give their views later, he said. "We want to discuss what is feasible, and come up with some sort of plan that we can take to the public for people to discuss and then add their views on," said John. "The plan will include some short-term goals that are easily achievable because they won't require a lot of funding. "Longer-term projects where we would need to find funding, and then schemes that we know will take some time to realise, such as regenerating Hyperion corner, alongside the bus station, making them more attractive." Hyperion corner could be completely transformed with new buildings. (Image: Town Team) He said the owners of the buildings were on board with the idea. Among the most striking suggestions are additional mooring pontoons at The Quay, designed to encourage more people travelling on the Great Ouse to stop and spend time in the town. The Town Team says extra visitor berths could bring more people to shops and other amenities, accommodate more boats and create opportunities for river events. It believes pontoons could also improve safety along the water's edge. The bus station could be given a makeover to make it more appealing to look at. (Image: Town Team) Another major idea would see part of Market Hill pedestrianised, particularly around the Oliver Cromwell statue, Town Hall, Free Church and Corn Exchange, and local MP Ben Obese-Jecty has launched a poll on the St Ives Serious Discussion Facebook page asking people for their views on potential pedestrianisation. John said: "This project is about far more than pedestrianisation; we want a vision for St Ives that will make it more attractive, while helping it to prosper." He said he has been pushing for various improvements in the town since 1996, when he was a town councillor. He believes the time is now right for progress. The Octagon could become a venue for daily farmers' markets. (Image: Town Team) "There has not been the political will before, but I believe it is there now, and so this is our chance to do something good for St Ives, and it's probably my last chance to see my ambitions for the town realised in my lifetime," said John. The Town Team's vision suggests reducing parking in Market Hill to create more community space, potentially featuring trees for shade and a covered area inspired by traditional market halls. Changes could also be made to Crown Street, Bridge Street and Merryland, with the Town Team suggesting pedestrianisation while retaining access for residents and delivery vehicles. Public transport is another key part of the vision. One idea is to reroute Cambridge buses through The Broadway, Crown Street and Market Hill, bringing passengers closer to shops and boosting footfall. The document also suggests the existing bus stop in Station Road could be relocated to the Sheep Market. Meanwhile, the area around the bus station is identified as a potential regeneration opportunity, including the historic Octagon. The document envisages a development featuring shops, an improved antiques centre, flats and an historic auction room. The Octagon itself could potentially become a daily indoor produce or farmers' market, while also being used for antique auctions and as a tourist information point because of its proximity to the bus station and main car park. The vision also calls for efforts to revive the town's markets, improve cleanliness, tackle commercial waste and wheelie bins in sensitive historic areas, and boost tourism. It also suggests creating an innovation hub, using vacant properties for pop-up businesses and conference facilities. The Town Team says the updated document aims to spark debate about what could be achieved and inform the Town Council's Neighbourhood Plan. It says St Ives should build on its independent shops, historic streets and riverside setting rather than copy other town centres. The document says some major projects will take time, while others could improve the town quickly. It says: "We understand that no town can stand still and rest on its laurels, and every community needs to assess and reassess itself to ensure it is taking advantage of all the opportunities that exist."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Six passenger planes across Europe, including two UK departures, are being inspected following suspected bomb threats. A flight from London Heathrow to Warsaw-Chopin Airport was diverted to Warsaw-Modlin Airport in Poland on Tuesday, temporarily closing the airport. Another flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw-Chopin landed as scheduled and was subsequently inspected by authorities. Elsewhere in Europe, a Ryanair flight from Manchester to Murcia in southern Spain was also subject to a bomb threat, while Bulgarian media reported a flight from Israel to Sofia received a threat via email before landing. The diverted flight, operated by Polish carrier LOT, was carrying 118 people and led to a partial closure of the airport. Francisco Lucas, the Spanish government’s delegate in the Murcia region, said 121 people were on board the Ryanair flight. He added that the plane was being inspected and security protocol was underway. Murcia-Corvera Airport’s fire brigade was also mobilised. In Bulgaria, Lyubomir Nikolov, chief secretary of the Ministry of Interior, said counter-terrorism teams were examining the aircraft for explosives. Sources have also told the BBC that two Ryanair flights, one from Lisbon and the other from Dublin, were searched following anonymous tips regarding potential bomb threats. Flight cancellations can quickly turn travel plans upside down, but passengers are not without rights when journeys are disrupted. Under UK law, airlines are required to provide care and assistance in the event of a cancelled flight, regardless of the reason for the disruption. The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) has clarified what travellers are entitled to, including accommodation, meals, and transport between the airport and hotel if re-routed to the following day. The CAA said: "The airline must provide you with these items until it is able to fly you to your destination, no matter how long the delay lasts or what has caused it." If airlines are unable to arrange assistance due to large-scale disruption, passengers are advised to organise their own accommodation and transport and reclaim the costs later. The CAA said: "If you end up paying for things yourself, keep every receipt and do not spend more than is reasonable. "Airlines are unlikely to refund you for things like luxury hotels or alcohol. "Some will provide guidance on reasonable costs." Travellers must also be given the choice between a full refund for unused parts of their ticket or an alternative flight. Compensation may be available depending on the cause of the cancellation. The CAA said: "Disruptions caused by things like extreme weather, airport or air traffic control employee strikes or other ‘extraordinary circumstances’ are not eligible for compensation." Compensation is also dependent on the notice given and the timing of the replacement flight. The CAA said: "If you received less than seven days’ notice of the cancellation, you can claim compensation based on the timings of the alternative flight. "If your new flight departs no more than one hour before the scheduled time of your original flight and your new flight arrives less than two hours after the scheduled time of your original flight, you are not entitled to financial compensation." More detailed information on entitlements and compensation can be found on the CAA website. Have you ever claimed compensation from a flight being cancelled or delayed? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Sole traders and landlords earning more than £50,000 have just days left to submit their second Making Tax Digital update, with HMRC clearing up five common mistakes ahead of the deadline. Thousands of sole traders and landlords face another important tax deadline this week, as HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) reminds people to submit their second Making Tax Digital (MTD) quarterly update by Saturday, November 7. The requirement applies to sole traders and landlords earning more than £50,000, with the new digital reporting system becoming mandatory for them from April 6, 2026. But after the first quarterly update was submitted in August, HMRC says it has been answering a number of common questions and misconceptions about what people need to do next. HMRC has now highlighted five things customers should know before submitting their latest figures - including whether they need to pay tax, what happens if they make a mistake and whether they can leave their submission until Saturday. One of the biggest misconceptions is that a quarterly update is effectively another tax return. HMRC has stressed that this is not the case. An MTD quarterly update is simply a summary of income and expenses from self-employment and property, which must be submitted using compatible software. There is no tax calculation involved and, importantly, no payment is due when the update is sent. Customers' overall tax position will only be calculated when they submit their tax return for the 2026 to 2027 tax year. Anyone who successfully submitted their first quarterly update in August does not need to contact HMRC again for reassurance that it has been received. Instead, customers can check their submission history whenever they want by logging into their HMRC online account or checking through their Making Tax Digital software. HMRC says there is no need to call or use webchat simply to confirm that an update has gone through. Another concern is that Making Tax Digital means customers must purchase complicated or expensive accounting packages. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Holidaymaker's horror as 'refund' from Ryanair turned out to be £900 scam
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A holidaymaker was scammed out of £900 after complaining online about soaking wet seats on a flight. Sharon Morrell thought she was receiving a £400 compensation payout from Ryanair after rain poured into the cabin before takeoff. The 48-year-old bus driver had booked a four-night package holiday flight from Bristol to Palma, Majorca, alongside her husband and two children on Saturday, October 24. Mrs Morrell said 11 seats near the open aircraft door were left sitting in puddles following heavy downpours. A holidaymaker who complained online about rain-soaked seats on a Ryanair flight was scammed out of £900 after fraudsters offered fake compensation. (Image: Kennedy News and Media) Cabin crew handed passengers paper towels from the toilet to mop up the water themselves before departure, she claimed. Mrs Morrell said: "We were waiting on the stairs for everyone to board the plane, so we were getting soaked then as well. "Obviously Ryanair can't help if there's downpours. "So we got inside the plane and the seats on the left and right side were soaking wet. "Even the seats behind were soaking too. "There were 11 overall that were soaked. "This was all our family's seats and the people behind us. "They weren't just a little bit wet - there were puddles." She said passengers were expected to sit on wet chairs for a two-hour flight, adding: "There was definitely an inch of water. "I said to the staff 'are we expected to just sit on this? This is ridiculous.' "They said 'we'll sort it out in a minute, just get seated so we can get everyone boarded.'" After arriving in Majorca, the mother-of-two shared her frustration on social media. She was shocked when an unknown caller rang her shortly afterwards claiming to represent the airline's compensation team. The caller offered £200 each for her and her husband, and instructed her to download two mobile phone apps to transfer the money safely. Mrs Morrell said: "He said 'no problem, and we can compensate you £200 each for me and my husband for what's happened.' "He sounded genuine." She followed the instructions, only to see funds flowing out of her account instead of coming in. Mrs Morrell said: "I said 'why are there payments leaving my account when it should be the other way around?' "He said 'it's normal process and it's actually payments we're putting into your account.' "He was so clever." The scammer asked for her account balance when payments were declined, prompting her to hang up as transactions totalling £900 went through to Kenya. Mrs Morrell is now disputing the transactions with her bank and warned others against falling for similar traps. She said: "It's so easy to be sucked in and I just can't believe how easy it is to get scammed. "Anybody can fall for these scams. It's my own fault, I got sucked into this." Ryanair said rainwater entered the cabin during boarding due to Storm Boelo. A spokesperson for the airline said: "Due to adverse weather conditions (Storm Boelo) during boarding at Bristol on 24 Oct, a small number of seats near the aircraft door became damp from rainwater entering the cabin. "Crew assisted affected passengers by wiping down the seats and this flight operated normally from Bristol to Palma de Mallorca."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Knife attacker 'spat at' police detention officer on train, court told
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The man accused of a knife attack on board an LNER train in Huntingdon last year "spat at" a police officer on a train travelling to Peterborough, a court has heard. Multiple people were injured on the service travelling to London King's Cross on November 1, 2025 which was forced to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon. Anthony Williams, 33, denies 14 counts of attempted murder: ten of them in relation to the LNER train, three said to have happened in Peterborough and one at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London. Earlier this month, Williams pleaded guilty to 10 counts of wounding with intent relating to the incident on the LNER train, the wounding with intent of a man at Pontoon Dock DLR station in the early hours of November 1 and to the wounding with intent of a 14-year-old boy in Peterborough on October 31, as well as a number of other offences. At Cambridge Crown Court on November 3, Prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC told jurors that a man, agreed by the prosecution and defence to be Williams, 'spat at' a passenger, Jordan Morley, on a train travelling to Peterborough at around 8am on November 1, 2025. Mr Morley, a police detention officer at Islington Custody, was on his way home from work and had boarded the 7.16am service at King's Cross St Pancras, the court heard in a statement read out by the prosecution. He "felt what I would describe as a spray of spittle" as he sat on the train which had just stopped at Hitchin, the court heard. The court heard how Mr Morley was "almost in disbelief that he had spat at him". He had no previous interaction with the male who spat at him, the court was told. Mr Morley exited the train at Biggleswade and sent a text message to British Transport Police at 8.18am on November 1, 2025, the court heard. Williams has pleaded guilty to common assault on a Thameslink train travelling between London and Biggleswade on November 1. The trial continues.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Further details behind closure of much-loved village pub emerge
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
For months now mystery has shrouded the fate of a popular village pub in Huntingdonshire which closed its doors without explanation. The Black Bull, on Church Road, in Brampton, announced it had closed "for the foreseeable future" in August. The 16th century venue was run by Malcolm Beswick and is operated by the UK's largest pub company, Stonegate. Now, ex-staff have come forward to reveal further details surrounding the watering hole's sudden closure. They claim "things took a turn for the worst" in February when the pub began "running out of stock", including soft drinks and kitchen supplies. "The place wasn't really managed, if I'm honest, it was all over the place," one ex-employee, who asked to remain anonymous, told The Hunts Post. However, stock would turn out to be the least of the pub's worries as a subsequent Food Standard's Agency inspection revealed. The premises was slapped with a zero food hygiene rating by the independent government body following a review of the site on May 6. It said "major improvement" was necessary in areas including "management of food safety" as well as "cleanliness and conditions of facilities and building". "The kitchen hasn't had a deep clean in a number of years and we were finding food that was out of date," a former employee said. "We once served a whole table with mouldy Yorkshire puddings which had been prepped the week before. "The hygiene was really bad, staff would go outside, smoke a cigarette, go back in and not wash their hands." Read more Eaton Socon home with one-bedroom annexe on sale for £500,000
    All the Cambridgeshire finalists in the British Kebab Awards 2027
    Ouse Valley and Black Cat Radio begin broadcasting on DAB across Hunts
    Care Network celebrates 40 years after helping thousands across Cambridgeshire
    Hunts dog lover's event sees 300 labradors gather at Jeremy Clarkson’s pub Former staff said the hygiene rating forced the closure of the kitchen, but claim that despite this it was still not professionally deep-cleaned. "It was quite uncertain and a lot of us were message each other about the future of the pub," they added. "We didn't know if the pub was going to be open and if we were going to have our jobs back which caused a lot of stress." Describing the culture at The Black Bull, one ex-employee even claims they often had no designated break unless they requested one. Mr Beswick revealed the pub would close "permanently" in a WhatsApp message sent to staff on August 13. The correspondence, seen by this newspaper and verified by two sources, confirmed the reason behind the closure in a bid to "avoid speculation". "Thank you all for your patience, I'm afraid we have to close permanently. "To avoid speculation I found out today that the brewery filed a bankruptcy petition over a £21,000 debt for buying out of tie. "I'm afraid I dropped the ball on that and it has cost everything including sadly your jobs," it added. According to The Gazette, a petition to declare Mr Beswick bankrupt was filed at Cambridge County Court on March 16. The application was lodged by the creditor Unique Pub Property Limited, which is a subsidiary of Stonegate. A bankruptcy order has since come into effect and will automatically discharge on June 10 next year, the Individual Insolvency Registers shows. In a statement, Stonegate said it is unable to comment on "any alleged legal or financial matters concerning individual third parties". A spokesperson said: "We are actively seeking a new tenant to take on the Black Bull, Brampton. "The Black Bull is a valued local pub with an important role to play in the community, and our priority is to secure the right operator to take the business forward. "We are keen to see the pub reopen as soon as possible and are actively seeking a new tenant who can build on its potential and re-establish it as a thriving venue." Mr Beswick has been approached for comment. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk or newsdesk@huntspost.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire joins major UK trial testing new Alzheimer’s treatments
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire and Peterborough have enrolled their first participants in a major UK trial for Alzheimer’s treatments. The study, supported by Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust (CPFT), is part of the AD-SMART trial—a national effort to accelerate the search for effective therapies. Dr Ben Underwood, director of research and development at CPFT and the trial’s local principal investigator, said: "We are delighted to welcome Angela and Steve to join the trial with us at CPFT and hope this research will directly benefit them and countless others living with Alzheimer’s disease. "Our research would not be possible without people like them coming forward to help us. "We will support them throughout their research journey and hope that many others will join to help test promising dementia treatments and ensure the most successful ones can be brought to NHS clinics as soon as possible." The AD-SMART trial is the first of its kind to test multiple drugs at the same time, beginning with two medicines already used to treat type 2 diabetes and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Angela and Steve Bucksey, residents from Cambridgeshire who joined the study, said: "Following Angela’s diagnosis, we decided to take part in a study at a local friendly research unit without having to travel into London, and it feels good to be doing something about it." The trial will involve up to 20 NHS sites over the next 12 to 18 months, with more than 30 planned in total. Researchers aim to recruit 1,200 participants across the UK. Researchers expect to finish evaluating the first drugs in 2030. Individuals with a confirmed diagnosis of Alzheimer’s who wish to take part can contact the CPFT Research team at RandD@cpft.nhs.uk or call 01223 219753. For more information on dementia research and other clinical trial opportunities, visit Join Dementia Research.

The National Farmers’ Union (NFU) has called for investment to build resilience in the sector, arguing that a sustainable farming industry is crucial for the rural economy, environmental stewardship and food security. Tom Bradshaw, president of the NFU, said: "This was an opportunity for the government to act on the warm words it made over the summer. NFU Cambridgeshire County Chair Alison Morris (Image: Alison Morris) "It has failed to act and has left farmers and growers feeling abandoned. "The OBR (the Office for Budget Responsibility) has reflected that the food price inflation outlook is significantly higher than previous forecasts. "Yet the government has failed to link domestic food production to food-price inflation, has missed the opportunity to deliver on its commitment that 'food security is national security' and failed to give farm businesses the 'breathing space' that the Chancellor said this Budget was for." The government did announce the removal of tariffs on certain foods and fertilisers to help reduce costs. Chancellor John Healey prepares to deliver the Budget 2026 (Image: John Healey) However, the NFU said most fertiliser already arrives in the UK without tariffs, and any savings would depend on whether benefits are passed down the supply chain. Alison Morris, chair of the NFU Cambridgeshire, said: "This Budget has done nothing to help our farmers. "We need help now not words of we understand. "We urgently need support from the Keep Britain Growing Loan so that we can afford to harvest the crops still in the ground and plant next year’s crops. "Increasing the Annual Investment Allowance to at least £5m, including structures and buildings, scrapping the family farm tax would have gone some way to restoring much-needed confidence."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Walkers recalls crisps over health concerns as shoppers warned 'do not eat'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Walkers snack sharing box is being recalled over undeclared wheat. PepsiCo is recalling its Walkers Variety Snacks Sharing Box after wheat was left off the outer packaging, creating a possible risk for some people with allergies or coeliac disease. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) says the affected boxes have best-before dates of November 21, 2026, or January 16, 2027. The alert applies to crisps sold in England, Scotland and Wales. The problem concerns an 85g packet of Monster Munch Giants Roast Beef inside the box, which contains wheat and gluten not declared on the outside of the sharing box. The FSA said: "This product contains gluten making it a possible health risk for anyone with an allergy or intolerance to wheat or gluten, or with coeliac disease." Affected boxes weigh 655g and contain six packs of snacks. The batch code to look for on the affected boxes is 107543. Anyone who has bought an affected box and has an allergy or intolerance to wheat or gluten, or has coeliac disease, is advised not to eat it. Instead, the FSA says customers can call the PepsiCo Consumer Care Line on 0800 274 777 or visit contact.pepsico.com/walkers to receive a full refund. PepsiCo has issued a point-of-sale notice explaining the recall and what customers should do. The NHS says a food allergy is different from a food intolerance and that allergic reactions can be serious for some people. It advises calling 999 if, for example, someone's lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or they are struggling to breathe. If someone having a serious allergic reaction has an adrenaline auto-injector or nasal spray, the NHS says to use it immediately and call 999 even if they seem to be feeling better. Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition in which eating gluten causes the immune system to attack the body's own tissues, damaging the small intestine, the NHS says. Symptoms can include diarrhoea, abdominal pain and bloating, and a gluten-free diet helps control symptoms and prevent long-term complications. The FSA explains that a food may be withdrawn from sale when there is a problem that means it should not be sold. A recall is when customers are asked to return the product, rather than it simply being taken off shelves. Food can be withdrawn or recalled because allergy information is missing or incorrect, or because there is another food allergy risk. When there is a food allergy risk, the agency issues an allergy alert.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts Phil to perform songs by composer killed on Somme at Remembrance event
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A "distinguished" amateur choir in Huntingdonshire will hold a Remembrance event with songs by a composer killed on the Somme. Huntingdonshire Philharmonic, also known as Hunts Phil, will perform at St Mary’s Church, Godmanchester, on Saturday, November 7, at 7.30pm. The first half of the programme will feature six songs from George Butterworth’s A Shropshire Lad, sung by baritone Caleb Richards. Butterworth was killed by a sniper at Pozières on the Somme in August 1916, aged 31. Before leaving for France, he destroyed the manuscripts he was dissatisfied with, fearing he would not come back to revise them, and left the rest to his friend Ralph Vaughan Williams. The rest of the programme includes Vaughan Williams’s Lord, Thou Hast Been Our Refuge, John Ireland’s Greater Love Hath No Man, and Herbert Sumsion’s They That Go Down to the Sea in Ships. The second half is Matthew Coleridge’s Requiem. Classic FM has described it as a modern choral classic. The concert is in the middle of Hunts Phil’s 50th anniversary season, which opened on October 17 to a capacity audience. The choir is conducted by Nicholas Morris.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The government has confirmed it intends to proceed with plans to use a former sheltered living complex to house asylum seekers. In a letter, the Home Office confirmed its decision to use Roman Court, in Leverington, near Wisbech, to house mothers and babies. It comes less than two weeks after a fire ripped through a disused building at the site, which police are investigating as arson. Fenland District Council said the decision "demonstrates a complete disregard for the serious risks the plans pose to public safety, community cohesion and civil unrest." Concerns have been raised about the site which was earmarked as part of government plans to move asylum seekers out of hotels and into longer-term homes. Police continue to investigate a fire which ripped through a disused building at the site (Image: Colin Martin) Cllr Sam Hoy, Fenland District Council portfolio holder for housing, said: "We are extremely alarmed by the Home Office’s decision which has been taken despite extensive evidence from the Council and our partners highlighting serious concerns about the suitability of Roman Court and the risks associated with this proposal. "What is particularly troubling is that the Home Office has chosen to proceed at a time when there has already been significant unrest linked to these plans, including public protests and the fire at the site, which remains the subject of an ongoing police investigation. "These events have demonstrated the strength of local concern and the heightened tensions that exist within the community. "We do not believe those circumstances can simply be dismissed as issues that can be managed through routine arrangements. "Our position remains unchanged. Roman Court is the wrong location for this proposal, and we remain deeply concerned about the impact on both future residents and the wider community. "We will continue to make our objections known to the Home Office and work with our partners to ensure local concerns are heard and appropriately addressed." As the contracted accommodation provider, Serco will be required to demonstrate the site meets legal, regulator and property requirements before occupation. "This will include the relevant safeguarding, welfare, security, fire safety and operational arrangements," the letter reads. "Where site-specific action or mitigation is required, this will be taken forward with Serco and the relevant partners as the site progresses. "The accommodation will not become operational until the applicable requirements have been met, with input from relevant partners sought through the appropriate channels where required."
