summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: No trains between Peterborough or Letchworth and London due to weekend works
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: No trains will run between Peterborough or Letchworth and London later this month due to engineering works. The disruption will take place on Saturday, November 28 and Sunday, November 29, as part of the £1.4 billion East Coast Digital Programme (ECDP), which will replace traditional signals with real-time, in-cab digital signalling. Passengers are advised to check their journeys and expect rail replacement services on affected routes. No Thameslink or Great Northern trains will run between Moorgate, London St Pancras or London King's Cross and Letchworth Garden City or Peterborough all weekend. Rail replacement buses will be operating on the following routes: Most LNER services will start and terminate at Peterborough, with rail replacement coaches connecting customers to Bedford where Thameslink trains will operate to London St Pancras. Ricky Barsby, head of access integration (ECDP) for Network Rail, said: "We have begun to introduce digital in-cab signalling to the East Coast Main Line and we’re getting ready to extend its use to more services. "When all trains operate with digital signalling there will be reliability benefits through less reliance on trackside equipment and better ability to recover from disruption. "We are also taking the opportunity to do other vital engineering work on the track and lineside to improve the reliability of day-to-day services. "We’re sorry to anyone whose journey will be affected. "Those customers who have choice about when they can travel may want to consider travelling on days before or after, which are unaffected by work. "For those who need to travel on the affected weekend, we have plans in place to keep passengers moving." A spokesperson for the train operators said: "We’re working with Network Rail to help passengers plan their journeys while these important upgrades take place. "No trains will be able to run on the East Coast Main Line between Peterborough or Letchworth Garden City and London on November 28 and 29. "Passengers should check before they travel and allow extra time, as services will be significantly altered and rail replacement services will be in operation for many journeys."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire police officers added to barred list doubled in last year
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The number of Cambridgeshire police officers who were added to the barred list doubled in the last year, according to new data. College of Policing figures show 20 Cambridgeshire officers were barred in 2025/26, up from 10 the previous year and three in 2023/24. The College of Policing is an independent body for everyone working in policing. Introduced in 2017, the barred list names officers, special constables and staff dismissed from policing after investigations. Nine Cambridgeshire officers were barred in 2022/23, compared with two in 2021/22 and three in 2020/21. This means more Cambridgeshire Police officers were added to the barred list in 2025/26 than in any other year since 2020. Nationally, 757 police officers were banned from serving after they were sacked for breaching professional standards in the year to the end of March 2026, up from 735 in 2024/25 and 594 in 2023/24. The College of Policing said on November 3 that it was the highest annual total since the barred list began. Assistant Chief Constable Arman Mathieson, director of operational standards at the College of Policing, said: “Policing is built on trust and these figures show we will not hesitate to act when that trust is broken. “757 officers have been removed and barred from ever serving again, including those who retired or resigned while under investigation. “This represents 0.5% of all serving officers, with the vast majority of officers serving with courage, professionalism and integrity. “We all deserve a service that roots out those who fall short. "Where standards are breached, we will find out and we will act. “Since the barred list was introduced in December 2017, 3,591 regular officers have been added in total, with the pace of dismissals accelerating markedly: 757 officers were barred last year alone, more than in any single year since the list began and over twice the annual average of the preceding four years.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: £120,000 conservation project launched to protect historic Houghton Mill
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Conservation work is underway to protect a historic watermill in Huntingdonshire. The project aims to safeguard Houghton Mill, one of the country’s few surviving watermills, from the pressures of age, weather, and seasonal flooding. Funding has come from the Wolfson Foundation, contributing to the estimated £120,000 cost of the scheme. Isabel Sedgwick, visitor operations manager at Houghton Mill, said: "Houghton Mill is a remarkable place, and we’re incredibly fortunate to be able to care for a building with such a rich history while keeping it working for visitors today. "This project is about making sure we can continue to share the sights, sounds and stories of the mill for many years to come. "The support from the Wolfson Foundation is helping us tackle some really important repairs and protect the mill’s character for future generations." External Repairs - Houghton Mill (Image: National Trust Images Mike Selby) The first phase of work will address the north and east sides of the mill, following detailed surveys that identified urgent repairs. A key focus will be the conservation of the north lucam, the overhanging timber hoist once used to lift grain into the mill. Specialist craftspeople will stabilise and repair the historic structure using traditional methods. The project will also include roof repairs, replacement of lead flashings, and restoration of weatherboarding, windows, and dormers. A Cambridgeshire-based firm, Brown and Ralph Ltd, is carrying out the work. The conservation is expected to be completed by January 2027, with the mill due to reopen to the public at Easter. Paul Ramsbottom, chief executive at the Wolfson Foundation, said: "Houghton Mill is an important part of our industrial heritage – there has been an active mill on this site for over 1,000 years. "We are pleased that our long-standing partnership with the National Trust can help support this essential restoration."

Isaiah Idris, then aged 17, was attacked on a DLR train in London in the early hours of November 1 last year, Cambridge Crown Court was told. Anthony Williams, 33, denies 14 counts of attempted murder: ten of them in relation to an incident on an LNER train in Huntingdon, three said to have happened in Peterborough and one relating to the incident on the DLR train. Earlier this month, Williams pleaded guilty to 10 counts of wounding with intent relating to the LNER train incident, the wounding with intent of a man at Pontoon Dock DLR station in the early hours of November 1 and to the wounding with intent of a 14-year-old boy in Peterborough on October 31, as well as a number of other offences. In a video-recorded interview played to jurors on November 3, a witness who was on the train said that the attacker "was specifically targeting a boy". She said: "There was nobody to help, we were very much on our own. "We didn't have anything to defend us. "It was a very scary moment." The witness added that it appeared to her that the attacker had "a psychotic episode". She said: "He was seeing things that weren't clear to the rest of us. "The attacker for some reason thought that this boy was the devil and wanted to harm him." The witness added that the attack was "completely out of nowhere". Judge Mr Justice Calver earlier told jurors that whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question, but they must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals when he carried out the attacks. The trial continues.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Eight sieges for every battle: new exhibition reveals Civil War reality
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Sieges, not battles, take centre stage in a new exhibition in Huntingdon. The Cromwell Museum's latest display, Besieged: Sieges of the Civil War, reveals the overlooked reality of the English Civil Wars. While just 28 major battles took place in England between 1642 and 1648, 189 locations were besieged, and more than 1,000 fortified sites could be found across the British Isles. Stuart Orme, curator of the Cromwell Museum, said: "When people think of the Civil Wars they tend to think of the great battles like Edgehill, Naseby, or Worcester, but there were eight sieges for every one of these. "Places all over Britain and Ireland were fortified and then besieged as part of this brutal conflict, dragging many thousands of ordinary people into the front line of the conflict and leaving scars on the landscape and many of our historic buildings that can still be seen today." The exhibition, which runs from November 3, 2026, to April 4, 2027, explores why so many towns and castles were fortified, how earthwork defences were constructed, and how siege tactics developed throughout the conflict. It also examines the roles of those involved, from engineers and soldiers to civilians and women who defended their homes. Visitors can view original artefacts including siege plans, musket balls, a cannonball from the siege of Sheffield Castle, and a scale model of Earith Bulwark. The only surviving Civil War siege helmet in the UK is also on display. Case studies of key locations feature throughout the exhibition, including Oxford, Bristol, Leicester, Skipton Castle, Pontefract, and Hull. Entry is free, though donations are welcome. The museum is open Tuesday to Sunday from 10am to 3.30pm. More information is available at cromwellmuseum.org.

The 27-year-old hid behind a nearby van, leaving his front-seat passenger trapped in the vehicle with serious injuries. Members of the public who witnessed the collision chased Ionescu and detained him, before officers arrived and arrested him. Ionescu’s 27-year-old passenger suffered a brain injury, multiple fractures and was in a medically induced coma for two weeks as a result of the crash. He admitting to causing serious injury by dangerous driving, using a motor vehicle without insurance, and using a motor vehicle without a valid license. Sentencing, Judge Andrew Hurst, commented on the fact that the victim is now unable to work and is "confined by his own fragile mental health". Detective Constable Lauren Byrne, from the force’s Serious Collision Investigation Unit, said: "Firstly my thoughts go out to the victim and his family. "This crash has had an extensive impact on them all and I wish the victim a speedy recovery. "This was a serious, but completely preventable crash, caused by Ionescu’s careless and reckless driving. "The impact of the collision goes far beyond the victim’s physical injuries - he will likely suffer from the ongoing emotional and psychological impact, especially as he is unable to work or continue his life as it was prior to the crash. "The fact Ionescu tried to flee the scene is cowardly and shows his lack of remorse and compassion for the victim, so I am pleased he is now behind bars and will be held accountable for his actions."

For years, a flaw in the benefits system meant that those who tried to work more hours, take on extra shifts or do better paid work were often left financially worse off. Now, new changes to Housing Benefit rules mean residents aged 16-25 will keep more of what they earn.  Around 30,000 young people living in supported housing receive Housing Benefit. Centrepoint welcomed the new changes by hosting a visit from Department for Work and Pensions Minister Stephen Timms MP to one of its East London supported accommodation services.  There, the Minister met Sadaf, a 19-year-old resident who talked about her hopes for the future. Throughout her time with Centrepoint, Sadaf has overcome difficulties but remains committed to her long-term aspiration to study medicine and build a better future for herself. Like many young people transitioning towards independence, Sadaf viewed employment as a positive step towards self-sufficiency. Her intention in seeking work was not only to gain financial independence but also to fund her education and create future opportunities. Sadaf said: "Working made me feel like I was moving forward. I finally felt like I was doing something productive and taking responsibility for my future." However, gaining employment triggered a significant reduction in Sadaf’s Housing Benefit entitlement. The reduction created a substantial gap between her accommodation costs and available income, resulting in rent arrears that eventually approached £5,000. Rather than creating greater financial stability, employment created financial uncertainty.  The impact extended far beyond finances alone. Housing uncertainty affected her future plans, educational opportunities, relationships and overall wellbeing. Now that the system is working better, Sadaf is actively seeking employment again.  She said: "There were times when it felt like working made everything harder, but I still believe education and employment are the way forward for me. I want to build a future where I can support myself, help other people and become the person I've always wanted to be.” Seyi Obakin OBE, Chief Executive Officer at Centrepoint, said: “This is a landmark win for young people, and we commend the government for getting this change over the line.  For too long, young people in supported housing, particularly those at the start of their careers, have had their ambitions blocked by a system that punished them for working harder. "This is what it looks like when the system works for young people, and we hope it creates a smoother transition from benefits into work for them.” An incredible evening was had on Tuesday 13th October at London's Bloomsbury Ballroom for the annual Centrepoint Awards. (Image: devantayj) The event, hosted by broadcaster and long-time Centrepoint supporter Gaby Roslin, celebrated the achievements of inspirational young people who have been supported by Centrepoint and, with the foundation of a safe and stable home, have gone on to establish themselves in their careers, interests and relationships. The night was opened by the London Cabaret Club's resident singer Sofia Klimovsky, who got the crowd in the celebratory mood before the award winners were announced. Videos showcasing the young people's stories brought tears to the eyes of many attendees. The awards included categories like Rising Star, won by a young person whose aim is to build the next unicorn and feature on the Forbes 30 Under 30 list, and the Arts and Educational Excellence Award, won by a young care leaver who has just started his first year at Oxford University studying Philosophy, Politics and Economics. Centrepoint were joined on the evening by some of their longstanding partners, including award sponsors the cardfactory Foundation, ASOS Foundation and Clarksons. Seyi Obakin OBE, Chief Executive at Centrepoint, said: "These awards are a poignant reminder that we are surrounded by talented young people, but the opportunities are not always there or equal. The success of the winners shows what happens when young people are given not just an opportunity to shine, but the support to do it." Following World Homelessness Day last month, contemporary artist Hugh Miller has dedicated his latest oil-on-canvas painting to Centrepoint. (Image: Anne-Marie Doohan) As a young aspiring artist, Hugh did a lot of chalk drawings on pavements near London’s famous landmarks and met inspiring young homeless people along the way. His early years led him to take an interest in the charity’s work. Miller’s Houses of Parliament oil-on-canvas painting is the latest in a series designed to "celebrate the aesthetic beauty of cities in the United Kingdom". The artist was given a rare chance to access the Speaker's Terrace in Parliament last month to complete a section of his painting. The visit attracted the attention of cross-party MPs and raised the profile of Centrepoint and youth homelessness in Parliament. His latest painting - which will take another eight months to finish - will form part of his Centrepoint series collection, with all proceeds from the artwork going to the charity to help end youth homelessness. To find out more about Hugh Miller and his work, visit www.hughmillerart.co.uk Last year, over 118,000 young people faced homelessness. That’s one young person every four minutes. At a time of life when most of their peers are trying new things and taking their first steps into adulthood, these young people found themselves alone and afraid, and unsure where to turn. It doesn’t have to be like this.  With the right support at the right time, these young people can escape homelessness or avoid it altogether. At Centrepoint, we provide more than a bed for the night. We provide a safe place to rebuild, support into education and work, and the confidence to believe in a better future. Youth homelessness is not inevitable. With the right help at the right time, it can be prevented and it can be ended. Our mission is to end youth homelessness – and you can help us. Whether it’s running a marathon or holding a sleep out, you, your friends, family and co-workers can join our movement to end youth homelessness and give vulnerable young people a brighter future. To find out more, donate or get involved, please visit our website http://www.centrepoint.org.uk/newspaper Thirty-seven young people experiencing homelessness had their deaths registered in England and Wales last year, according to the latest figures released by the Office for National Statistics. Of the 37 deaths of young people aged between 16-24 years old, 29 were male and eight were female.  This marks a 2.8% rise from the year before. Overall, 974 people died while experiencing homelessness in England and Wales in 2025.  This marks a 77% increase compared to when the figures were first collated in 2013, rising from 550 to 974.  London had the highest estimated number of deaths in English regions, followed by the North-West and the South-East. Matt Bawden, Director of Progression Housing at Centrepoint said: "Even one death of someone experiencing homelessness is too many. These sobering figures represent countless individual tragedies but are also indicative of a system that is failing. The need to work collaboratively to fix that system and to deliver high-quality housing and support is more urgent than ever.  We believe that every young person should be given the opportunity to lead a fulfilling, healthy life where they can realise their potential."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Andy Burnham hails local news as 'critical' as PM backs Journalism Matters campaign

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has spoken out in support of the Journalism Matters campaign, emphasising the crucial role of news media in democracy, accountability, and community life. The campaign, coordinated by the News Media Association, highlights the value of journalism and will run from November 2 to 8. Mr Burnham said: "I am proud to support this year's Journalism Matters campaign, which is about recognising journalism not as a nice-to-have, but as part of the national infrastructure of a healthy country and democracy. "It holds power to account, strengthens our resilience and connects people to the places they call home." He stressed the importance of local journalism in the Government’s devolution plans, saying that returning power to communities must go hand in hand with local accountability. Mr Burnham said: "Local reporters are the people sitting in council chambers, courts and planning meetings, asking the questions that need to be asked. "They shine a light on decisions made in people’s name and give communities a voice." He also highlighted the vital role of trusted journalism during times of crisis. Mr Burnham said: "At moments when communities are at their most vulnerable, good local journalism can bring people together and separate fact from fiction. "We saw that after Southport and, more recently, in Belfast, when trusted reporters challenged lies and misinformation being spread online." This year’s Journalism Matters campaign will see the news industry come together to celebrate the role journalism plays underpinning national infrastructure. A recent global report by UNESCO found that countries with a strong, independent press enjoy significant economic and security benefits. News Media Association Chief Executive Theo Bamber (Image: NMA) Theo Bamber, chief executive of the News Media Association, welcomed Mr Burnham’s support but called for practical action. Mr Bamber said: "The Prime Minister is absolutely right to point to the critical role that independent journalism plays in our society and particularly how important local news will be to the success of his own sprawling devolution agenda. "Now, the support shown by the Prime Minister must turn into real action that demonstrates the government understands the changed environment that journalists and news publishers are operating in and strengthens their ability to do more of what they’re brilliant at—chasing stories, uncovering the truth and holding power to account." He called on the Government to protect and promote a diverse media ecosystem. The Journalism Matters campaign runs from November 2 to 8, 2026.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Andy Burnham - 'Journalism is a vital part of our national infrastructure'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Too much power in this country has flowed one way: towards Westminster and away from the places where people actually live their lives. This government is changing that. We are putting power and resources back into the hands of communities. Because I want people in local communities to have a bigger say over the decisions that shape their area. But with greater local power must come local accountability. And that is why local journalism matters. Local reporters are the people sitting in council chambers, courts and planning meetings, asking the questions that need to be asked. They shine a light on decisions made in people’s name and give communities a voice. But their role goes much further than holding power to account. At moments when communities are at their most vulnerable, good local journalism can bring people together and separate fact from fiction. We saw that after Southport and, more recently, in Belfast, when trusted reporters challenged lies and misinformation being spread online. And I saw its power myself as Mayor of Greater Manchester. When the Manchester Evening News campaigned for free bus travel for homeless children living in temporary accommodation, it didn't just report what was wrong, it brought people together to get behind the change that was needed. That is exactly what this year's Journalism Matters campaign is about: recognising journalism not as a nice-to-have, but as part of the national infrastructure of a healthy country and democracy. It holds power to account, strengthens our resilience and connects people to the places they call home. And yet access to good local journalism is becoming increasingly unequal. Ninety-five per cent of adults access local news, but the market alone will not sustain it everywhere. Up to 37 local authority districts now have no dedicated outlet of their own, leaving as many as 4.4 million people in local "news deserts", disproportionately in some of our most deprived urban communities. I've spent my career arguing that where you live should not determine the opportunities you get. I believe exactly the same principle applies to information. People in every part of the country deserve trusted local news, scrutiny of those in power and a strong voice for their community. Through our Local Media Action Plan, the new Local News Fund will provide up to £12 million over two years. This is part of a wider package of measures we're delivering to support local journalism. This year, local newspapers, websites and independent television and radio stations in England and Wales have been able to bid for up to £125,000 to invest in their future, whether that's new technology, multimedia journalism, reaching younger audiences or finding new ways to bring in revenue. We have also made up to £275,000 available for projects that strengthen the wider industry. And in the second year, £1 million will help communities bring local journalism back where it has disappeared, whether by reviving a dormant title, expanding a neighbouring publication or establishing a community-owned outlet. We’re doing this because devolution cannot simply mean moving power from one set of politicians to another. It has to mean giving people more of a say. For that to work, they need to know what is being done in their name. They need journalists willing to ask difficult questions, expose wrongdoing, challenge misinformation and champion their communities. That is why I am proud to support this year's Journalism Matters campaign, and why this government will work to ensure trusted local journalism remains at the heart of communities across our country.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Why the UK government must act to protect trusted local journalism
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Where does a news story come from? A scandal exposed, a failure revealed, a decision brought into the open that someone would rather have kept private. Behind each is work we rarely see. We read the story, take it in and move on. In short, we take journalism for granted. Someone had to find that story, check it, check it again, and then tell it. That takes skill, experience and painstaking work, sometimes over hours, sometimes over days, weeks, months or years. The published story is the bit we all see, and if we want that to continue, we must protect the people and the industry that makes it possible. This year’s Journalism Matters campaign is a chance for us to reflect carefully on what journalism does for all of us, and what we would lose if we didn’t have it. In an article launching this year’s campaign, Prime Minister Andy Burnham cites the enormous benefits that independent journalism delivers for our society and the critical importance of local news media to the devolution agenda. He is absolutely right to do so. Journalism is part of the national infrastructure we all rely on, and the benefits it delivers go far beyond the stories themselves. A global report published by UNESCO earlier this year found a raft of economic and security benefits connected to journalism in countries with an ecosystem which supports an independent free press. So how do we make sure more journalism can happen? It’s clear that there is plenty the government can do to strengthen the conditions that the industry operates in and it must use this opportunity to affect real change. In an article launching this year’s campaign, Prime Minister Andy Burnham cites the enormous benefits that independent journalism delivers for our society and the critical importance of local news media to the devolution agenda (Image: Carlos Jasso/Press Association) This should start with digital markets, and creating an ecosystem which can support and maintain a plural and diverse range of media outlets. This increases user choice and allows publishers that invest in reporting to get a fair return for their work. Meta, always ready and willing to play the role of the tech giant bully, recently launched an assault on journalism with its attempt to force publishers and other businesses to hand over all their content to train its AI products. It was a move right out of the tech platform playbook - bury the crucial detail in a ton of paperwork and then feign disbelief and surprise at the horrified reaction from the business community. This can’t continue and, if the government supports journalism in the way the Prime Minister has outlined, it must back the Competition and Markets Authority to the hilt. The CMA is tasked with making the tech platforms play fair, and to do this job effectively it needs full-throated political support. Nothing else will do. But getting the platforms to play fair is just the start. Government must also make sure that its own policies support journalism, not undermine it. The news prominence regime, as proposed in the Media Green Paper, will have a damaging and distortive effect on the news media landscape if implemented in its current form. Inevitably, local news will be hit particularly hard and the lack of clarity on how platform compliance will be enforced does little to boost our confidence that the policy won’t deliver myriad dangerous, unintended consequences. Ministers must also ensure that the BBC Charter Renewal results in a BBC which partners with the commercial sector rather than competing aggressively against it. And, at a local level, transparency must be maintained as power is shifted out of Westminster to the regions, including by keeping public notices in highly trusted local news media. As the noise around us gets louder and more complex, we still need people intent on establishing the truth. The real, actual truth. This is what journalism does, and this is why bold government support for the industry should be non-negotiable. Without it, we’ll lose our ability to understand the world around us and be consigned to a world where decisions that happen behind closed doors never see the light of day and stories that change lives are never told. That is not an acceptable future for a modern-day democracy such as ours. The Journalism Matters campaign runs from November 2 to 8, 2026.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: One million people warned to act before major UK landline change
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: One million people risk losing landline phone access unless they upgrade to digital lines The warning comes as the UK prepares to retire its old analogue phone network and complete the switch to digital lines. BT-owned Openreach are phasing out the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN), a system in place since the 1870s, with a full shutdown planned for January 31, 2027. James Lilley, director of customer migrations at Openreach, said: "It’s very hard to get [customers] to read and react and do something." Moving to digital lines is expected to provide a more reliable service, better-quality calls and improved blocking of unwanted calls. Despite these benefits, around one million residents and businesses remain on the old network. Those who do not upgrade in time could lose service or be transferred to a basic emergency phone system without features like voicemail. The UK government says the transition is necessary due to the declining reliability of the copper-based PSTN, and Ofcom has said most users are unlikely to experience significant disruption. The original switch-off date was set for December 31, 2025, but concerns about the impact on vulnerable and rural users, particularly those relying on telecare alarms, led to a revised timeline. Under the PSTN Charter, providers have agreed not to migrate customers using telecare devices unless their equipment is confirmed to be compatible with digital lines. Telecom companies, including BT, are supplying vulnerable customers with free back-up battery packs to ensure phones remain operational during power outages. Read More Unlike the digital system, the traditional PSTN does not depend on mains electricity and will continue to function during a power cut. Openreach has stated that there will not be a single day when all customers lose service. Tens of thousands of customers are reportedly switching to the new system each week, Lilley said a rise in scams had made it harder to get consumers to respond to letters about the change. Have you switched to a digital phone service yet? Let us know in the comments.

Piyush said: "Before this, I worked as an accountant, where success was measured in financial figures. "Now, those numbers are replaced by student outcomes and the difference we’re making to young people’s lives." The business supports children who struggle with mainstream education, including those with special educational needs and mental health difficulties. Piyush recalled the progress of one student who was selective mute, particularly in educational settings. He said: "At the start, they found it a challenge communicating with their tutor. "After several months, they gradually began talking to their peers and became more comfortable around our team and even volunteered to welcome new students." His wife Smita joined the business five years later, bringing more than 20 years of primary education experience. She said: "I’ve never seen Piyush happier in his work, and I’ve learnt so much from him too. "It’s been lovely to bring my expertise into the business in order for us to support even more local students." The couple’s two sons have also been involved, with their eldest now working full-time, making it a true family business. Smita said: "All the relationships we’ve built over the years have been amazing. "Our staff and tutors have been especially important for us, and we couldn’t have achieved what we have done without them." Piyush said he is proud of how far the business has come. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A knifeman who stabbed 10 people on a London-bound train was described by a boy he stabbed the day before as having ‘his eyes wide open like he was on something’, a court heard. Several people were injured on an LNER train from Doncaster to London King's Cross on November 1, 2025 which was forced to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon, where CCTV of the knife attack was shown in court. Anthony Williams, 33, denies ten counts of attempted murder relating to the incident. He also denies the attempted murders of three people in Peterborough on October 31, and of a 17-year-old boy at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London in the early hours of November 1. His trial opened at Cambridge Crown Court on Wednesday, October 28. Judge Mr Justice Calver earlier told jurors at Cambridge Crown Court that whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question but they must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals when he carried out the attacks. Cambridge Crown Court (Image: LDR) A 14-year-old boy, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, told police in a video-recorded interview played in court on Friday that he was stabbed on Halloween last year. He said he was going to go trick or treating with friends and was walking over a bridge behind an Asda store in Peterborough when a man ‘just pulled out a knife and stabbed me’. He described the person as "this random guy" and said it happened shortly after 7pm as he was walking with a friend, along a footbridge near Henry Penn Walk. "We’ve pretty much got right up close to him as we’re walking past him and he’s pulled out a knife and just stabbed me," the boy said. He added: "I didn’t feel like he was mentally sane. "His eyes were wide open like he was on something." He said the man "shouted something, I don’t know what he said". "I jumped back a little when I saw he was reaching for something and I started running," the boy said. He continued: "He was screaming something. "My friend said he was shouting something like 'are you involved?'." He said he and his friend ran and hid in bushes and called the police. Asked what force the man had used, the boy said: "It was strong, like it pushed me back a little bit. "He was using his full force, his arm was fully stretched out." He said the man was dressed in black and he believed the knife was around 10 inches long. A group of police officers stand close to the emergency equipment left behind after an incident at Huntingdon train station (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire) The boy’s friend, who also cannot be identified for legal reasons, said the man who he described as a black male had shouted "are you two involved?". In a statement read in court, he said the man "pulled out a large knife" from a rucksack, describing the knife as a "type of zombie knife or Rambo-style knife". Williams is accused of the attempted murders of two others in Peterborough on October 31, Dawid Taborski and William Ogelby. Mr Taborski said in a video interview that he had been on his way to a rave when a man he had never seen before "kept saying are you involved, are you involved?" He said he "didn’t know what he (Williams) was on about, I was really confused" and he initially thought it may have been "a Halloween thing". "As soon as he took that knife out I ran," he added. "It happened so quickly." The scene at Huntingdon train station after the incident last year (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire) Detective Constable Ryan Burke said he was on high-visibility foot patrols when Mr Taborski approached him by Charters bar in Peterborough and told him "someone had attempted to stab him but they hadn’t been able to do so". The officer said in a statement that Mr Taborski told him the man had "brandished a long silver blade" and "lunged attempting to stab him". Mr Ogelby told police he had been walking to a cashpoint to get money out when a man walking towards him said "wagwan" to him, which he understood to be a greeting. "I’ve said (it) back and he’s pulled a knife out and tried to stab me three times in my stomach and once in my chest," he said in a video interview played to jurors. He said he ran home "as fast as my legs would carry me" and "checked myself to see if I was bleeding – I wasn’t bleeding". "I thought he was going to kill me," he said. Jurors were shown a photo of Mr Ogelby wearing a jacket which had what prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC described as a "knife cut" to it. The trial continues, with jurors asked to return to court on Monday, November 2.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Are you owed £8,000? HMRC is sending out 311,000 new letters to people due money
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Thousands of people - mostly mums - are due money back from historic State Pension errors, as HMRC has sent out 311,000 letters to people who could be missing out. The letters are aimed at parents and carers who may be missing Home Responsibilities Protection (HRP) from their National Insurance records, potentially leaving them with a lower State Pension than they should receive. HMRC says the latest mailout will run until the end of March 2027, with 215,000 letters going to people who have already reached State Pension age. The department says the letters will include a claim form for the first time, making it easier for people to apply for HRP without having to download or print the paperwork themselves. Official figures show that more than 25,000 people have had HRP added to their National Insurance records since HMRC began sending letters in September 2023. Nearly all were above State Pension age, and they have received a share of more than £100million in pension arrears. The average arrears payment has been around £8,000, although the amount an individual receives depends on their circumstances and whether they are eligible. Home Responsibilities Protection was introduced to help protect the State Pension entitlement of parents and carers who took time away from paid employment to raise children or care for others. People who claimed Child Benefit between 1978 and May 2000 may be affected if HRP is missing from their National Insurance records. During this period, people claiming Child Benefit were not always required to provide their National Insurance number. HMRC says that while HRP was automatically added to the records of people who supplied their NI number, some people who did not provide it may have missed out. HRP reduced the number of qualifying years a person needed on their National Insurance record to receive a full basic State Pension. The scheme was replaced by National Insurance credits in 2010, meaning people who started claiming Child Benefit after that date will not be affected by this particular issue. HMRC and the Department for Work and Pensions have been contacting people who may be missing HRP for the past three years. The department says it has already sent 340,000 letters inviting people to check whether they qualify. Following a successful trial of a revised letter, a further 311,000 are being sent out by next March. The latest letters will include the CF411 claim form, which recipients can complete with their personal details and return by post. HMRC says checking eligibility online remains the quickest option for people who can use the service. Claimants can use the GOV.UK eligibility tool to check whether they may be missing HRP and submit a claim online. Myrtle Lloyd, HMRC's chief customer officer, said: “We're hopeful that by including the claim form in the letter, people are more likely to fill it in, send it back and find out quickly and easily whether their entitlement will increase on retirement or, if they've reached State Pension age, they're owed a payout.” Pensioners with income up to the value of the full new state pension (to be £13,040 from April 2027) will not pay tax. Mechanism not stated, I suspect there will be an effective increased pensioner allowance with a clawback for income above that. More when I know more. #Budget2026 — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) October 28, 2026 HMRC says people do not need to use a third-party company to check their eligibility or submit an application, meaning they can avoid paying a firm a share of any arrears they receive. Anyone who needs help can call the National Insurance Helpline on 0300 200 3500. Further support is also available online. Research published by the Department for Work and Pensions in May 2025, based on work carried out by Verian, examined why some people did not respond to the earlier campaign. The research identified several possible reasons, including fears that letters could be scams, confusion about the terminology used and uncertainty about whether the recipient was eligible for money. Some people struggled to understand how HRP related to their own circumstances. Others were concerned that making a claim could leave them worse off or lacked confidence in completing the process online. The findings highlight the challenge of reaching people who may be entitled to arrears but do not realise that the letters apply to them. Elaine Walker, director of AskRose, said: “The government's own research tells us exactly why so many people didn't respond last time. "Letters didn't arrive, people didn't think they applied to them, they couldn't see what they stood to gain, and many understandably feared the letter was a scam.” Recommended reading: HMRC is encouraging people who have retired or are approaching retirement to check their National Insurance records for gaps that could affect their State Pension entitlement. The main steps are: Not everyone who checks their record will be entitled to arrears. The amount, if any, will depend on their National Insurance history and individual circumstances.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Wrong council tax band? What it could mean for your £100 bank energy payment
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Around 20 million households will receive a £100 energy payment this winter under plans announced by Chancellor John Healey in the Budget. Households in council tax bands A to D in England are expected to receive the money through the council tax system from January 2027, most likely paid directly into their bank accounts, according to Martin Lewis. The scheme will cost £2.6 billion, with funding also being provided to devolved administrations so they can introduce similar support elsewhere in the UK. Mr Healey said the payment would help families cope with rising energy bills during the coldest months. He told the Commons: “This winter, for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D, I am announcing a £100 energy payment for households, paid directly into people’s bank accounts to deal with rising energy bills. “That’s a £2.6 billion scheme to take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people though to the spring.” Mr Healey urged devolved administrations to “do the same and give people of all nations in the UK breathing space on their energy bills this winter”. But how can you tell if you are eligible for the £100 payment, and what happens if you think you are in the wrong Council Tax band? It's not clear what the deadline will be for this yet, but Martin Lewis has previously shared his advice about what to do if you think your council tax bill is too high. The consumer champion explained how two simple checks can lower your Council Tax bill this year and forever - but it has to be done with care. He explained: "Up to 400,000 people in England and Scotland are in the wrong band, a higher band, and I've been looking at how you can challenge this since 2007. "Effectively, what you need to do is go onto voa.gov.uk to check your council tax band of an identical property, or if it's Scotland, saa.gov.uk. "If you're in a higher band, the name is in identical properties, then you need to work out what bad you would have been in 1991 if that shows you had a band. "Then you need to look at going forward to get your band lower." 'What can you do if your council tax is going up?' - @susannareid100@MartinSLewis explains what you can do, as he points out that many people could be missing out on discounts. pic.twitter.com/VkucbcAS2K — Good Morning Britain (@GMB) April 1, 2025 Council tax bands were drawn up in 1991 based on drive-by valuations of homes at that time. They are subsequently out of date and many people may actually be in the wrong council tax band. In 2007, financial expert and Money Saving Expert founder Martin Lewis started a campaign to show how you might be able to challenge it. The Check and Challenge approach made huge headlines that year and many people have been able to use it to save themselves money since then. Here’s how it works: You can find out more about Martin Lewis' method - read it carefully before making any challenge. The Check and Challenge method has two steps, and it is absolutely vital you do both before deciding whether to get your council tax banding assessed. Step one involves finding out if your band is higher than neighbours in similar or identical properties. Thankfully, this is public information, so you don’t need to go and ask them. England valuation bands are listed here, and the valuations are here. The band of every property in Scotland can be found on the Scottish Assessors Association website. All domestic properties in Wales are put into 9 tax bands (bands A to I). The tax bands are based on how much a home and the land it is on is worth. The Valuation Office Agency (VOA) values properties for Council Tax purposes. They are the government's property experts for Wales and England. When comparing your band with your neighbours’, make sure the properties are as close in size and value as possible, and would have been in 1991. If neighbours in similar properties are in a lower band than you, then you may have a claim. However, you could land yourself in bother if you don’t do the next step. If your band is different to your neighbours’ and you’re in similar properties, then it could be that their band is wrong and not yours, and you could actually end up landing them with a larger bill if you appeal - you risk becoming an unpopular neighbour. So here is an important next step before deciding to challenge… A post shared by Martin Lewis (@martinlewismse) A second crucial step is to estimate what your home was worth in 1991, as that's when and how the council tax bands were defined. If you bought your house after 1991, you can simply use its price and date of sale to do this. If you rent or bought earlier, you'll need to find an estimated price. It's also worth doing this with similar neighbouring properties. To find a price quickly, you can use a website which offers free historic sales price information such as Zoopla or Rightmove. Enter your street name and it'll tell you the prices of all properties sold there since 2000. Find the most recent sale price of a similar property to yours in your street. Now note down both the price and the date of sale. Once you have that information, you can use it to estimate what your property would've been worth back in 1991, and what band it's in. There is a calculator you can use here, which uses house price data from Nationwide. Recommended reading: This will only give a rough indication, but it gives an idea. You may be in a higher band than your neighbours because they’re in the wrong band, not you. In that case, if you appeal and stay in the same band, but their band is increased, you might not make many friends. Now you've worked out roughly what your property was worth in 1991, you can compare this to a table here to see what band you should have been put in, based on that home value. If you're convinced your property band is unfair after all the checks, you could challenge it. In Scotland, the SAA deals with council tax bands. Enter your postcode in the council tax bands search box on the homepage. Select your property from the list. If you want to challenge the banding, click on "Make a proposal". You can then fill in an online form which will be sent to your local assessor, who will contact you. But do remember, you can’t just ask for your band to be lowered, only for it to be reassessed, which means it could be moved up or down. This is why it’s important to do both checks and think about whether you’ve added an extension to your home or bought extra land or outbuildings.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Drivers warned over viral fuel-saving petrol pump trick that experts say won't work
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A motoring expert has debunked a viral fuel-saving tip making the rounds on social media. The so-called "slow squeeze" method, gaining traction on TikTok and Instagram, claims that gently squeezing the fuel pump trigger while filling up will get motorists more petrol or diesel for their money by reducing air bubbles and foam in the tank. The theory has gained attention online, with one TikTok post under the tag "Fuel Prices UK" reaching almost 250,000 views. However, Graham Conway, managing director at Select Car Leasing, said the advice is misguided and unlikely to deliver any real benefit. Mr Conway said: "The ‘slow squeeze’ hack is popular on platforms like TikTok and Instagram, but you’re highly unlikely to see any real benefit. "Modern fuel pumps have clever systems designed to prevent air or vapour from affecting the measurement of fuel that comes out of the nozzle. "You can’t somehow game the system with the trickle method. "The only thing that might happen is that you take ages to fill up, angering other drivers patiently waiting behind you." The creator of the trend argued that filling up too quickly creates bubbles in the tank, similar to pouring a fizzy drink too fast. Despite Mr Conway’s explanation, some social media users remain convinced the method works. One commenter said: "I always fill up holding the lever halfway and my petrol lasts way longer. "By holding the lever in all the way in we are paying for a lot of air too." Another claimed that it could "make a litre or two difference in a fill up." Mr Conway also used the opportunity to warn against another common mistake at the pump: topping off the tank after the nozzle clicks. He said: "Squeezing the fuel pump trigger after the nozzle has automatically clicked off, also known as ‘topping off,’ might seem like a sensible way to squeeze a little extra fuel into your tank. "But doing so repeatedly could actually end up damaging your car, potentially leaving you facing an expensive repair bill. "Most modern petrol cars are fitted with an evaporative emissions control system, which captures petrol vapours from the fuel tank and stores them in a charcoal canister, preventing them from escaping into the atmosphere. "However, if you continue forcing petrol into an already full tank, liquid fuel can enter parts of this system that are designed to handle vapour rather than liquid. "This can damage the charcoal canister and other components, potentially triggering an engine management warning light and even contributing to an MOT failure. "Although diesel vehicles generally don't use the same charcoal-canister system, overfilling can still cause fuel to spill or interfere with the tank's venting arrangements. Read More "Repairs to a damaged evaporative emissions system can run into hundreds of pounds, depending on the vehicle and the extent of the damage. "So, while an occasional extra squeeze isn't guaranteed to cause problems, it's best to stop filling when the nozzle automatically clicks off. "That way, you can avoid the risk of an unnecessary repair bill." The warnings come as UK motorists continue to look for ways to cut costs at the pump amid persistently high fuel prices. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Village’s only café scales back hours
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridge village’s only café has been warned it will ‘run out of money’ if it doesn’t make major changes. The Cherry Branch café in Cherry Hinton has faced major finanial issues in its first year. Cambridge City Council owns the building, which includes the library, with the kitchen, café and meeting rooms rented by the charity Cherry Hinton Community Benefit Society (CHCBS). Kate Jones, one of the cafe’s trustees, said a business consultant told them, “there’s no two ways about it – you’re going to run out of money”. The 51-year-old said: “It’s difficult when something like this happens – which nobody wanted – and understandably people were upset.” The group said they were required to pay a facilities management charge of £32,000 per year as part of the lease agreement with the city council. This covered building maintenance such as cleaning, gardening and repairs but left the group unable to hire their own contractors meaning they had to do some tasks themselves. Ms Jones said: “That contract meant we were paying a lot of money as a small charity, bearing in mind this is our first year.” The CHCBS also hired a catering manager as a contractor instead of an employee – which would have been cheaper – as they said the council wanted their contract to be terminated more easily if the lease ended. They said the fees for this on top of the facilities management charge were too much as they could only make money from café sales and hiring out meeting rooms. The group took the decision to end the catering manager’s contract and the council has frozen the facilities management charge until March 2027. Ms Jones said: “What we were finding was trustees were doing day to day work in the hub – including the chair actually cleaning the toilets. That meant our ability to have that thinking time was taken away – every time there’s a regular booking someone needs to be here. Now we need to focus on making the hub sustainable – the council have been super helpful and have offered us a hub manager.” The cafe will now be able to stay open with scaled back hours after closing temporarily. A meeting was held this month to reassure Cherry Hinton residents that it is not closing. Ms Jones added: “I think the meeting was good because we were able to just address some of the things people had heard that weren’t right. “We wanted to reassure people the hub is still here, the café is still open, and the trustees are absolutely committed and working extremely hard to deliver this community facility to the people of Cherry Hinton.” Cllr Mike Todd-Jones, the council’s cabinet member for communities, said: “I’m determined to work in partnership with the Cherry Hinton Community Benefit Society to help put the Hub on a sustainable financial footing for the future. “Through workshops with the CHCBS, and support from local councillors and the council team, we will work hard together to develop a plan that means the Hub will be in a strong position to serve the people of Cherry Hinton for many years to come.” Be sure to set CambridgeshireLive as your preferred news source to make sure you never miss a story. Simply click here and tick the box. A spokesperson for Cambridge City Council said they were helping to support the CHCBS “through this tricky period”. They said: “Cherry Hinton Hub and Library is a vital focus for the local community and Cambridge City Council is fully committed to its success having redeveloped the former library at a cost of over £1.5 million – funding from the City Council and S106 developer contributions. “The first year or two operating a community facility and establishing a café can be really tough. Maximising income from room hire and the café in this early period is difficult and, combined with the expenses associated with opening new premises, this has proved financially challenging. “The city council has already stepped in to support the CHCBS, suspending facilities management charges from June 2026 to March 2027 alongside other financial help that should save CHCBS around £30,000. The city council is also proposing to pay for an interim Hub manager.” The cafe will be open from 10am to 2pm on Wednesdays only.

Grantchester has long been associated with literary figures including Rupert Brooke, while its centuries-old Church of St Andrew & St Mary stands at the heart of the community. The village gained international recognition through the ITV drama Grantchester, which introduced its idyllic streets to television audiences around the world. For those seeking a quintessential English village experience, Grantchester delivers in abundance. With historic pubs, charming architecture and a setting that feels timeless, it is easy to see why so many people consider this riverside gem a must-visit location. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A university scientist living in Cambridgeshire has been named as one of 69 people killed in a deadly high-speed train crash in Spain. Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling on one of the trains involved in the collision near Urda, south of Madrid, on Wednesday (October 28). Her death was confirmed by the Centre for Research in Molecular Medicine and Chronic Diseases (CiMUS) three days after the disaster. In a statement posted online, the centre, based in Santiago de Compostela, paid tribute to the "brilliant young researcher". At least 69 people have been killed in the rail disaster (Image: Manu Fernandez/AP) It reads: "The CiMUS community would like to express its support and deepest sympathies to our dear PI María José Alonso, following the death of her niece, Marta Shahbazi, in the railway accident that occurred on 28 October. "Marta was a brilliant young researcher, Group Leader at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology and Affiliate Associate Professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute, University of Cambridge. "At this difficult time, we extend our heartfelt condolences to María José and her family, as well as to Marta Shahbazi’s colleagues and collaborators. "Our thoughts are with them all, and we wish them strength and comfort as they come to terms with this profound loss." The 41-year-old had been travelling to receive the scientific excellence prize from the Spanish Society for Developmental Biology. She had been nominated for her research into stem cells and the early stages of human development. Born in Spain, the mum-of-two had been living with her living with her children, aged three and seven, in Cambridge. Authorities have since blamed the crash on a computer failure and human error. (Image: Juanma Jimenez/Europa Press via AP) Dr Shahbazi began her career at the Autonomous University of Madrid where she received an undergraduate degree in Biology. She also received an MSc in Molecular Biomedicine before obtaining her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre. In 2019, she received the 3Rs Prize for "providing an opportunity to replace and reduce the use of mice in developmental biology studies." The affiliate associate professor at the University of Cambridge led a group of researchers at the MCR Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB). The Laboratory had previously confirmed Dr Shahbazi was on one of the trains but said here whereabouts were "unknown". In a tribute on its website, the LMB said it is "deeply saddened" by the "tragic death" of the "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist". "Her death is a profound shock and a huge loss. Our thoughts are with her family, friends and colleagues at this extremely difficult time. "The LMB is offering support to members of its community as they navigate this tragic loss." The collision occurred when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company. It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. Authorities have since blamed the crash on a computer failure and human error. Mr Pratt said: "The completion of the Rothbury Estate purchase is a defining moment for Northumberland and the North East. "Opportunities of this scale and significance are incredibly rare. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Fake beauty products found to contain mercury, lead, nicotine and methanol
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Counterfeit beauty products containing mercury, lead and methanol are putting consumers at risk, following testing of hauls seized by Trading Standards. The toxic chemicals were found in fake cosmetics, skincare and perfumes seized during recent investigations, with four in 10 seized cosmetics found to contain potentially harmful substances. Among the most alarming discoveries was a skincare product containing 13,200 parts per million of mercury, as well as high levels of lead in lipsticks, eyeshadows and contour products. Nicotine was also found in some counterfeit perfumes, and one fake fragrance was made up of approximately 80 per cent methanol. The Intellectual Property Office has issued warnings. (Image: IPO/Press Association) Rani Ghosh, an independent toxicologist, said: "When you hear that mercury has been found in face cream, lead in make-up or nicotine in perfume, it raises serious questions about what is going into these products and how they are being made. "Some reactions to unsafe cosmetics may be visible, such as irritation, swelling or changes to the skin. "But what concerns me as a toxicologist is what you might not see. "Substances such as mercury and lead can affect the body internally, and those effects may not be immediately obvious. "Counterfeit beauty products can look incredibly convincing. "You cannot tell from the packaging what chemicals are inside, how the product has been made, or what risk it might pose. "That is why knowing where your beauty products come from matters." The Intellectual Property Office’s (IPO) latest Counterfeit Goods Tracker revealed that one in five 18 to 24-year-olds who bought beauty products last year knowingly bought counterfeits, up from six per cent in 2023. In July, the Police Intellectual Property Crime Unit and Greater Manchester Police seized 1,666 counterfeit hair products, including extensions, shampoos and conditioners, from a warehouse in Manchester. A separate raid in Bolton uncovered £2 million worth of fake goods. This included perfume, cosmetics, clothing and vapes. The IPO’s Face the Fakes campaign is working with content creators and the beauty industry to raise awareness of the potential harms of counterfeit beauty products. Helen Barnham, head of enforcement engagement at the IPO, said: "These findings show why counterfeit beauty products can pose such serious risks to consumers. "Products can look remarkably convincing, but behind the packaging they can contain dangerous substances that have no place in the cosmetics people use every day, and can be made in appalling, unhygienic conditions. Counterfeit manufacturing equipment. (Image: IPO/Press Association) "Counterfeiters exploit the names and reputations of brands that consumers know and trust, while bypassing the rigorous safety standards that legitimate businesses work hard to meet. "With our latest research showing a sharp rise in counterfeit beauty buying among young adults, we want to make sure people understand the potential risks and know how to protect themselves. "Our Face the Fakes campaign is giving consumers practical advice to shop more safely, including checking who is actually selling a product and choosing trusted sources." Dr Emma Meredith, director-general of the Cosmetic, Toiletry and Perfumery Association, said: "There is a rigorous safety framework behind every legitimate cosmetic product sold in the UK. "Ingredients are carefully controlled, products have to be made in clean and hygienic conditions, and they must undergo a safety assessment. "Companies have clear legal responsibilities for the products they place on the market."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Ryanair confirms luggage rule change impacting thousands of travellers
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Ryanair has confirmed it will be making a major change to its luggage rules, and it is set to be enforced next month. The change is expected to affect millions of people who fly with Ryanair. If you are taking a trip soon and are flying with Ryanair, it is worth keeping up to date with the airline’s policies to avoid being caught out at the airport. A post shared by Ryanair_European_Airline (@ryanair) Ryanair has confirmed it will be changing its rules around airport check-ins and bag drops. From November 10, the airline will be giving passengers less time to drop off their luggage before their flight. The new rule means Ryanair will close all of its airport bag drop desks and physical check-in counters 60 minutes before the flight’s departure time. Previously, the airline allowed passengers to drop off their luggage up to 40 minutes before their flight. The change is hoped to give passengers more time to clear airport queues, such as security checks and passport control queues, before their flights. The airline has said the extra 20 minutes will help to run operations more smoothly. Ryanair has said the change should help reduce the number of travellers who miss their flights because of delays at the airport. The rule impacts anyone with checked luggage or those who require physical check-in assistance at the airport. If you have either a 10kg or 20kg checked bag, you must make sure it has gone through the bag drop at least an hour before your scheduled flight time. Ryanair CMO, Dara Brady, said: “From Tues, 10 Nov, bag drop services at all Ryanair airports will close 60 minutes before scheduled departure, instead of the current 40 minutes. “This small change will give the 20% of Ryanair passengers who check in a bag, more time to clear airport security and passport control queues and get to their departure gate before boarding begins, particularly during busy travel periods when airport queues can be longer. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Disabled Huntingdonshire tenant raises asbestos fears over deteriorating floor
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A disabled tenant fears his Huntingdonshire home is unsafe because its asbestos-containing floor is deteriorating, but his housing association says a survey found it poses a “very low risk”. Michael Cook moved into the Places for People property in Chapel Close, Needingworth, in June, and says the bitumen floor should have been sealed and covered first. He says the bitumen is now breaking up and becoming sticky in places, with residue transferring onto his belongings, clothes and the paws of his dog, Spike. Places for People tenant Michael Cook says flooring in his flat contains asbestos and is a health risk, however the landlords say surveys show it is 'low risk'. (Image: Michael Cook) Places for People disputes claims that the deterioration poses an asbestos risk. A Places for People spokesperson said: “We take concerns about the safety and condition of our customers’ homes seriously, and we’re sorry for the worry and frustration Mr Cook has experienced. “Our survey confirmed the presence of asbestos in the adhesive beneath the floor, but it is encapsulated and very low risk, with no evidence of fibres being released into the home. Places for People tenant Michael Cook says flooring in his flat contains asbestos and is a health risk, however the landlords say surveys show it is 'low risk'. (Image: Michael Cook) “The surveys identified no risk requiring emergency action, and there is no requirement to stop vacuuming, sweeping or mopping, or to avoid laying laminate flooring.” Mr Cook and his advocate, his mum Ilya Kennard, say surveys carried out in 2026 found chrysotile asbestos in the bitumen adhesive beneath floors in several rooms. Mr Cook says the deteriorating floor has left the material inadequately protected and should have been sealed and covered before he moved in. Places for People tenant Michael Cook says flooring in his flat contains asbestos and is a health risk, however the landlords say surveys show it is 'low risk'. (Image: Michael Cook) Mr Cook has also reported plumbing and drainage problems, including flooding in the wet room. Mr Cook also says he was told not to vacuum, sweep or mop the affected floor because it could be disturbed. Places for People disputes this and says its surveys found no need for such restrictions. Concerns have also been raised about how the case was handled and communicated to Mr Cook, who is disabled and takes morphine and pregabalin for a broken back. The spokesperson added: “While the reported deterioration of the floor is not causing asbestos fibres to become airborne, we have assessed the property and are laying new flooring throughout. “There were, however, shortcomings in our communication with Mr Cook and his appointed advocate. “We apologise for the stress this may have caused and will ensure appropriate support is in place in future.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts council leader slams latest 'deeply disappointing' LGR delay
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A council leader has slammed the latest government update on Local Government Reorganisation, calling the lack of action "deeply disappointing". Sarah Conboy, leader of Huntingdonshire District Council, criticised the update, which confirmed that no final decision had been made on Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. LGR would see the two tier system of county and district councils in Cambridgeshire replaced with a number of unitary authorities across the county. An announcement on the form this would take was expected in July, but the Secretary of State for Local Government at the time, Steve Reed, delayed the decision until October. On October 29, Jim McMahon MP, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Local Government, Devolution and Regional Growth, announced in Parliament that only five of the 14 areas under review would be proceeding. Cambridgeshire and Peterborough was not included in the five. Cllr Conboy said: "Today's announcement is deeply disappointing for Huntingdonshire and the wider Cambridgeshire and Peterborough area. "After months of work developing and assessing proposals, we had hoped the Government would provide certainty about the future of local government in our area. "Instead, residents, businesses and councils are being asked to wait longer for a decision. "We will continue to work constructively with our partners while seeking greater clarity from Government on the next steps and timescales." The Government says it expects to make a final decision by early next year. In the meantime, HDC will continue to work with regional partners to assess the implications of the announcement and plan for the next phase of the LGR programme. The council confirmed there will be no immediate changes to council services, which will continue to be delivered as normal while councils await further details. The Government said all options would remain under consideration, with a further update due by Christmas and outcomes for every area expected early next year.
