summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: We visited Cambs garden centre’s new pottery studio - here's what we thought
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Nestled into Huntingdon Home & Garden’s spacious restaurant area is its newest attraction – The Potting Shed Studio. Immediately after walking through its doors, the sage green interior decor gives an instant feeling of calmness. It really is a place to unwind and let your imagination takeover. The staff – a small team led by studio manager Sophie – are equally as welcoming, leading us to the well-stocked display. It can be tricky deciding what to paint due to the vast selection, but don’t worry as they have every age covered. From cute little animals to small plates, platter plates, jugs and photo frames, the £1 booking fee per person is redeemable against the price of your pottery. Though it’s not quite as well equipped as some of the longer established pottery studios – for example Center Parcs – this can be forgiven as the studio only opened its doors in late March. Nonetheless, we as a family loved our experience; our two young children had great fun mixing the different squeeze paints together in their palette and getting creative. It’s worth noting, however, that they were not provided with or offered aprons, but we have been assured that the paint comes off very easily in the wash. Something else to bear in mind is that the turnaround is up to two weeks, so you will have to make a return visit for collection — though this isn’t really a problem as Blue Diamond has its customers covered. The Potting Shed Studio has been open for around two weeks (Image: Ben Jolley/Newsquest) Visitors can get topped up on your fresh fruit and veg, browse the clothing range, enjoy a cuppa and a slice of cake, and even refresh your fish tank by popping into Maidenhead Aquatics. Overall, The Potting Shed Studio is a great addition not only to the garden centre – which gave out a complimentary glass of bubbly upon entry to celebrate one year of being open – but for the wider Cambridgeshire area. Alongside being great for families, it would make for a quirky few hours out to get the girls together or even for part of a date day. And, with plans to run exciting events in the future, make sure to keep your eyes peeled on their socials. Visit https://events.bluediamond.gg/event-tickets/75710?branches.branchID=3618 to book.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Why Hamerton Zoo Park is one of Cambridgeshire’s best attractions
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: When it comes to a day out at the zoo, the UK’s biggest are likely the first ones that spring to mind. But, much closer to home, there’s a more local alternative that’s equally worth visiting: Hamerton, near Sawtry, between Huntingdonshire and Peterborough. What began its life as a private collection when it first opened its doors to the public in June 1990, has since grown into a park that is home to many rare and unusual animals. Fast forward 35 years, and not only has the number of distinct breeds massively increased, the entrance area has had a makeover and there’s a brilliant new park (Treetop Adventure Play) that has just as much to occupy children as it does adults. Tree Tops Adventure Play(Image: Newsquest) This includes an obstacle course in the sky that’s connected with ladders and ropes, a great zipwire, plenty of slides and a disorienting Rubix cube-like climbing puzzle that’s sure to challenge parents. Onto the zoo’s main attraction, and there are countless stunning animals to see and learn about: from cute common marmosets that would fit in the palm of your hand to swinging lemurs, to tiny dik-dik deers, hopping white wallabys and adorable lettuce-munching tortoises of all sizes. Read more Witnessing the Greater Flamingo stood on parade is a sight, too, as is being able to walk through the bird enclosure as a myriad of colours zoom past your eyes. Though acclimatised to living in dark, the sloths are equally mesmerising to watch, clinging to branches and ropes while somehow managing to eat upside down. It’s entrancing to witness them move along at such a slow pace, especially in such close proximity. The same can be said for the reptile and rodent house, which has all manner of rare lizards and snakes. It’s worth noting that all the enclosures are incredibly well kept and presented, especially in the bird area (a highlight of which is the strikingly colourful Scarlet Ibis). The flamingos(Image: Newsquest) The meerkat enclosure, meanwhile, has had an upgrade with two new bubble head viewing platforms that provide a great photo opportunity - little ones are sure to want to go through the tunnel on repeat, and they may even be able to snap a selfie with a meerkat. A word of warning, though: it might be a bit tiring for adults - especially those who are taller. As if all that isn’t enough, there are also swimming otters, miniature donkeys, zebra, massive camels, several tigers and, if you’re lucky like we were, one or more of the Syrian Brown Bear family might pop out to say hello. The animal-spotting doesn’t stop there, though, as even while enjoying a tasty panini and delicious cake, there are opportunities to spot some impressive aquatic species. The viewing platforms inside the meerkat enclosure(Image: Newsquest) With all this and more for an affordable price - £19.99 an adult, £15.99 a child, free for under threes and carers - it’s a great value experience. Undoubtedly one of Cambridgeshire’s best attractions, you can easily spend the whole day at Hamerton Zoo Park, and its annual pass option makes for a perfect family gift that’s guaranteed to create lots of special memories. To book, visit https://hamertonzoopark.com

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: We visited bird sanctuary in Cambridgeshire and here’s what we thought
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Ben Jolley reports back from a visit to The Raptor Foundation in Woodhurst, Cambridgeshire It’s more important than ever to support local attractions - especially ones that are making a real difference. A registered charity for over 30 years and situated at its current site for the same amount of time, visiting The Raptor Foundation is not only fun for all ages but you'll be supporting a crucial cause too. Having started its life in Ramsey St Mary, before moving to its current, bigger premises in the late 1990s, the sanctuary is home to around 170 birds of prey, including between 35 and 40 different species. The Buzzard Lawn (Image: Newsquest) As the majority of these have come from a rescue background, money spent (entry is very affordable at £8 for adults, £5 for children and free for under threes) goes towards rescuing, rehabilitating and then returning native birds of prey back to the wild. Open to the public all year round, and currently appealing for builders to help create new aviaries, time spent at the foundation is both exciting and educational. The bird of prey displays - which feature rare owls and falcons soaring overhead - are thrilling to watch. If you’re lucky, some may even decide to perch on the seat next to you, which takes the phrase up close and personal to a whole new level. Action from the bird of prey display (Image: Newsquest) Having trained the birds inside out, the keepers and handlers are incredibly knowledgeable, informative and able to answer any question posed to them. This extends to the talks and feeding sessions throughout the day which offer further meet and greet opportunities; a parrot might even land on your shoulders. It’s not just birds, however, as the reptile house is home to a gigantic tortoise (and many smaller ones), as well as lizards and snakes. Beyond animals, there is also a play area and pond that will amuse younger children and a tearoom serving food and drink. Read more The foundation also runs experience days which, ranging from one-to-one handling to junior keeper days, would make for a perfect Christmas present. It also hosts photography tours and is an ideal venue for birthday parties. As if that wasn't enough, there is also the option to stay overnight, at either the Falcons Nest guest accommodation or the caravan site. Whilst we didn’t spend the whole day at The Raptor Foundation (largely due to the weather), there's no question that it is one of Cambridgeshire's most treasured gems.

Millions of pumpkins usually end up being thrown away by Brits every year   (Image: PA) Pumpkins can be used for a variety of foods once they have been cleaned out. Dominique Delacour, dairy expert at CAMBOZOLA, shared: “The best way to recycle your pumpkin after Halloween is to cook with it - never throw it away! "Both the flesh, puplp and the seeds can be turned into something delicious. "Roasted pumpkin works beautifully with creamy cheeses in puff pastry parcels, pasta bakes or toasties, while the seeds can be washed, seasoned and baked until golden for a crunchy topping or snack. "It’s an easy way to cut down on waste and turn your Halloween leftovers into something comforting and indulgent for autumn.” Grating the pumpkin pulp you pull out when carving could also be ideal for use in a pumpkin loaf, pie or muffin. The fruit is high in vitamins A and C, as well as being a good source of fibre. Pumpkins don't just have to be used for food after Halloween, with several creative ways to give them a second life. One option is to turn your pumpkin into a seasonal candle. Clean out the inside before adding melted wax, spices such as cinnamon and ginger, and a wick to fill your home with autumnal scents. Leftover pumpkins can also be turned into planters. Remove the inside, add drainage holes and fill with potting soil and your choice of plants. Another option is to make a bird feeder by cleaning out the pumpkin, cutting openings into the sides and filling it with bird seed before hanging it outside. Pumpkins can be composted (PA)  (Image: PA) Using pumpkin in a DIY face mask can be beneficial. AHAs, or alpha hydroxy acids, are widely praised in the skincare world for their ability to help exfoliate and renew skin, and pumpkins are packed full of them. Josh Novell, Director of Polhill Garden Centre, has shared that pumpkins can be used in your garden once they have been cleaned out. He said: "Next, break the pumpkin up into small chunks. Large pieces take much longer to decompose. "Cutting them into fist-sized chunks or smaller helps them break down quickly and release nutrients evenly into the soil. “One of the biggest mistakes people make is scattering pumpkin pieces across the surface; that’s an open invitation for rats and slugs. "Always bury your pumpkin a few inches deep in the soil as this keeps pests away and helps the microbes get to work faster.” “If you’re digging pumpkins into borders or beds, mix in some dry garden materials like leaves, straw or old compost. "That stops the soil from getting too wet or slimy, and it balances out the carbon and nitrogen levels as the pumpkin breaks down.” If you do need to get rid of your pumpkin, then composting it would be the best option. Chris Taylor from Chris Taylor Gardening shared: "Pumpkins break down quickly and make great compost material. "Just remove any candle wax or decorations, chop it into smaller chunks, and add it to your compost heap. Recommended reading: "The high moisture content helps balance drier materials like leaves or cardboard." You could also offer it up to any gardeners or allotment owners who might be interested in taking it off your hands Aside from that, putting it in a food waste recycling bin also works. What do you do with your pumpkin once Halloween is over? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: I'm a personal finance writer - here are the 8 Budget changes I'm most pleased to see
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Budgets always have winners and losers, but this week there are some genuinely welcome bits of news for many people, and as a personal finance writer, I'm particularly pleased to see help for households facing rising energy bills, pensioners getting a boost, more money for workers and new support for people hoping to buy their first home. Chancellor John Healey has announced a package designed to give families, savers and businesses some breathing space during a challenging economic period. And while there's no magic wand to make the cost of living disappear overnight, I think there are some measures worth celebrating. From £100 landing in millions of bank accounts to a higher State Pension and a new scheme to help first-time buyers, here's what I'm taking away from the Budget – and what it could mean for your money. One of the biggest wins for families is the £100 energy support payment - and the fact that they have chosen to put it in people's banks and not give it directly to the energy companies. Around 20 million households in council tax bands A to D will receive £100 from the Government this winter, with the money expected to arrive directly in bank accounts from January - a time when most people will need it most. I particularly like that families will be free to spend the money however they choose. Whether it's going towards an energy bill, the weekly food shop or another household essential, it gives people a little more flexibility. Some may say it'll get frittered away, but I like the idea that billpayers get to choose - if that's a day out with the kids or new school shoes or even a drink with mates, a cash boost could help the economy as tills ring with a tiny bit more optimism. There's more good news for energy customers, too. The Government plans to move some of the cost of standing charges on gas bills into the unit rate. Around 60% of households are expected to save an average of £45 a year. The removal of VAT from electricity bills is also being extended until July 2031. Of course, households using more energy could end up paying more under the standing charge changes, so it's worth keeping an eye on how your own bill is affected. But overall, I welcome the focus on making energy costs more manageable. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey delivering his Budget in the House of Commons, London. (Image: House of Commons/UK Parliament/PA Wire) There's some particularly good news for pensioners, with the State Pension set to rise to £13,036 a year from next April under the triple lock. For millions of people who rely on their State Pension to cover everyday essentials, this increase will be an important boost. I also think the announcement of a new tax allowance for pensioners on lower incomes is worth highlighting. The measure is designed to protect pensioners from being dragged into paying income tax simply because their State Pension has increased above the £12,570 personal allowance. This is particularly welcome for those who rely largely on the State Pension and don't have significant additional retirement income - the people who really need some help. Did you spot some good news for savers, too? The planned reduction in the annual cash ISA allowance from £20,000 to £12,000 has been scrapped. That's a big win for anyone who likes the flexibility and tax-free benefits of a cash ISA. It feels like trusting people to make the right choice with their own money rather than legislating where and how they can save. It means savers can continue to put away up to £20,000 a year across their ISAs, subject to the usual rules. I think this is particularly important at a time when people are trying to build emergency savings, put money aside for a deposit or simply earn a return on their hard-earned cash. However, there is a sting in the tail (when isn't there?). Tax on savings income is set to increase from April 2027. Basic-rate taxpayers will pay 24%, higher-rate taxpayers 44% and additional-rate taxpayers 49%. This makes making the most of tax-efficient savings options even more important. My advice is to review where your savings are held and check whether you're making full use of your available ISA allowance. A post shared by Martin Lewis (@martinlewismse) One of the most interesting announcements for aspiring homeowners is the new £4.7 billion Your First Home scheme. The aim is to help around 70,000 households in England take their first step onto the property ladder. The scheme will offer first-time buyers 20% equity loans, potentially reducing the deposit and mortgage they need to find themselves. There will be household income limits of £110,000 outside London and £140,000 in London. For anyone who has been saving for years but struggling to get together enough money to buy a home, this could be a welcome opportunity. There's also a new First-Time Buyer ISA coming in April 2029, which will replace the Lifetime ISA. For eligible buyers, it's certainly an announcement worth watching. This is another announcement I'd put firmly in the positive column. The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage will rise by 3.9% in April 2027. For workers aged 21 and over, the hourly rate will increase from £12.71 to £13.21. For those aged 18 to 20, it will rise from £10.85 to £11.27. Around 2.3 million workers are expected to benefit. For people on lower incomes, even a modest increase can make a difference to the monthly budget. With food shopping, transport and household essentials continuing to put pressure on finances, having more money coming in is certainly welcome. However, income tax thresholds remain frozen, meaning some workers could find more of their earnings falling into a higher tax bracket as their pay increases. It's a reminder that it's not just your headline pay rise that matters, but how much you actually take home. There's good news for motorists too, and goodness knows, we need it. The fuel duty freeze has been extended, keeping the rate at 52p a litre and cancelling a planned increase in January. For anyone who relies on their car, this is another welcome measure. There's also good news for people who use their own vehicles for work, with the higher tax-free mileage allowance of 55p being made permanent. That should provide some reassurance for employees who use their cars for business journeys and claim mileage expenses. With motoring costs adding up quickly, keeping these allowances in place is a positive step. Pensioners with income up to the value of the full new state pension (to be £13,040 from April 2027) will not pay tax. Mechanism not stated, I suspect there will be an effective increased pensioner allowance with a clawback for income above that. More when I know more. #Budget2026 — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) October 28, 2026 I'm also encouraged by the business rates announcement. The threshold for small business rates relief for retail, hospitality and leisure businesses is increasing from £12,000 to £18,000. The Government estimates this will take around 70,000 additional businesses completely out of paying business rates. That's potentially a significant saving for independent shops, restaurants, cafés and other businesses that are the backbone of our local communities. For businesses trying to keep their prices competitive, invest in their premises or take on staff, reducing overheads could make a real difference. A thriving high street is good news for everyone, so I'm pleased to see measures aimed at supporting the businesses that keep our communities going. The global economic picture is undoubtedly challenging, particularly with the conflict in the Middle East putting pressure on energy prices. But there are some encouraging signs in the forecasts. The OBR has increased its growth forecast for 2026 from 1.1% to 1.2%. While growth for 2027 has been downgraded to 1%, the longer-term forecasts point towards growth of 1.6% in 2028, 1.8% in 2029 and 1.7% in 2030. There is still work to do, but I think it's important to look beyond the immediate economic headlines and recognise that there are opportunities for improvement. The big priority now must be making sure economic growth translates into better wages, more jobs and more money in people's pockets. Let's face facts - times are pretty tough. Most people are struggling - food and fuel cost far too much. But, for me, the biggest takeaway from this Budget is that there are some practical measures that could make a difference at different stages of our financial lives, and no big shocks to make matters worse. Whether you're a pensioner, a first-time buyer, a family with young kids, a saver or a small business owner, there is something in this Budget that could help. I'm particularly pleased to see the State Pension increase, the protection for lower-income pensioners, the decision to retain the £20,000 ISA allowance and the new support for first-time buyers. The £100 energy payment and minimum wage increases are also welcome measures for households feeling the squeeze. Recommended reading: Of course, there are still challenges ahead. Inflation, borrowing costs and weaker growth forecasts show that the economy isn't out of the woods yet. But I think it's important to recognise the positives too. My advice? Take a fresh look at your finances and make the most of any changes that could benefit you. Check your pension, review your savings arrangements, look at your ISA allowance and, if you're hoping to buy your first home, keep an eye on the new scheme. It's not a Budget that's going to change everyone's financial fortunes overnight, but there are some encouraging steps in the right direction. And with household budgets needing all the help they can get, that's certainly something worth celebrating.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Legal expert reveals your rights if trick-or-treaters disturb you on Halloween
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Halloween is an exciting time for many families who will be dressing up and trick-or-treating this weekend. Many houses will be decorated with pumpkins and will be handing out chocolates and sweets to children. However, some people are not a fan of this holiday and will be keeping their doors shut during the evening. A property law expert has revealed what homeowners can do if they want to avoid being disturbed on Halloween. If you do not decorate your house, it indicates to people that you do not want to be disturbed. (Image: Getty) Janet Lane, a property law expert from Rogers and Norton, has shared a few steps that homeowners can take to indicate to trick-or-treaters that they do not want to be disturbed. She said: “There is generally an implied permission for somebody to walk up the usual route to your front door and knock, which is why a delivery driver, neighbour or other caller does not normally need express permission first. “But homeowners can make it clear that they do not want Halloween callers. “A locked gate, or a simple and prominent ‘no trick-or-treaters’ notice on the door, gate or window is one of the clearest ways of communicating that visitors are not invited to approach.” Legal action or police involvement is only necessary if the situation escalates into criminal damage, harassment, or anti-social behaviour. Throwing things at a property like eggs, flour, rocks, and silly string or damaging walls, windows, and vehicles falls under criminal damage, according to the Criminal Damage Act 1971. The Public Order Act 1986 states that using abusive, threatening or insulting words or behaviour that causes alarm or distress is also an offence. Lane added: “There is an important difference between a child innocently knocking on the wrong door and behaviour which becomes intimidating or destructive.” “A single knock is one thing. “Repeatedly banging on somebody’s door after being asked to leave, damaging their property or throwing objects at their home is something very different and should never be dismissed as simply part of Halloween.” Janet says that using a clear sign that says ‘no trick-or-treaters please’ and not putting out pumpkins or decorations will signal to people that you do not want to be disturbed. You should also keep gates closed and make sure any signs are visible before people reach your front door. Do you love Halloween or will you be keeping your door closed this year? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Council-owned developer may not be able to pay back loans
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A council-owned developer has said they may face a multi-million pound cash shortfall as the housing market faces an “economic squeeze”. This Land, which is owned by Cambridgeshire County Council, could face a shortfall of as much as £7.7m in March 2029, against its loan obligations. A report said the company may not be able to pay back the loans and interest it took from the council under the current forecasts. Michael Hudson, the council’s executive director of finance, told a meeting of the shareholder sub-committee this was not an “immediate insolvency event”. He said that “national market factors” were increasing risks of cash shortages for housing developers and other businesses “as the economic squeeze hits harder and harder”. Set up by the county council in 2016 to build homes and sell land to other developers across Cambridgeshire, the company currently owes the council £58m and a further £22.5m in interest. The report said they expect losses of around £2.7m, around £400,000 worse than planned, by the end of the 2026/27 financial year partly driven by delayed sales at Eddeva Park. Approved in 2021, the development just south of Cambridge of up to 230 homes is a mix of detached, terraced and apartments, with 40 per cent marked as affordable. Rob Williams, chief executive officer of This Land, said that “sales are taking a bit longer at the moment” and “things are slow” in both house building and the wider economy. He said: “The planning system is getting slower if anything. “I think the raft of improvements that have come from central government, whilst they are positive, are taking time to embed and for planning authorities to get their heads around.” The report said council officers are working with This Land “to assess options to protect the council’s position and address the 2029 cashflow risk”. These include “close management of the principal receipts, potential rephasing of disposals, management of loan and interest timing and consideration of the company’s future operating model”.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Bar Hill Christmas tree grant approved despite concerns over heatwave maintenance
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A Cambridgeshire village has been given funding for a permanent Christmas tree – though concerns were raised over its ability to survive a heatwave. Bar Hill Community Association applied to plant the Christmas tree on land owned by the parish council ahead of the lights switch-on scheduled in November. They told South Cambridgeshire District Council that the scheme would be a “long-term community asset” and help “enhance community cohesion”. The report said it would cost a total of £2,807.20 with £1,000 funded by the parish council and asked the district council for a grant to cover the rest. This was broken down into £1,129.20 for the lighting and electricity, £1,278 for the tree and installation, £150 for a banner and £250 for Christmas presents. William Scantlebury, ward councillor for Bar Hill, wrote in support of the application and said it would be a “simple but meaningful addition, helping to bring residents together and add some festive spirit to the heart of Bar Hill”. Cllr Dr Richard Williams, vice chair of South Cambs Council’s grants advisory committee, said it’s “a lovely thing to have” but the costs “jump out a bit”. Cllr Eileen Wilson, of Cottenham, said: “The one thing that came to my mind when I was reading about this was the ongoing maintenance after the heatwaves that we had this summer. “Have they got provisions in place to maintain the tree, to keep it watered if we have a heatwave, because seeing the example of the trees along the A14 that have perished, it does take quite a lot to keep trees going when they have these very big heatwaves.” Emma Dyer, development officer with the communities team, said she’d check the tree management policy but assumes that would be covered. She said: “I think it’s something that they want to keep as an asset so I should imagine they would take a lot of care and look after it.” Cllr Farhan Hussain, of Shelford, said he grew up in Bar Hill and it is “quite an isolated village”. He said: “I think it’s quite a good, community spirit thing to have and I know a lot of villages are isolated at the moment. “Having that in place might actually help out a lot of low disposable income families. You know, things are quite tough at the moment. “I think this is a nice way to do it, but I think it would be very good to just clarify the detailed cost of how they’ve come to that price.” Councillors decided against delaying the application for more details about the pricing as it would mean it wouldn’t be decided until after Christmas. Cllr Williams said: “I think it’s a lovely idea, I really wouldn’t like to delay it and then miss Christmas”. The grant was approved unanimously.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The stunning Cambridgeshire walk with incredible views and riverside tea room
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: For those looking to escape the crowds and discover a quieter side of Cambridgeshire, the St Ives and Hemingfords Walk is one of the county's best-kept secrets. Beginning at Houghton Mill, this picturesque route follows the banks of the River Great Ouse through water meadows and historic villages. The five-mile circular walk is largely flat, making it accessible for most abilities, and offers a constantly changing landscape. Walkers pass through the peaceful Ouse Valley and enjoy long stretches beside the river before reaching the charming villages of Hemingford Grey and Hemingford Abbots. Along the way are postcard-worthy cottages, medieval churches and waterside views that feel a world away from nearby towns and cities. Those with time to spare can visit Holt Island Nature Reserve in St Ives, explore the town's historic centre or stop by the Norris Museum before continuing through the meadows. The route starts and finishes at Houghton Mill, the National Trust's historic working watermill, where visitors will find a gift shop and a popular riverside tea room. Further refreshments can be found in the nearby villages, including traditional pubs that make ideal stopping points on a warm afternoon. What makes this walk so special is its sense of tranquillity. Even during the summer months, there are stretches where the only sounds are birdsong, rustling reeds and the gentle flow of the river. For anyone seeking a hidden riverside route packed with scenery, wildlife and heritage, this walk is certainly a rewarding day out. Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The best woodland walks in Cambridgeshire to discover this autumn
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From ancient woodlands and National Trust estates to wildlife-rich nature reserves, Cambridgeshire offers far more woodland scenery than many people realise. Showcasing some of the county's most attractive forest and woodland walks, here are six beauty spots to discover this autumn. While best known for its wetlands, Wicken Fen also contains areas of woodland and scrub that create a wonderfully varied walking experience. The reserve's network of paths passes through reedbeds, grassland and developing woodland, offering visitors the chance to spot everything from dragonflies and marsh harriers to grazing Konik ponies. The ever-changing landscape and huge skies make every walk feel different, whatever the season. One of the county's most important ancient woodlands, Monk's Wood is a haven for wildlife and a favourite among walkers seeking tranquillity. The reserve's oak and ash trees line peaceful trails that weave through centuries-old woodland. During spring, woodland flowers brighten the forest floor, while birdwatchers can enjoy sightings of woodpeckers, nuthatches and other woodland species. The largest country estate in Cambridgeshire offers far more than historic architecture. Its extensive parkland includes pockets of mature woodland, tree-lined avenues and scenic walking routes stretching across the estate. Visitors can wander beneath ancient trees before emerging into open countryside with far-reaching views. Managed by the National Trust, it combines woodland beauty with some of the county's most impressive landscapes. Famous for its gardens, Anglesey Abbey also boasts beautiful woodland walks that are particularly spectacular during autumn. Shaded paths wind through mature trees and carefully designed landscapes, creating a peaceful retreat from nearby Cambridge. Seasonal colour is a major draw, while the estate's varied habitats support a wide range of birds and other wildlife. It is one of the most picturesque places for a gentle woodland stroll in the county. Covering more than 170 acres, Hinchingbrooke Country Park combines mature woodland with lakes, meadows and open countryside. Well-maintained trails guide visitors through shady woodland areas rich in birdlife and seasonal wildflowers. The park's accessibility and variety of routes make it popular with families, dog walkers and runners alike, while its peaceful setting provides a welcome escape from nearby Huntingdon. Overshadowed by some of the region's larger historic sites, this riverside retreat combines heritage, wildlife and scenic walking routes. At the heart of the site is Houghton Mill, the last surviving working watermill on the River Great Ouse. Visitors can explore the historic building and discover how grain was transformed into flour using traditional machinery, with volunteer millers helping bring centuries of history to life. During the operating season, the giant waterwheel can still be seen turning, offering a glimpse into a way of life that once powered communities across the country. Beyond the mill lies the beautiful Waterclose Meadows, a landscape of riverside grassland, wildlife-rich habitats and tranquil walking paths. Footpaths lead through the meadows and along the river towards the picturesque villages of The Hemingfords, making it a favourite spot for walkers, photographers and nature lovers. In summer, the meadows buzz with insects and birds, while the river provides a constantly changing backdrop. Despite its rural atmosphere, visitors will find plenty of amenities. The on-site tea room enjoys a picturesque riverside location and serves freshly made cakes, scones, light lunches, hot drinks and seasonal treats. Indoor and outdoor seating allows visitors to relax beside the water after exploring the site. There is also parking, a gift shop, toilet facilities and accessible routes around much of the property. Families are well catered for, with open green spaces, picnic areas and easy riverside walks providing plenty of opportunities to enjoy the outdoors together. The site is also popular with cyclists thanks to nearby links with the wider cycle network. For those looking to discover a quieter side of Cambridgeshire, Houghton Mill and Waterclose Meadows offers history, scenery and relaxation in equal measure. It may be one of the county's hidden gems, but once visited, it is unlikely to remain a secret for long. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Local government shakeup in Cambridgeshire slammed as ‘gut punch’
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
A planned local government shakeup has been slammed as a “merry-go-round” as the plans face further delays. Local councils in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough were set to be dissolved in government plans for local government reorganisation (LGR). They were set to be replaced with a number of unitary councils which would handle both county and district level responsibilities. An announcement on what form this would take was expected in July, but the Secretary of State for Local Government at the time, Steve Reed, delayed the decision until October. At the time, he said the “shadow elections” planned for May 2027 for the newly-created authorities would still take place. But in September, the government said local elections would go ahead for Peterborough, East Cambridgeshire, Fenland and Cambridge City in 2027. South Cambridgeshire and Huntingdonshire already held their elections in May. All six councils and Cambridgeshire County Council were set to be replaced with two or three bigger councils under the plans, with the shadow elections setting the stage for a transition the next year. Currently, lower-tier district councils look after things like bin collections, leisure facilities and council tax, while the upper-tier county council is responsible for road maintenance, public health and education, including special educational needs and disabilities. Today, it was announced that the transition would face a further delay. Jim McMahon MP, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Local Government, Devolution and Regional Growth, announced in Parliament that only five of the 14 areas under review would be proceeding. These are East Sussex and Brighton and Hove, Gloucestershire, Oxfordshire and Warwickshire and Worcestershire. He said: “To be clear, all options and proposals in these areas will remain under consideration and I will approach all decisions with an open mind. “As such it should not be assumed the same proposal will automatically
  be selected. It is important the process is allowed to run its course and allow full and proper consideration.” To help with the “costs of uncertainty” he said all areas would receive half of transition funding – £450k per new unitary previously announced and £500k for each area in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough and West Sussex. He said there would be a further update by Christmas and every area will have outcomes by early next year. Pippa Heylings, Liberal Democrat MP for South Cambridgeshire, said: “Local Government Reorganisation has become a merry-go-round of changing decisions. “First, we were promised elections in May 2027. Then the decision for Cambridgeshire and West Sussex was delayed, while ministers still insisted elections would go ahead in May 2027. “Just two months later, the whole scheme was put on hold. Now it’s back, with a new date of 2028. Businesses need certainty to invest and plan. “Councils need certainty to set budgets and invest in our communities. the electorate deserve a clear and transparent process and council staff deserve certainty about their jobs and their families’ futures. “Instead, they’ve had shambolic U-turns and no certainty whatsoever. “Business owners across South Cambridgeshire have told me how badly this uncertainty has hurt them, putting their businesses at risk when they could least afford it. “Today’s delay is another gut-punch to Cambridgeshire’s businesses and councils, and it does nothing to solve the uncertainty that has plagued this whole process. “How can businesses and council leaders trust that we won’t be back here in a couple of months facing yet another delay? “I’ll keep pressing the Government until our communities get the certainty they deserve.” Leader of Cambridgeshire County Council, Councillor Lucy Nethsingha, said: “This is a bitter disappointment and once again shows we have a Government incapable of making decisions or following through on its own policies. “Cambridgeshire and Peterborough were already stuck in ‘LGR limbo’ and to simply extend that further beggars believe. “Continued uncertainty simply creates increased risks, prevents us from making long-term plans and all at a time when the demand for and the costs of providing council services are rising. “In particular, the anxiety and uncertainty that this creates for the hard-working staff in the seven councils in this area is intolerable. “We risk being unable to retain and recruit good people, we risk being unable to plan financially over the longer term and we risk being forced into making more short-term procurement and contract decisions, all because this Government can’t get its act together. “Our residents and communities deserve better; our staff deserve better and the democratically elected councillors across this area deserve better. “This Government may have changed Prime Minister, but it remains firmly mired in chaos. “Yes, decisions have consequences, but indecision, dither and delay also has consequences, in this case for local public services, the people we employ and the people who rely on us. “Despite this further indecision, we will remain our focussed upon delivering our services for residents and communities and doing the very best for Cambridgeshire, while once again waiting on the Government.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire firms left with ‘more questions than answers’ after Budget
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Business leaders say the latest Budget offers "more questions than answers" for firms across Cambridgeshire. The Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce has welcomed some of the Chancellor’s announcements, including changes to business rates and investment plans, but criticised the lack of support on employer National Insurance contributions, energy costs, and export provision. Charlotte Horobin, chief executive of the Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce, said: "The Budget leaves many businesses in Cambridgeshire, Peterborough and Stamford with more questions than answers. "The business-rates threshold increase is a step in the right direction but falls short of what the British Chambers of Commerce called for. "The absence of employer NIC relief, business energy support and export provision means the short-term pressures most businesses are facing remain largely unaddressed." Charlotte said the real impact of the Budget will depend on how quickly the measures translate into tangible benefits. She said: "There are encouraging signals on place-based growth and devolution, but the practical test is simple: how quickly will these measures translate into lower operating costs, stronger investment and real opportunities for businesses on the ground?" The Budget includes a rise in the small business rate relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000, removing rates for 70,000 more businesses and freezing business rates for two years. Other measures include a 3.9 per cent increase in the National Living Wage and National Minimum Wage, a tripled trading allowance, and a new entrepreneur’s allowance intended to cover a year of living costs. The Chancellor also announced a scale-up programme for female founders, new founders’ Capital Gains Tax relief, and a fiscal devolution roadmap to expand local powers for mayoral authorities, and referenced the Cambridge Development Corporation. Funding for a local apprenticeship service was also included, alongside a plan that fully funds the defence investment plan and a new defence spending taskforce.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Former Cambs councillor and cadet leader guilty of rape and child sexual offences
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A former Cambridgeshire councillor and Army Cadet Force leader has been found guilty of rape and multiple child sexual offences. Rylan Ray, 26, from Westgate, Peterborough, was convicted of 23 offences following a 24-day trial at Ipswich Crown Court. The former Peterborough City Councillor had already pleaded guilty to three other offences before the trial began. Ray used his role as a detachment commander in the Army Cadet Force (ACF) to contact young people on WhatsApp under the guise of discussing cadet duties. He then encouraged them to move conversations to Snapchat, where the messaging became sexual. Ray created a fake Snapchat account posing as a teenage girl named Chelsie to obtain intimate images from his victims. He was linked to the account after a phone call from one victim to Chelsie was answered by Ray. Another fake account was traced to his flat through its IP address. Photos of Chelsie, including the Snapchat icon, were found on Ray’s phone, along with intimate images from six victims that had only been sent to the fake accounts. He also told a 16-year-old cadet that he could get him into clubs without ID because he was a Peterborough licensing officer. Rylan Ray was a former Peterborough City Councillor (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) The offences, involving 11 victims, came to light in 2025 after two 16th birthday parties were held at Ray’s home. The parties were attended mostly by cadets or people connected to the ACF. Parents raised concerns about drinking and behaviour at the parties, prompting complaints to the ACF. When officers spoke to children who attended the parties, several disclosed sexual messaging with Ray. He was also involved with the Combined Cadet Force (CCF) at Stanground Academy and Nene Park Academy in Peterborough. Police were notified in May 2025 and launched an investigation, where some children reported not only sexual messages but also sexual assault. Ray was arrested that same month. In a prepared statement during his police interview, he admitted he "may have" engaged in inappropriate conversations but denied any sexual motivation. He said he was "truly shocked and disgusted" by the allegations and claimed they had "ruined his career." He then gave no further comment. In later interviews, Ray admitted receiving topless images from one child and acknowledged that some messages were sexual in nature. He also admitted sending a photo of his genitals and pornography to the same boy. Ray was charged with 25 offences. Following media coverage of the charges, another victim came forward and reported that Ray had raped him after a night out in Peterborough in 2019. Before the trial, Ray pleaded guilty to two counts of causing or inciting a boy aged 13 to 15 to engage in sexual activity and one count of causing a child aged 13 to 15 to look at an image of sexual activity. During the trial, he admitted two further offences of making indecent images of children. He was found guilty of 23 additional offences, including rape, sexual assault, and sexual communication with a child. Ray will be sentenced at Ipswich Crown Court on January 8. Detective Constable Gordon Logan, who investigated, said: "The roles Ray held allowed him trusted access to young people, and he seized these opportunities to abuse them sexually. "We would like to praise the bravery of the children involved in confiding in others what had happened to them. "Doing so takes a lot of courage but it was so important that they did, because we then began investigating. "Many of the victims involved felt they had no choice but to engage in the chats with Ray. "In an increasingly digital world, mobile phones and social media mean children can be vulnerable to those who prey on their innocence and exploit their trust. "We encourage all members of the public to be aware of adults who pay an unusual amount of attention to a child – no matter their profession. "Sharing any concerns, no matter how small, can make all the difference."

This was due to the dividing of the school hall to allow for a third bedroom, but residents submitted 17 letters in support of the plans. Philippa Hope, of Bluntisham Parish Council, told the council’s development management committee the building “needs to be preserved”. She said: “It has a resonance for the people of Bluntisham – and is integral to the spirit of place. “However, it is no longer a school and could never be used as a school again. “To convert any building into a home internal changes are inevitable – the school building is the same and any changes are justifiable in securing the long-term future of this vacant listed building.” A previous proposal was refused in 2025 despite concerns that the building hasn’t been properly maintained since it stopped being used as a school in 1968. Councillors had concerns with the proposed rear extension which was reduced in size in the resubmission, with the hall division the last remaining concern for officers. Simon Claridge, the applicant, told the committee he cares “deeply about the building” which had continued to “deteriorate through vandalism, broken windows, water ingress, roof damage and even attempted arson”. He said: “We’ve listened, compromised and repeatedly amended our proposals. Given the resources already invested though – this really is our last attempt to save this building. “Every year that passes more of the very heritage we’re trying to protect is lost. “I understand the conservation’s desire to retain the school hall as one open space – however, a completely open hall simply does not provide a practical family home.” He added that the partition would be “reversible” as a “further compromise” and the proposal was the “only way of ensuring that this building will continue to stand”. Cllr Paul Hodgson-Jones, speaking as ward councillor for Holywell-cum-Needingworth, said the school hall would “not be open to the public to see”. The Conservative councillor said: “They will still be able to see that it’s an old school hall from the outside because it’s evident from the architecture.” Cllr Julie Kerr agreed that the hall would be too big for a room in a home of that size and couldn’t be maintained “as a viable room”. The independent councillor said: “The person who owns it is clearly passionate about the building, he lives next door, he cares about it, he cares about the village. “I couldn’t think of a more suitable person to renovate it.” Cllr Peter Gammons said it was a “very emotionally challenging thing” being faced with the possibility “it could collapse and be lost forever”. But, the Reform UK councillor, said this should “perhaps have been considered before buying it”. He said: “I don’t know that we can vote against the conservation officer on things which are regarded as being of historical importance. “But the other side of it is, we want to see this building preserved – we don’t want to see it lost.” The committee voted to approve the plans.

Sentencing him at the same court, Judge Stephen Robbins imposed a nine-month prison sentence and ordered Alford to pay £3,000 in costs. On November 10, 2004, the star was convicted of using disorderly behaviour or threatening words "likely to cause harassment, alarm or distress". Less than two years later, on January 9, 2006, Alford was sentenced at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court after admitting to drink driving. He was handed a 16-month driving ban after crashing his Rover into three cars in Islington, north London, on April 2 the previous year. Alford pleaded guilty to a minor road traffic offence which occurred on the same date and was fined £150 and ordered to pay £100 in costs. He next appeared at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court on October 10, 2018, accused of smashing the window of a council bin lorry. He pleaded guilty to a charge of criminal damage but entered a not guilty plea to two counts of assault on a police officer. Alford later pleaded guilty to two counts of resisting an officer and was given a 12-month community order at a sentencing hearing on January 29, 2019. He was also ordered to pay a total of £400 in compensation, complete a rehabilitative activity and serve a curfew on an electronic tag. Born in Glasgow, Alford rose to fame as fireman Billy Ray in ITV drama London’s Burning (Image: Dominic Lipinski/PA Wire) Police records reveal Alford was also issued with two fixed penalty notices between December 2010 and 2017. The first was issued on December 2, 2010, after he was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in a public place. The second was issued on September 7, 2017, when Alford was again arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly. Officers were called to a McDonald's restaurant but the actor left the scene and was later "found by police nearby walking in the road, causing cars to swerve to avoid him". Alford was found unresponsive on his bed when staff opened his cell door at HMP Bure near Norwich and medics were called. Norfolk Coroner's Court opened an inquest into the death of the 54-year-old on June 16 with his provisional cause of death given as ischaemic heart disease. The Prisons and Probation Ombudsman confirmed it is conducting an independent investigation into the death. During his trial last year, the court heard Alford sexually assaulted the girls while they were drunk following a night out at the pub. The offences took place at the home of a third girl whose father was friends with Alford. The disgraced actor purchased £250 worth of food, alcohol and cigarettes from a petrol station in the early hours of the morning. Alford then had sexual intercourse with the 14-year-old girl in the garden and downstairs toilet of the home. He also inappropriately touched the 15-year-old girl as she lay half asleep on the living room sofa. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Sir David Attenborough issues heartfelt message as he thanks the public
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Sir David Attenborough has thanked the public after the successful purchase of a 9,500-acre estate in north-east England. The Rothbury Estate in Northumberland, acquired by The Wildlife Trusts and Northumberland Wildlife Trust following a two-year fundraising campaign and priced at £30 million, marks the largest land purchase in England in decades. Sir David, president emeritus of The Wildlife Trusts, said: "The Wildlife Trusts called for your support and you answered in your thousands. "The appeal to secure the future of the Rothbury Estate in Northumberland has been successful and now the opportunity to bring the vision of a landscape where nature and people thrive side by side can become a reality. "This will be a place where nature, community, farming and heritage can combine to create something very special for generations to come. "Thank you very much." The project will focus on nature-friendly farming, restoring bogs, and enhancing wildlife across the estate. Sir David’s early backing generated more than £1 million in donations within a week. The scheme received around £1.9 million from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, as well as £5 million from the National Lottery Heritage Fund. Public donations totalled £17 million, with contributions from more than 25,000 people across 50 countries. Eilish McGuinness, chief executive at The National Lottery Heritage Fund, said: "By working with local communities to develop new approaches to land management, this transformational project has the potential to deliver nature recovery at a grand scale, helping to reconnect people to the unique natural and cultural heritage of this remarkable and nationally significant landscape." A post shared by A Life On Our Planet (@davidattenborough) Mike Pratt, chief executive of Northumberland Wildlife Trust, described it as a "remarkable achievement." Mr Pratt said: "The completion of the Rothbury Estate purchase is a defining moment for Northumberland and the North East. "Opportunities of this scale and significance are incredibly rare. "By securing this extraordinary landscape, we’ve the potential to create a flagship for nature recovery supported by sustainable farming, whilst delivering lasting benefits for wildlife, local people and the rural economy for generations to come." Portions of the estate have already been secured, and initial work is under way to survey wildlife, landscapes, and historical features. Sir David has previously praised the estate’s remote beauty, where visitors can explore crags and prehistoric rock art.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Fake beauty products found to contain mercury, lead, nicotine and methanol
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Counterfeit beauty products containing mercury, lead and methanol are putting consumers at risk, following testing of hauls seized by Trading Standards. The toxic chemicals were found in fake cosmetics, skincare and perfumes seized during recent investigations, with four in 10 seized cosmetics found to contain potentially harmful substances. Among the most alarming discoveries was a skincare product containing 13,200 parts per million of mercury, as well as high levels of lead in lipsticks, eyeshadows and contour products. Nicotine was also found in some counterfeit perfumes, and one fake fragrance was made up of approximately 80 per cent methanol. The Intellectual Property Office has issued warnings. (Image: IPO/Press Association) Rani Ghosh, an independent toxicologist, said: "When you hear that mercury has been found in face cream, lead in make-up or nicotine in perfume, it raises serious questions about what is going into these products and how they are being made. "Some reactions to unsafe cosmetics may be visible, such as irritation, swelling or changes to the skin. "But what concerns me as a toxicologist is what you might not see. "Substances such as mercury and lead can affect the body internally, and those effects may not be immediately obvious. "Counterfeit beauty products can look incredibly convincing. "You cannot tell from the packaging what chemicals are inside, how the product has been made, or what risk it might pose. "That is why knowing where your beauty products come from matters." The Intellectual Property Office’s (IPO) latest Counterfeit Goods Tracker revealed that one in five 18 to 24-year-olds who bought beauty products last year knowingly bought counterfeits, up from six per cent in 2023. In July, the Police Intellectual Property Crime Unit and Greater Manchester Police seized 1,666 counterfeit hair products, including extensions, shampoos and conditioners, from a warehouse in Manchester. A separate raid in Bolton uncovered £2 million worth of fake goods. This included perfume, cosmetics, clothing and vapes. The IPO’s Face the Fakes campaign is working with content creators and the beauty industry to raise awareness of the potential harms of counterfeit beauty products. Helen Barnham, head of enforcement engagement at the IPO, said: "These findings show why counterfeit beauty products can pose such serious risks to consumers. "Products can look remarkably convincing, but behind the packaging they can contain dangerous substances that have no place in the cosmetics people use every day, and can be made in appalling, unhygienic conditions. Counterfeit manufacturing equipment. (Image: IPO/Press Association) "Counterfeiters exploit the names and reputations of brands that consumers know and trust, while bypassing the rigorous safety standards that legitimate businesses work hard to meet. "With our latest research showing a sharp rise in counterfeit beauty buying among young adults, we want to make sure people understand the potential risks and know how to protect themselves. "Our Face the Fakes campaign is giving consumers practical advice to shop more safely, including checking who is actually selling a product and choosing trusted sources." Dr Emma Meredith, director-general of the Cosmetic, Toiletry and Perfumery Association, said: "There is a rigorous safety framework behind every legitimate cosmetic product sold in the UK. "Ingredients are carefully controlled, products have to be made in clean and hygienic conditions, and they must undergo a safety assessment. "Companies have clear legal responsibilities for the products they place on the market."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New DWP bank checks begin for people claiming three benefits
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: New bank checks targeting people claiming three benefits have begun as part of a major Department for Work and Pensions crackdown on fraud and error. The DWP has issued its first Eligibility Verification Notice, requiring banks and other financial institutions to check information relating to some benefit-receiving accounts. The new system can be used in relation to Universal Credit, Pension Credit and Employment and Support Allowance (ESA). It is designed to identify cases where someone may have savings which affect their entitlement or has remained abroad for longer than benefit rules allow. However, the DWP has stressed that the powers do not give officials access to people's bank accounts, transactions or information about their spending habits. Instead, financial institutions will be asked to check relevant benefit-receiving accounts against specified eligibility rules and flag cases where further investigation could be required. A flag will not itself mean somebody has committed benefit fraud or done anything wrong. The Government also says no decision about a person's benefit entitlement can be made solely using information provided through the new system. Undeclared savings and the amount of time claimants spend outside the country are two of the areas the Government hopes the checks will help identify. The DWP estimates fraud and error involving undeclared savings and time spent abroad in relation to Universal Credit and Pension Credit cost taxpayers £1.5 billion in 2025-26. The Eligibility Verification Measure is expected to generate £1.2 billion in savings by 2030-31. Minister for Innovation, Fraud and Debt Lilian Greenwood said: “Benefit fraudsters should be looking over their shoulder. These new powers will help us crack down on those who deliberately abuse the system, while ensuring people receive the right support at the right time. “We are not interested in where people do their weekly shop or how much they’re spending on new clothes. Banks will simply be asked to identify if somebody may no longer meet the rules for the benefits they receive, allowing us to investigate further where necessary. “With £1.2 billion in savings expected by 2030/31, this is a major step forward in tackling fraud and error, protecting public money and ensuring support goes to those who genuinely need it.” Being flagged through the system will not automatically result in someone's benefits being stopped. The DWP says a flag does not establish fraud or wrongdoing and further enquiries would have to be made. The measure is initially being introduced through a "test-and-learn" phase and will be subject to independent oversight before any wider rollout. The powers were introduced through the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Act 2025 and form part of the Government's wider efforts to reduce fraud and incorrect benefit payments. Further measures are also planned, including 2,000 additional anti-fraud specialists being deployed to Jobcentres and tougher checks involving Universal Credit claims from people who have gone abroad. The Government says its broader package of measures is intended to save taxpayers £14.6 billion over the next five years.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 12 ways John Healey’s Budget 2026 plans could affect your money
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Chancellor John Healey has unveiled a series of measures aimed at easing the cost of living, supporting pensioners and helping households manage their finances. From £100 energy payments and changes to pension tax to a freeze on the cash ISA allowance and new help for first-time buyers, the Budget contains several announcements that could affect what people pay, save and receive. Here are 12 key changes and what they could mean for your money. Around 20 million households in council tax bands A to D will receive a £100 payment directly into their bank accounts this winter to help with rising energy bills. The Government said the scheme would cost £2.6billion and provide support during the coldest months. The Chancellor also extended the cut to VAT on electricity until July, which he said would take £50 off the annual price cap. Pensioners whose income is no higher than the value of the full new State Pension will not pay income tax under the Government’s new pension tax allowance during this Parliament. The measure is intended to protect pensioners receiving the full new State Pension from income tax as payments rise. However, pensioners with additional private pensions, earnings or savings interest could still need to consider their total taxable income. More than 13 million State Pension recipients are set to receive a 3.9% increase from April next year under the triple lock. The increase will provide a boost to pensioners’ regular income, although the amount each person receives will depend on their entitlement and whether they receive the new or old State Pension. The Chancellor also promised that every penny of the pension fund surplus for ex-mineworkers would go to miners, alongside a commitment to continue working towards the full transfer of the guarantor’s fund. Martin Lewis said the Chancellor had told him that gas standing charges would be scrapped in 2027. The MoneySavingExpert founder said the charge currently costs around £108 a year, but warned that the cost would be shifted to unit rates. That means households would pay more for each unit of gas they use instead. Mr Lewis estimated that around 60% of people could pay less, while 40% could pay more, depending on their consumption. The Chancellor is also expected to discuss removing electricity standing charges with Ofgem, although this is considered more complicated. Motorists will continue to benefit from the 5p-a-litre fuel duty cut until July 2027. The Chancellor said the extension would help households, hauliers and farmers amid continued pressure on fuel prices. He also announced that the higher mileage allowance for people using their cars for work would increase from 25p to 35p per mile. The increase to the standard mileage rate introduced earlier this year will also become permanent. Savers will be able to continue putting up to £20,000 a year into a cash ISA without paying tax on the interest. The Chancellor abandoned a planned reduction to the tax-free cash ISA limit, saying the allowance would remain unchanged for people of all ages. He also announced plans to work with the sector to create a new Starter ISA aimed at rewarding first-time investors. The decision will be welcome news for savers who want to keep their money in cash while protecting the interest they earn from tax. The Chancellor announced £4.7billion in Government-backed lending for a new Your First Home equity loan scheme, due to launch next spring. The scheme is intended to help first-time buyers who do not have financial support from family. He also announced plans for a new First Time Buyer ISA to replace the Lifetime ISA. In addition, the Government will end the Lifetime ISA penalty for people buying homes costing more than £450,000. Those affected will get back at least what they paid in, according to the Chancellor. The changes could be significant for aspiring homeowners struggling to save a deposit or facing property prices above the existing Lifetime ISA limit. The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage will increase by 3.9%, benefiting 2.3 million of the lowest-paid workers. The Chancellor said the increase was intended to help people manage everyday costs, including the weekly shop. The actual benefit will depend on the rate each worker currently receives, their age and the number of hours they work. The Government will change Carer’s Allowance rules so people no longer lose their entire benefit because they earn just a penny above the earnings limit. The Chancellor said the cliff edge would be removed, allowing carers to keep some support as their earnings rise. The change is intended to make it easier for people to combine paid work with caring responsibilities without risking the loss of their entire allowance over a small increase in income. The Government is suspending tariffs on more than 100 supermarket products in an attempt to keep prices down. The Chancellor said the move was intended to help households with the cost of the weekly shop. The impact on individual shoppers will depend on how retailers pass on any savings, so it does not guarantee that every affected product will become cheaper. The Chancellor announced changes to how self-assessed income tax is collected, with affected taxpayers expected to make smaller, more regular payments rather than facing large bills that can be harder to pay. The changes could help people manage their cash flow and budget for tax more consistently. However, the announcement concerns the timing of payments rather than an automatic reduction in the amount of tax owed. The Chancellor also announced that the tax-free trading allowance for people earning money from a new venture would rise from £1,000 to £3,000. Self-employed fathers and partners will become eligible for paid parental leave for the first time. The Chancellor described the announcement as a first step towards wider change, saying he had listened to calls from MPs about paternity leave. The measure could provide additional financial support to eligible self-employed parents following the arrival of a child. The announcement did not set out all the detailed eligibility rules or payment arrangements, so further information will be needed to establish exactly who qualifies and how much they will receive. Recommended reading: The biggest immediate help announced by the Chancellor includes the £100 energy payment for eligible households, the extension of the electricity VAT cut and the continued fuel duty reduction. Pensioners will also be watching the new pension tax allowance and the 3.9% State Pension increase, while savers have been given certainty that the cash ISA allowance will remain at £20,000. Other measures, including the gas standing charge changes and new first-time buyer support, will take longer to come into effect.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Coffee sold at TK Maxx recalled over mould toxin above legal limit
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A batch of ground coffee has been recalled over a mould toxin. Bialetti's Perfetto Moka caramel-flavoured coffee, sold at TK Maxx, contained ochratoxin A above the permitted limit, according to recall notices from the retailer and manufacturer. The recall applies to 250g packs with batch code LC5 BD149T and a best-before date of May 29, 2027. TK Maxx said the coffee was sold in its stores between July and November 2025. An urgent recall has been issued for the Bialetti Perfetto Moka Ground Coffee Flavoured with Caramel after it was found to contain levels of Ochratoxin A above the permitted limit (Image: Kennedy News & Media) Customers with the affected coffee are being told not to consume it and to return it. In its recall notice, TK Maxx said: "This product is being recalled because testing identified levels of Ochratoxin A above the permitted limit." The retailer said the coffee could be returned to any TK Maxx or Homesense store for a full refund or replacement. Bialetti said customers returning the affected batch to the point of purchase would receive a full refund even without a receipt. Ochratoxin A is a naturally occurring toxin produced by certain moulds, according to the Food Safety Authority of Ireland, which also issued an alert about the batch. The authority said consuming the affected product does not pose an immediate health risk, but continuous consumption over a long period may pose a potential risk. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: £100 energy bill support to be sent directly to bank accounts for 20 million people

The £2.6billion scheme is designed to give families breathing space during the coldest months, as households face pressure from energy costs and the impact of conflict in the Middle East. Announcing the measure in his Budget, Mr Healey told MPs: “Madam Deputy Speaker, let me say this to families at home: I know that with the conflict in the Middle East, rising energy bills are a real worry. “I know that people look to government at times like this not to solve all their problems, but to give them a bit of breathing space. “So today, I'm taking one further step. He added: “Madam Deputy Speaker, 50 pounds off VAT, 100 pounds off council tax, for this winter two tax cuts for next year fairer bills, and for the long term radical reform of the energy market to produce cheaper power.” The payment is intended for households in council tax bands A to D, with the money paid directly into bank accounts. The announcement sets out a £100 payment for eligible households this winter, but further details on how payments will be administered and when the money will arrive have not been provided in the statement quoted above. The Chancellor said the devolved governments would receive funding to support households in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, but called on them to take their own action to provide similar help. The energy payment is part of a wider Budget package that Mr Healey said would support working people while maintaining the Government's commitment not to raise taxes on “working people”. The Chancellor told MPs that the Budget was designed to provide breathing space on the cost of living and the cost of doing business, support businesses and growth, and tackle longer-term challenges including energy, national security, public services and housing. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Chancellor John Healey announced he will increase the national minimum wage and national living wage by 3.9%, taking the over 21 rate from £12.71 to £13.20 an hour. He said: "For 2.3 million of our lowest paid workers, I am increasing both the national minimum wage and the national living wage by 3.9%.” Mr Healey opened his Budget statement by saying it is for “the working people of Britain, for British businesses, big and small”, built on “fiscal discipline”. He said: “First, by giving Britain some breathing space on the cost of living and the cost of business, “Second, backing the enterprise of British business to unleash innovation and growth in every postcode “And third, by tackling the big challenges on energy, on national security, on public service transformation and on housing.” The real Living Wage and the Government’s National Living Wage are often confused, but they are different pay rates with different purposes. The National Living Wage is the legal minimum employers must pay eligible workers aged 21 and over. The real Living Wage is a voluntary rate calculated independently to reflect the cost of living, with a separate, higher rate for London. The real Living Wage currently stands at £14.10 an hour across the UK and £15.45 in London. The key difference is that the Government’s rates are legal minimums, while the real Living Wage is a voluntary benchmark based on the cost of living. Recommended reading: The real Living Wage is a voluntary employer commitment that covers workers aged 18 and over. Nearly 17,000 employers, including IKEA, KPMG and LUSH, have signed up to pay it, according to the Living Wage campaign. The movement says almost half a million workers receive a pay increase each year as a result. However, workers do not automatically have a legal right to the real Living Wage. They are entitled to the statutory minimum that applies to them unless their employer has committed to a higher rate or their contract provides for one.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire council pledges £2m to tackle EHCP assessment delays
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Long waits for vital education, health and care plan (EHCP) assessments could finally be addressed as part of a new funding push in Cambridgeshire. The funding was approved at a meeting of the council’s children and young people committee on Tuesday, October 20. Cllr Edna Murphy, chair of the committee, said: "We know that the council’s performance on EHCP assessments has not been good enough. "While service delivery has improved significantly over the last year, these improvements have been outstripped by a continued unprecedented increase in demand. "I want to apologise to the families who have been kept waiting, in some cases far beyond the statutory deadline, and reassure them that improving the timeliness and quality of the EHCP processes is an absolute priority for us. "We’re working hard to provide fair opportunities and the best possible start in life for all Cambridgeshire’s children and young people, regardless of need – so I’m really pleased we have today supported additional investment that aims to tackle the long waiting times for assessments. "We will be carefully and closely monitoring the impact of this new programme, which I fully expect will prove to be a decisive turning point for the waiting families across our county." Under current law, assessments must be completed within 20 weeks, but rising demand has led to significant delays in Cambridgeshire. The additional investment will fund a 12-month recovery programme, prioritising the longest-waiting and highest-risk cases, subject to final approval by the council’s strategy and resources committee.
