summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DWP new State Pension to rise almost £500 to more than £13,000 a year
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of State Pension recipients are on course for a pay rise next April, with the full new State Pension set to increase by nearly £490 over the year. The increase is 3.9% under the Triple Lock, after Chancellor John Healey confirmed the figures in his first Budget. This follows official figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS), which showed average earnings growth of 3.9% between May and July. This was higher than September's Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation rate of 3.5% and the Triple Lock's minimum increase of 2.5%. The Triple Lock means the State Pension rises each April by whichever is highest out of average earnings growth, inflation or 2.5%. The figures point to a weekly increase of £9.40 for people receiving the full new State Pension, taking payments from £241.30 to around £250.70. That would mean an extra £488.80 over a full year, with the annual payment rising from £12,547.60 to approximately £13,036.40. The full new State Pension would therefore pass £13,000 a year for the first time. But, it's important to say that pensioners aged 75 and over are on the older basic system of pension, which is still lower. The expected 3.9% increase would also apply to the full basic State Pension, paid to people who reached State Pension age before April 2016. The projected rates for the 2027/28 financial year are: Full new State Pension Full basic State Pension These figures are projections based on a 3.9% rise. The actual amounts will depend on the Government's formal uprating decision and rounding. It is important to remember that not everyone receives the full State Pension. The amount paid depends on an individual's National Insurance record and other entitlement rules. People are able to claim the new State Pension when they reach State Pension age if they are: Older pensioners get the basic State Pension, and some also get Additional State Pension. Recommended reading: Labour has pledged to maintain the Triple Lock for the duration of the current Parliament. Changes to the State Pension uprating system are scheduled to take effect from April 2030. The latest earnings figures mean the 2027 increase is expected to be driven by wage growth rather than inflation. September's CPI inflation rate was 3.5%, up from 3.1% in August. ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said increased fuel prices were again the main driver, with diesel prices reaching their highest level since July 2022.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Ahead of the Budget 2026 tomorrow Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey have announced five “everyday fixes” covering work-related travel, food prices, parental pay and support for unpaid carers, alongside plans to make sending and returning parcels easier. The measures are expected to feature in Wednesday’s Budget, with Mr Burnham promising further action to help families and businesses. Millions of employees and self-employed people who drive for work are set to benefit from changes to the tax-free mileage allowance. The Government will make the existing 55p-a-mile rate permanent for the first 10,000 business miles. For mileage above that threshold, the rate will increase from 25p to 35p per mile. The Government expects the overall package to help around three million workers. Shoppers could save money on their food bills after ministers announced plans to remove tariffs on more than 100 products. Popular items including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins are among the goods covered by the changes. The Treasury estimates the tariff cuts will save households around £21 on food shopping over the course of a year. The changes are also intended to reduce costs for farmers by cutting tariffs on fertilisers, while households that use kerosene for heating could benefit from a separate tariff reduction. More than 150,000 parents a year are expected to benefit from an extension to parental pay. The changes will include self-employed fathers who have previously missed out on the support. The measure is intended to give more parents financial support during the early weeks of their child's life. Further details are expected as the Budget measures are set out. The Government has promised to end the controversial Carers’ Allowance earnings cliff edge. Under the current system, unpaid carers can lose their entire benefit if they earn even a few pence above the weekly earnings limit. The Government plans to introduce a taper instead, reducing the benefit by £1 for every £1 earned above the limit. The change is intended to prevent carers from suddenly losing all their support when they take on extra paid work. The Government is also rolling out hundreds of additional Post Office drop boxes. The aim is to reduce the number of people who have to queue at counters to send or return parcels. The extra facilities are expected to be particularly useful in the run-up to Christmas, when parcel volumes typically rise. The Prime Minister said the Government wanted to address everyday financial pressures alongside its wider economic plans. He said: “We are taking on the big challenges facing the country. But that doesn’t mean losing sight of the everyday problems that cost people money or simply aren’t fair. “If you’re a nurse driving for work, a parent spending those precious first weeks with your new baby, or an unpaid carer picking up an extra shift, these changes will make life a little easier and put more money back in your pocket. “And at Wednesday’s Budget, we’ll go further to give families and businesses the breathing space they need today, while we build a stronger economy, transform our country and bring down cost for people long-term.” Chancellor John Healey said the measures were only a small part of the Government's plans to ease pressure on household budgets. He said: “Today’s everyday fixes are just a small part of what we are doing to give families a bit of breathing space. “Conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting families here at home through higher everyday costs. “We can’t control global events, but we can act where we can make a difference.” Recommended reading: The Budget is also expected to deliver a £432million boost to help get homeless people off the streets by Christmas. Mr Burnham said he wanted to ensure “every single person” sleeping on the streets received an offer of help by the end of the year. The Prime Minister has indicated that further measures to support families and businesses will be announced in Wednesday’s Budget.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire MP is calling for the government to protect kidney care during a major hospital redevelopment. He visited the renal unit, spoke to staff and patients, and raised concerns about dialysis under the New Hospital Programme. Mr Obese-Jecty said: "Visiting the unit and speaking directly with patients and staff brought home just how vital this service is to our community. "Haemodialysis is physically exhausting and emotionally demanding; local patients should never have to carry the additional anxiety of travelling miles out of our area simply to access life-sustaining treatment." Mr Obese-Jecty has submitted written parliamentary questions to the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC), requesting transparent funding commitments and clear confirmation that constituents will not be forced to travel outside Huntingdonshire for regular treatment. He said: "While the rebuild of Hinchingbrooke Hospital is an essential milestone to modernise our health estate and removing reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete (RAAC), facility improvements must protect core clinical specialities. "I have taken our community's case to Westminster to secure binding commitments from ministers that renal dialysis will stay right here in Huntingdon for the long term." Patients with end-stage kidney conditions often attend dialysis sessions several times a week. If the service were moved, patients would face lengthy journeys to Addenbrooke’s Hospital in Cambridge or Peterborough City Hospital. Hinchingbrooke Hospital was added to the New Hospital Programme in May 2023. North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust invited the public to have their say on site accessibility and navigation; the desired patient and visitor experience, including digital technology and single rooms; and how the hospital can better support community health and wellbeing. The redevelopment programme is designed to address the challenges associated with ageing hospital infrastructure. A new hospital is expected to be delivered on the existing site, due to open by the end of 2032.

The victim attended Hinchingbrooke Hospital for treatment for serious but not life-threatening injuries. Officers located the victims at their nearby home and they were taken to hospital, where they were treated for multiple serious but not life-threatening stab wounds. He pleaded guilty to two counts of wounding with intent and possession of a bladed article in a public place. O’Donnell, 21, of Tilling Way, Littleport, pleaded guilty to affray and was sentenced to 19 months in prison, suspended for two years. He must also carry out 100 hours of unpaid work. Detective Constable Charmaine Wood, who investigated, said: "This was a completely unprovoked attack on two men. Although the education watchdog said it does not comment on individual providers, its guidance on suspension is clear. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: What will Budget mean for pensioners as State Pension set to hit £13,036?
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of pensioners are waiting to see whether Chancellor John Healey will announce a major change to the tax-free personal allowance in the Budget 2026. The Government is expected to set out how it will protect people whose only income is the State Pension from paying Income Tax, after next April’s increase is set to push the full new State Pension above the existing £12,570 personal allowance. According to some reports, ministers are considering raising the tax-free threshold for low-income pensioners to £13,036, matching the projected annual value of the full new State Pension from April 2027. This could shield almost one million pensioners from Income Tax and cost around £200million a year by the end of the decade. However, the reported plan would not mean every pensioner becomes exempt from tax. People with private pensions, savings income or other sources of taxable income could still face an Income Tax bill. The full new State Pension is on course to increase by 3.9% from April 2027 under the triple lock. This would take the weekly payment from £241.30 to £250.70, an annual increase of around £489, bringing the yearly total to approximately £13,036. The increase reflects earnings growth, which is one of three measures used to determine the annual State Pension rise. A post shared by Martin Lewis (@martinlewismse) Under the triple lock, payments increase each April by whichever is highest of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5%. The projected increase would take the full new State Pension above the current £12,570 Income Tax personal allowance for the first time. The personal allowance is the amount someone can earn in a tax year before they start paying Income Tax. Without a change to the rules, pensioners whose only income is the full new State Pension could technically have a small amount of income above the standard tax-free threshold. The Government has previously promised that people whose only income is the State Pension will be protected from paying Income Tax, with further details expected in the Budget. The Times reports that ministers intend to achieve this by increasing the personal allowance for low-income pensioners to £13,036. If introduced as reported, the measure could mean almost one million pensioners avoid paying Income Tax on their State Pension. The proposed threshold would also rise in line with increases to the State Pension during the current Parliament, according to the newspaper. However, the details of how eligibility would work have not yet been confirmed. Steve Webb, a partner at pension consultants LCP, warned that the policy could create difficulties if the higher allowance is restricted to people on low incomes. He said: “The gap between the new state pension and the tax threshold is set to grow every year, which will make the policy hard to switch off. “But if it continues, the cost will grow and grow. And if the extra allowance is available only to those on a low income, there could be a growing ‘cliff edge’ problem where those with very small amounts of private income lose the whole allowance and end up worse off than those with nothing.” The concern is that someone with a small private pension could lose access to the additional allowance and end up paying more tax than someone whose only income is the State Pension. Pensioners receiving the basic State Pension under the old system will also see their payments increase next April. Under the projected 3.9% rise, the full basic State Pension would increase from £184.90 to £192.10 a week. That would amount to around £9,989 a year, leaving it below the existing £12,570 personal allowance. However, many people who reached State Pension age under the old system receive additional payments on top of the basic pension. These can include additional State Pension entitlements, such as the State Earnings-Related Pension Scheme (SERPS), meaning their total income may be higher. The amount someone receives depends on their National Insurance record and individual circumstances. People with gaps in their contributions may receive less than the full new State Pension. The tax proposal comes as the Government has also announced plans to adjust how the triple lock operates from April 2030. Under the proposals outlined by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the State Pension would continue to rise by at least inflation or 2.5%, while still tracking average earnings over time. The Government says the overhaul would help fund a new National Care Service in England. Any change to the triple lock could have implications for pensioners' future income, particularly as the State Pension continues to rise alongside wages and inflation. Recommended reading: The Budget is also expected to settle questions about whether the Government will change the amount people can withdraw from their private pensions tax-free. There had been speculation that ministers were considering cutting the maximum tax-free lump sum from £268,275 to £100,000. People can normally withdraw up to 25% of their pension pot tax-free, subject to the relevant limits and protections. The normal minimum pension age is 55, rising to 57 from April 2028 for most people.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Home Bargains hot water bottle warning after customer's horror burns
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A woman needed surgery after a hot water bottle spilled on her. Megan Shannon said she suffered first- and second-degree burns when the long bottle she bought from Home Bargains leaked in June 2025. She said she had wrapped the £7.99 Home Collections bottle around her waist to ease period pains and heard a pop after about 10 minutes. She said: "I just heard a pop, and felt the hot water trickle down my stomach, my legs, my thighs, my pelvis." Megan said the water was boiling hot and ran down her legs when she stood up. Megan was rushed to Whiston Hospital in Prescot, Merseyside (Image: Kennedy News/@meg.shann) Her boyfriend called an ambulance while she used cold water in the shower to cool her burns. She said: "It's the worst physical pain I've ever been in, it's like having my skin unpeeled multiple times in the same area." Megan, from Liverpool, was taken to Whiston Hospital in Prescot, where she said a team of plastic surgeons, doctors and nurses assessed her injuries. Megan said her groin, upper thighs and lower abdomen had first- and second-degree burns. Three days after the incident, she underwent a treatment called Recell, which she described as a skin graft treatment. She said: "It was petrifying. I had to have surgery, a treatment called Recell, it's a skin graft treatment. They take skin from somewhere in my body and spray it back on to me." Megan said doctors treated blisters and it took weeks before she could walk comfortably. She said: "To be comfortable walking it took weeks and because of the area I wasn't even able to wear underwear. My mental health went so down after that." She said the burns had mostly healed but marks remained and had left her feeling self-conscious. Megan said she would not use a hot water bottle again, adding that doctors had recommended a microwaveable wheat bag to her. Home Bargains said it was sorry to hear about her experience and encouraged her to get in touch so it could look into the incident. A spokesperson said: "We take the safety of our customers extremely seriously, which is why all our hot water bottles are stringently tested to ensure they meet the relevant safety standards and are labelled with appropriate safety warnings." The spokesperson added: "Hot water bottles can pose a risk of burns if they are not cared for or used correctly, which is why it is important that customers follow the safety instructions provided." NHS Scotland advises people not to use boiling water when filling a hot water bottle, and to let the water cool for a few minutes first. It also recommends filling the bottle no more than two-thirds full, carefully squeezing out the air and using a cover to protect the skin. The NHS says burns and scalds should be held under cool running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible, within three hours of the injury. It advises calling 999 or going to A&E for a very large or deep burn, or one affecting the face, genitals or bottom.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: JD Wetherspoon customers banned from wearing this item in all 800 UK pubs
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Meta Glasses are now banned at all JD Wetherspoon venues across the UK. Customers can no longer wear Meta glasses, or any other smart glasses, at any of its more than 800 pubs. The devices, which can record video, photos and audio, have raised privacy concerns due to their ability to film without drawing attention. The ban, announced in August, follows growing reports of people secretly recording strangers and sharing footage online. A JD Wetherspoon spokesperson, explaining the ban, said: "Like many hospitality companies, Wetherspoon has CCTV cameras for security reasons, but their use is strictly controlled by data legislation. "Apart from that, the general code that applies in our pubs, and most pubs, is that you can’t film customers or employees without their permission. "Meta glasses seem to breach this code, and common sense, by enabling surreptitious surveillance, so our instinct is to say turn off the cameras. "This is akin to our efforts to stop audible playing of videos in our pubs, which also invades people’s space." Meta reassured people that their glasses have a light that turns on to let people know when a photo or video is being taken. A spokesperson for the company added: "People use our glasses because they're helpful and help them stay in the moment, from listening to music to live translation or hands-free calls. "They also provide critical new technology for people who are low-sighted or hard of hearing and limiting how people can use this technology would be a major step backwards. "Naturally some places shouldn't be filmed at all and that's reasonable but rules should be applied consistently." Around 88% of Wetherspoon customers agree with the Meta Glasses ban. (Image: Patrick Glover) We asked readers whether they agreed with the Meta Glasses ban in Wetherspoon pubs, with 88% (4243 people) saying 'yes'. Around 9% (441) of people didn't agree with the ban, while 3% (141) said they weren't sure. Wetherspoon also recently banned customers from playing music out loud or taking calls on speaker at its UK pubs. While Meta Glasses, playing music out loud, and taking calls on speaker are all banned at Wetherspoon venues across the UK, poppies are not. The confirmation comes after customers at The Star, a JD Wetherspoon pub in Gosport, were denied entry on Sunday (October 25) for wearing poppies. The incident occurred during a day of demonstrations in the town, and among those turned away were veterans and members of the public, including Reform UK councillor George Madgwick. Cllr Madgwick said they were denied entry after door staff told them wearing poppies breached company policy. JD Wetherspoon has confirmed that poppies are not banned in its UK pubs. (Image: Getty Images) JD Wetherspoon has since insisted there is "no ban on poppies" in its pubs and apologised for the incident. A Wetherspoon spokesperson said: "Wetherspoon has been a long-standing supporter of the Royal British Legion Poppy Appeal, with poppies for sale in our pubs, including the Star. "There is no ban on poppies in Wetherspoon pubs. "However, there were some standard security measures in place today, as a result of demonstrations in the town. "Unfortunately, some members of the public, including some wearing poppies, did not gain entry to the pub. "The pub closed to all customers, on advice of the police, at 5pm and remains closed today. "We apologise to any regular customers who have been inconvenienced by today’s events and look to forward to welcoming everyone back tomorrow." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Budget 2026 what to expect from John Healey as Chancellor prepares major announcement
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: John Healey will deliver his first Budget as Chancellor today, October 28, with households and businesses waiting to see whether he will announce further help with the cost of living. Andy Burnham's Chancellor faces a difficult economic backdrop, with pressure on public finances compounded by higher borrowing costs linked to turmoil in international markets following the Iran war. Ministers have already unveiled a series of measures aimed at easing everyday costs, including changes to Carers’ Allowance, mileage payments and food tariffs. Further announcements are expected on energy bills, fuel duty, wages and public spending. But with the Government facing tight financial constraints, the Chancellor will also have to balance support for households against his commitment to meeting the fiscal rules. Here is what to expect from the Budget 2026, including the measures already announced and the policies reportedly under consideration. There's been much debate about how the state pension and personal allowance issue will be resolved, and given that the state pension is tipped to rise above the income tax threshold in April, today is likely to be the day that's finally sorted. In a post on social media, Martin Lewis highlighted that the full new State Pension is expected to rise to around £13,040 a year from April 2027, while the Income Tax personal allowance remains frozen at £12,570. Martin pointed out that John Healey has said the Government will honour former Chancellor Rachel Reeves' promise that pensioners whose only income is the State Pension will not pay Income Tax. He questioned whether that protection could create a cliff edge for those with even a small amount of extra income. “An important question for @JohnHealey_MP,” Martin wrote. He continued: “So the full new State Pension would normally attract tax. Yet you've said you'll honour former Chancellor Rachel Reeves' promise that those whose ONLY income is the State Pension won't pay tax. But will that be a cliff edge?” Of course, many would like to see the HMRC Personal Allowance increase for everyone. As Alex Beavis, Interim Director of Banking at LHV Bank, says, it's particularly key for savers. He's calling on the Chancellor to raise the allowance: "The biggest tax rise facing savers won't make the Budget headlines. It's already happening to your hard-earned cash, year after year. "The Personal Savings Allowance hasn't moved since 2016. With savings tax rates due to rise by two percentage points from April, more people will be taxed twice on the same money." Measures to ease pressure on household budgets are expected to feature prominently in the Budget. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked the Chancellor and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to examine whether standing charges on gas bills could be scrapped. Ministers are also looking at whether to break the link between wholesale gas prices and electricity bills, despite gas accounting for only a proportion of total electricity generation. Fuel duty is another key issue for motorists. Mr Healey is expected to cancel a planned January increase, keeping fuel duty frozen at 52p per litre for a 16th consecutive year. The reported move follows concerns about rising petrol and diesel prices and the impact of the Iran war. Ministers have unveiled five “everyday fixes” ahead of the Budget. These include: The Prime Minister has said further measures will be announced on Wednesday to give families and businesses more “breathing space”. The Chancellor is expected to announce an increase in the minimum wage. The national living wage is set to rise by nearly 4%, from £12.71 to £13.20 an hour. The reported plans would also end the trend of increasing the minimum wage for workers aged 18 to 20 by a larger percentage than the rate for older workers. Instead, the younger age group's minimum wage would rise at roughly the same rate as the national living wage, according to the report. The details remain subject to confirmation in the Budget. The Treasury estimates that reducing paperwork and other administrative requirements could save businesses around £800million. The proposals form part of efforts to reduce the burden on firms and support economic growth. Mr Healey has ruled out increasing capital gains tax in the Budget. The tax is charged on profits made when people sell certain assets, such as shares or second homes. Some Labour figures have called for capital gains tax rates to be brought closer to those applied to earnings, but the Chancellor has rejected a rise. A potential increase in the tax surcharge on banks is reportedly under consideration. The surcharge, currently set at 3%, could rise to 8%, reversing a reduction introduced by former chancellor Jeremy Hunt. The Trades Union Congress, which supports the proposal, said the increase could raise £2.25billion a year from banks' “bumper profits”. However, representatives of the financial sector have warned that a higher tax could discourage investment in Britain. It remains to be seen whether the Chancellor will include the proposal in his Budget. Mr Healey has promised to fill a £4.7billion shortfall in Britain's defence investment plan. The plan, one of Sir Keir Starmer's final major announcements as prime minister, promised an additional £15billion for the UK defence sector but allocated only £10.3billion, leaving the Chancellor to find the remaining funding. The additional spending would help raise defence expenditure to 2.7% of the economy by 2027. The Government's longer-term path towards NATO's target of 3.5% of gross domestic product by 2035 is due to be set out at next year's spending review. Mr Healey previously resigned as defence secretary in a dispute over funding, arguing that the Government needed a plan to reach 3% of GDP in 2030. The OBR estimates that reaching that level would cost an additional £17.3billion in 2029/30. More than £600million is set to be committed to projects supporting the development and safe use of artificial intelligence. The planned funding includes: The investment is intended to support the development of AI while strengthening safeguards against potential threats. A £7million fund will be used to examine the feasibility of a potential future bid to host the Olympic and Paralympic Games in northern England. The funding would support a study into whether such a bid could be viable. It does not mean a bid to host the Games has been confirmed. An initial £285million is set to be allocated as part of plans to give mayors and regional leaders in England greater funding and powers. The aim is to allow local leaders to invest in projects in their areas and have more control over regional priorities. More than £1billion is set to be allocated to social and affordable housing. The funding forms part of the Government's wider plans to address housing needs and increase the availability of affordable homes. The Budget is also expected to include an additional £432million for the rough sleeping programme in England. The aim is to help get people off the streets by Christmas. Mr Burnham has said he wants “every single person” sleeping rough to receive an offer of help by the end of the year. The funding was disclosed ahead of the Budget, with the Government expected to set out further details as part of its spending plans. The state of the public finances will be a central issue in Mr Healey’s first Budget. The Chancellor has retained the fiscal rules established by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves. These require day-to-day spending to be funded by tax receipts rather than borrowing by 2029/30, while public debt as a share of the economy must also be falling in the same year. In March, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) forecast that the Government had around £24billion of headroom against its fiscal rules. However, higher borrowing costs could significantly reduce that buffer. The Resolution Foundation estimates that headroom may have fallen to around £12billion, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) believes it could still stand at approximately £20billion. The figures highlight the uncertainty facing the Chancellor as he considers how much additional support he can afford to offer households and businesses. A post shared by Dan T | The Manc Investor (@dantinvests) The Chancellor say not, but some experts advise that it should. Antonia Medlicott, Founder and Managing Director of financial education specialists Investing Insiders, says: “I wouldn’t like to pay more income tax, and I’m sure nobody else would. But a transparent income tax rise is much better than a dozen smaller, stealthy tax grabs that sneak up on ordinary people and increase financial pressure on them. “The chancellor doesn’t have much headroom, and he has made a mistake by ruling out rises in income tax, employee national insurance, and VAT for working people. All three raise serious money. “The easiest of those to raise is the basic rate of income tax. A rise from 20 per cent to 21 per cent would raise about £8bn a year from 2027-28, according to HMRC. That’s about £224 a year for someone earning £35,000, or about £74 for a pensioner on £20,000. “Raising VAT would feed straight into inflation in the middle of an energy shock, while employee national insurance falls only on earnings, so the whole burden lands on workers. Income tax reaches pension income and rental income too, which spreads the load across a much wider base.” Recommended reading: John Healey will deliver the Budget on Wednesday, October 28, 2026. Households will be watching for announcements affecting wages, fuel costs, energy bills and benefits, while businesses will be looking for details on tax, regulation and investment. Although several measures have already been announced, other proposals remain based on reports ahead of the Chancellor's statement and should not be treated as confirmed until the Budget is delivered.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Martin Lewis celebrates end of 'energy poll tax' as £108 Standing Charge axed
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Martin Lewis is celebrating the Government's decision to scrap the £108 gas standing charge, declaring an end to what he has branded an “energy poll tax”. The Money Saving Expert founder said he was “very pleased” after meeting Chancellor John Healey, who confirmed the fixed charge will be removed in 2027. The move marks a major victory for Mr Lewis, who said he had campaigned against standing charges for around six years. Standing charges are added to gas bills regardless of how much energy a household uses, meaning customers can face costs even when they make efforts to cut consumption. Mr Lewis has long argued that the system unfairly penalises people who use less gas, including those trying to keep their bills down. Announcing the news, he said: “I have confirmation that the standing charge on gas bills is to be scrapped in 2027. I've been campaigning on this for about six years, so I am very pleased to hear it.” He added: “It is a moral hazard. It disincentivizes people from cutting their bills. It's a poll tax on energy, if you like.” The typical gas standing charge costs around £108 a year, according to Mr Lewis. Under the planned changes, the charge will be removed and the costs shifted into the unit rate customers pay for each kilowatt hour of gas they use. Mr Lewis said he did not yet know the final increase to unit rates, but estimated it could be just under 1p per kilowatt hour. The changes could come into effect with the October 2027 energy price cap, although January 2028 is another possibility. The exact timing has yet to be confirmed. For households that use very little gas, scrapping the fixed fee could mean no longer paying the same daily charge as a much heavier user simply for having a gas supply. The reform is expected to benefit around 60% of households, with the Treasury estimating an average annual saving of £45 for those who gain. Although Mr Lewis welcomed the announcement, he warned that the change would not mean every household pays less. Because the costs will be transferred to unit rates, people who use more gas could end up paying more. He estimated the dividing line could be around 12,500 kilowatt hours of gas a year, although the final figure will depend on the rates eventually set. Around 40% of households could pay more under the new structure, according to his estimate. Mr Lewis also cited research by Nesta suggesting the majority of people in income groups below £100,000 would be better off following the change. He said vulnerable households with high energy use may need additional support if energy prices remain elevated when the reform comes into force. The gas announcement could also be the first step towards a wider shake-up of energy bills. Mr Lewis said Mr Healey would speak to Ofgem about how electricity standing charges could be removed, too. However, he said the Chancellor had described this as “trickier” and indicated it would take longer. For now, the confirmed plan relates to gas standing charges, with no timetable announced for electricity. The reform will primarily affect standing charges under the energy price cap. Suppliers will still be able to offer different pricing structures on other tariffs. Recommended reading: Mr Lewis also reassured people who already have a fixed energy tariff, saying the planned changes should not alter the rates they have agreed to pay. He said: “As for those on fixes: if you get a fix now, the rate of your fix is fixed, so this should not affect it. You will pay what you pay and if it has standing charges they will continue.” For millions of households, the end of the fixed gas fee will be a welcome move away from paying a charge that stays the same regardless of how much gas they use.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Chancellor John Healey is reportedly preparing to reverse plans to cut the annual ISA allowance from £20,000 to £12,000 in a potential boost for savers. The Chancellor is said to believe reducing the amount people can save tax-free was the wrong way to encourage more Britons to invest in stocks and shares, according to the Financial Times. Instead, Mr Healey is reportedly considering focusing on educating savers about the benefits of investing in the stock market. UNCONFIRMED: Reports in FT 2027 cash isa reduction for under 65s to £12,000 to be scrapped so it will stay at £20,000. — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) October 28, 2026 The reported U-turn would reverse a decision announced by former chancellor Rachel Reeves at last year's autumn Budget. The proposed cut, which would apply to savers aged under 65, is due to come into force in April 2027. Individual Savings Accounts (ISAs) allow people to save or invest without paying tax on interest, dividends or capital gains within the account. The annual ISA allowance currently stands at £20,000, meaning eligible savers can put up to that amount into ISAs each tax year without paying tax on the returns. ISAs remain one of the UK's most popular savings products, with HM Revenue and Customs figures showing that around £135.7billion was paid into adult ISAs in the 2024/25 tax year. That was an annual increase of £32.7billion, with much of the growth coming from cash ISAs. Cash ISA subscriptions rose by 37.5%, an increase of £26.1billion, while subscriptions to stocks and shares ISAs increased by 19.7%, or £6.1billion. Lifetime ISA subscriptions also rose, increasing by 20.1%, equivalent to £472million. The figures suggest that cash ISAs accounted for much of the growth in ISA subscriptions, despite government efforts to encourage more people to invest. Recommended reading: The reported rethink would be a boost for savers who want to retain the flexibility to put up to £20,000 a year into tax-free accounts. It could also be welcomed by banks and building societies, which rely on savings deposits to help fund lending to households and businesses. The reported ISA U-turn would offer some relief to the banking sector ahead of today's Budget, with banks widely expecting the Chancellor to announce higher taxes on the industry. However, the ISA change has not been formally confirmed. The £12,000 limit remains a proposed change unless and until the Government announces otherwise.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Gas standing charges to be scrapped in major Budget energy bill shake-up
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of households are set to see gas standing charges scrapped from 2027, in a major shake-up that could save some families money on their energy bills. The Treasury has announced that Chancellor John Healey will ask energy regulator Ofgem to remove the fixed daily fees “in 2027 or as soon as possible after”. Standing charges are added to gas bills regardless of how much energy a household uses. They cover the cost of delivering gas to homes and businesses and currently cost a typical household around £108 a year. The change is expected to affect around 23 million homes, with the Treasury saying the move could save 60% of households an average of £45 a year. However, the charges will not simply disappear from the energy system. Instead, the fixed costs will be transferred to the unit rate customers pay for each unit of gas they use. This means households that use less gas could benefit, while those that use more may face higher costs per unit. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: “Abolishing gas standing charges is about basic fairness and giving people more control over their bills. “I am determined to reform our broken energy market, so it better serves the public interest.” Simon Francis, coordinator of the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: "Removing the gas standing charge will bring real relief to many low-income households who use very little energy and for prepayment customers it could stop debt building up in the summer months. "It's also welcome that the Chancellor acknowledges that wider measures are needed to bring down bills and we will wait to see if he matches these words with more action in the Budget later." Mr Healey added: “Gas standing charges are unfair and outdated so I am scrapping them to give millions of households a bit of breathing space. “My Budget will draw a line in the sand on an energy policy that has failed British billpayers for years, letting extra costs on bills pile high and leaving households even more exposed to global shocks.” Recommended reading: The announcement comes as Mr Healey prepares to deliver his first Budget in the Commons on Wednesday afternoon. The Chancellor said the change would give families “breathing space” while making the energy system fairer. The precise timing of the change will depend on Ofgem, which has been asked to implement the reform from 2027 or as soon as possible afterwards.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Celebrity asks to block sexual misconduct claims, citing 'potentially fatal' impact
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A celebrity has asked the High Court to block publication of sexual misconduct allegations, arguing it could have "potentially fatal" consequences. The unnamed public figure is seeking an injunction to prevent ITN and Guardian News and Media (GNM) from revealing claims that he used his status over many years to pursue "inappropriate sexual activities with a large number of girls and young women". The man denies all allegations, according to the BBC, including suggestions that he abused his position to contact and form relationships with teenagers and young women for sexual purposes. ‘Well-known individual’ suing two news outlets to halt publication of claims linked to 'inappropriate sexual activities' https://t.co/phZU4JS2oE — LBC (@LBC) October 28, 2026 Sara Mansoori KC, representing the celebrity, told the court that publication would carry a "potentially fatal impact," citing evidence of severe mental health risk. Ms Mansoori said: "The only reason they would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life. "This is not a case where an individual has spuriously raised 'mental health' concerns in the face of an impending publication that they do not wish to occur. "The claimant has attempted suicide twice as a result of these matters, been hospitalised for months, been the subject of involuntary detention and been examined by multiple – now more than 10 – doctors." She told the court that the man had already made one suicide attempt after receiving letters from the news organisations seeking his response to the allegations, and later attempted to take his own life a second time after absconding from hospital. The claimant, who is referred to in court as PPT, "has no intention of returning to public life," Ms Mansoori said. A medical report submitted to the court stated that inpatient treatment could offer "significant, but not complete mitigation of the risk," and that treatment, perhaps for months, had "a realistic potential to reduce the risk". Mr Justice Nicklin, who is presiding over the case, emphasised the public interest in the proceedings but warned against speculation or attempts to identify the individual. He said: "The existence of online speculation, however confidently expressed or widely repeated, does not authorise anyone to identify, or purport authoritatively to identify, PPT in connection with these proceedings. "Nor does repetition transform speculation into established fact." The judge clarified that the case is not about determining the truth or accuracy of the allegations, but rather whether they can be lawfully published. Gavin Millar KC, representing the news organisations, argued that there was a strong public interest in publishing the allegations, which he said formed a "pattern of behaviour." Mr Millar said "numerous allegations" had been gathered during a "wide-ranging and rigorous investigation", with reporters having spoken to more than 100 people. He told the court that "many of the women have been traumatised by the claimant's alleged conduct and have suffered mental health crises and mental illness as a result". Mr Millar acknowledged the seriousness of the suicide risk but argued that "the state may have a responsibility to protect life," but doing so in this case would require the state to "intervene in lawful journalistic activities to prevent an autonomous act by the claimant himself." He suggested that the risk could be mitigated and that there was "no proper basis to restrain the publication of public interest journalism." Justice Nicklin described the matter as "a difficult and important case" and said the court would determine the outcome "fairly, on the evidence and legal submissions." He confirmed that his decision would focus solely on whether the allegations can be published, not on their truth or accuracy.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Nine Cambs council workers sacked in one year after disciplinary hearings
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Nine county council employees were sacked last year following disciplinary hearings, data has revealed. A Freedom of Information Act request to Cambridgeshire County Council found that there were a total of 57 disciplinary hearings over the last three years. In the 2024/25 financial year, there were 22 disciplinary hearings with nine resulting in the employee’s contract being terminated. This was higher than the year before, 2023/24, when there were just seven hearings and less than five dismissals. To protect privacy, exact figures for numbers under five have not been provided. In 2025/26, there were 28 disciplinary hearings but less than five of these resulted in the employee being sacked. The most common reasons for disciplinary action were breach of policy and procedure and safeguarding, with 13 cases of each across the three years. This was followed by inappropriate communication or behaviour, with 11 cases, and health and safety with ten cases. There were less than five cases each of hearings for absence, bullying, harassment or discrimination, fraud, financial or theft, gross misconduct and negligence. A spokesperson for Cambridgeshire County Council said they pride themselves “on being a compassionate and inclusive employer”. They said: “That does not mean that we avoid dealing with inappropriate or unacceptable conduct by our employees – the council is equally committed to achieving high standards across our workforce of more than 4,500 people. “Disciplinary hearings, where necessary, occur following robust and fair investigation processes. “Importantly, disciplinary processes do not and should not always result in the dismissal of employees. “Other sanctions, such as warnings, are available to the council and are applied where appropriate. “The FOI request did not ask for details of these outcomes, it only asked about dismissals.” In 2025, a council worker was sacked after the county council was scammed out of more than £90,000 in a bank mandate fraud. A fraudster had submitted falsified documents to change the bank details of a contracted home-to-school transport supplier and four payments totalling £93,000 were sent to the fraudster’s account. By the time it was discovered, Cambridgeshire Police found that the “suspected fraudster had left the country,” according to council documents. The officer in charge of verifying changes of bank details said they called the supplier and spoke to the owner to verify the change, but the council found they had not done this. They were dismissed for gross misconduct after falsifying a document to say they had conducted these checks, which the council said could have prevented the fraud.

Sponsored walk for homelessness charity Emmaus Cambridge is a step in the right direction for World Homeless Day (Image: Emmaus Cambridge) The team set off from Northstowe and finished at the Emmaus Cambridge site in Landbeach, raising funds and collecting essential items for the charity’s residents along the way. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Co-op becomes first UK retailer to get viral sweet treat in 1,600 stores
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Co-op has claimed it has become the first retailer to bring a viral sweet treat to UK stores. Dot Cakes have amassed attention on platforms like TikTok recently, after a video from a New York bakery showing one off gained traction. The dessert is usually a small cake served in a cup, pot or ramekin, layered with sponge and buttercream, then topped with a thick layer of tiny round sprinkles. The cakes have since attracted millions of fans globally online, with many creating their own DIY versions at home. A post shared by Co-op (@coopuk) Co-op will now stock its own version in more than 1,600 stores across the UK for a limited period of six weeks. A spokesperson for Co-op said: "Staying true to the original flavours social media users love, Co-op’s Raspberry & Vanilla Dot Cake (166g, £2.50) combines vanilla flavour sponge, layered with raspberry jam and vanilla flavour frosting, topped with multi-coloured sugar decorations. "Chocolate lovers can also get their hands on the retailer’s Chocolate & Salted Caramel Dot Cake (177g, £2.50), featuring fluffy chocolate flavour sponge, layered with salted caramel and chocolate caramel flavour frosting, finished with white and milk chocolate crispy balls." Kevin Sargent, senior product development manager for cake at Co-op, said: "We're excited to be hot on the heels of one of this year's biggest food trends by being the first retailer to bring them to shops across the UK. The Dot Cakes come in two flavours in Raspberry & Vanilla and Chocolate & Salted Caramel (Image: Co-op) "They tap into everything people love right now – aesthetically pleasing, nostalgic treats that are as fun to eat as they are to share online. "With two delicious flavour combinations and that signature crunchy topping, we're making it easier for shoppers across the country to get their hands on the viral treat and see what all the fuss is about!" Back in September, Co-op brought back a popular crisp flavour after a three-year absence. The retailer originally launched Roast Potato Crisps in 2019, and they quickly gained a loyal following thanks to their "surprisingly bold taste". Combining sea salt, garlic, rosemary and black pepper, the crisps are designed to "capture the taste of a classic Christmas roast potato". However, they disappeared from Co-op shelves in 2023, prompting shoppers to call for their return. The flavour has now made a comeback as Irresistible Ultimate Roast Potato Crinkle Cut Crisps (150g), one of three flavours included in Co-op's new Christmas range for 2026. Recommended reading: Crisps, snacks and nuts development manager at Co-op, Natalie Dawe, said: "Our crisps have developed something of a cult following over the years, with our customers regularly championing their favourites. "This year, we're delighted to bring back our Roast Potato Crisps and what I love about them is that the flavour always sparks discussion… it’s much more than meets the eye. "Combining salt, garlic, rosemary and black pepper to recreate the taste of perfectly seasoned roasties." Will you be looking to get a Dot Cake in Co-op stores? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: WATCH: Disqualified driver who fled from officers sniffed out by police dog
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A disqualified driver who fled from officers and was sniffed out by a police dog has been handed a suspended prison sentence and a driving ban. Fabio Sanches-Kuiper, 19, of Dovecote Avenue, Great Cambourne, was spotted by officers getting into a BMW at Brampton Hut Services at 11.20pm on September 23. Police had intelligence that he was driving again despite court-imposed bans. Road Policing Unit officers deployed a stinger on the A141, but Sanches-Kuiper refused to stop, drove towards Brampton, then abandoned the BMW and fled into nearby bushes. He was arrested with the help of police dog Ghost. At Cambridge Magistrates’ Court on Monday, October 19, Sanches-Kuiper admitted two counts of driving without insurance, two counts of driving while disqualified and failing to stop. He was jailed for 20 weeks, suspended for 18 months, and given a six-month curfew from 11pm to 6am. He was also banned from driving for four years. PC Colin Dyer, of the Road Policing Unit, said: "Despite being disqualified from driving and previously serving a prison sentence for the offence, Sanches-Kuiper made the decision to get behind the wheel yet again and on one occasion attempted to evade officers. “Driving bans are imposed to protect the public and reduce the risk posed by dangerous drivers. "His repeated offending showed a complete disregard for those restrictions.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 5 locations to enjoy autumn walks in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From misty fenland and colourful woodland to tranquil lakeside trails, Cambridgeshire offers plenty of opportunities to enjoy the best of autumn. Whether you're looking for wildlife or a peaceful countryside escape, here are five places to enjoy a picturesque walk. Autumn is one of the most atmospheric times to visit Wicken Fen National Nature Reserve, one of Britain's oldest nature reserves. Walkers can follow the Four Lodes Trail or Adventurers' Trail through reedbeds, wetlands and open fenland, where grazing Highland cattle and Konik ponies can often be spotted. The Adventurer's Trail is a three-mile circular route, with grazing Highland cattle and Konik ponies among the wildlife visitors may see. As temperatures cool, migratory birds arrive and morning mists frequently hang over the landscape, creating stunning views across the reserve's unique habitat. Few places in Cambridgeshire rival Anglesey Abbey for autumn colour. The National Trust estate is famous for its tree-lined avenues, which transform into spectacular tunnels of gold, orange and red during October and November. Several walking routes wind through the grounds, passing formal gardens, woodland and open parkland. The changing leaves, seasonal flower displays and peaceful atmosphere make it one of the county's most photogenic autumn destinations. Part of Nene Park, Ferry Meadows combines lakes, woodland, riverside paths and open meadows across one of eastern England's largest country parks. Autumn brings vibrant colours to the woodland trails while the park's lakes provide beautiful reflections of the surrounding foliage. With a variety of circular routes available, visitors can enjoy anything from a gentle stroll to a longer waterside walk while taking in the seasonal scenery and wildlife. Located in the Great Ouse Valley, Paxton Pits Nature Reserve offers a mix of lakes, woodland, meadows and riverside footpaths. The reserve is particularly appealing in autumn, when trees around the former gravel pits turn rich shades of amber and bronze. The Heron Trail and Meadow Trail provide excellent opportunities for spotting wildlife, with water birds regularly gathering on the reserve's lakes as the seasons change. Tucked away beside the River Great Ouse in the heart of St Ives, Holt Island Nature Reserve is a hidden gem that feels a world away from the town centre. The reserve's raised boardwalk takes visitors through rare wet woodland, where autumn colours are reflected in the surrounding waterways. Wildlife is abundant throughout the season, and the tranquil setting makes this one of the county's most peaceful walks for anyone looking to escape the bustle of everyday life. One of Cambridgeshire's most celebrated natural landscapes, Wicken Fen is the National Trust's oldest nature reserve and one of Europe's most important wetlands. The reserve is home to thousands of species, including rare birds, dragonflies and wild plants. Visitors can explore miles of footpaths, boardwalks and cycling routes through a landscape that has changed little over centuries. Vast skies, peaceful waterways and abundant wildlife make it one of the county's most memorable beauty spots. Covering nearly 1,500 acres, Grafham Water offers some of the most spectacular waterside scenery in Cambridgeshire. The circular trail around the reservoir attracts walkers, runners and cyclists throughout the year. Meanwhile, expansive views across the water create a sense of tranquillity rarely found in the east of England. The site is also popular with birdwatchers, who regularly spot ospreys, grebes and other water birds against the backdrop of one of the county's largest open spaces. Nestled on the banks of the River Great Ouse, Houghton Mill combines beautiful countryside with fascinating history. The 18th-century watermill sits amid riverside meadows, willow-lined paths and charming villages. Visitors can enjoy leisurely walks through Waterclose Meadows, watch boats passing along the river and relax beside one of the most picturesque stretches of water in Cambridgeshire. The idyllic surroundings make it a favourite destination for photographers and walkers alike. Stretching along the River Nene, this vast green space is much more than a city park. Lakes, meadows, woodland and riverside trails combine to create a diverse landscape that attracts visitors throughout the year. At its heart lies Ferry Meadows, where miles of pathways provide opportunities for walking, cycling and wildlife spotting. Arguably the county's most iconic view, The Backs offers stunning vistas of the historic University of Cambridge colleges lining the River Cam. Mature trees, elegant bridges and perfectly maintained lawns combine to create a scene recognised around the world. Whether viewed on foot or from a punt, the area delivers some of the finest scenery in Cambridgeshire and remains a must-visit destination for locals and tourists alike. Famous for its landscaped gardens and extensive grounds, Anglesey Abbey is one of Cambridgeshire's most beautiful historic estates. Visitors can wander through woodland walks, colourful seasonal displays and carefully designed gardens that look spectacular throughout the year. Spring blossom, summer flowers and autumn foliage ensure there is always something worth seeing. As Cambridgeshire's largest country estate, Wimpole Estate offers an impressive combination of grand parkland, lakes, farmland and historic architecture. Visitors can enjoy far-reaching views across rolling countryside, explore woodland trails and discover picturesque corners throughout the estate. Managed by the National Trust, the site provides a striking contrast to the county's landscapes and remains one of the finest places to enjoy the great outdoors. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new set of stamps honouring the service of the nation’s armed forces has been revealed. Royal Mail will release six stamps on Armistice Day, November 11, marking 110 years since the Battle of the Somme, which began on July 1, 1916, and became one of the defining battles of the First World War. The stamps feature specially commissioned artworks by British artist Matthew Cook, who has served as a reservist in the Parachute Regiment and The Rifles and was deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan. David Gold of Royal Mail, said: "Remembrance holds a profound place in our national life. "Through these stamps, we pay tribute to the service and sacrifice of those who have served our country through two world wars and many other conflicts. Six new stamps have been released. (Image: Royal Mail/Press Association) "Matthew Cook’s poignant artworks provide a fitting and powerful way to reflect on the sacrifices made by so many courageous men and women across the generations." Cook said: “Remembrance has a very special place in my life, having served as a reservist in the Parachute Regiment and The Rifles and been deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan. “I was delighted to be asked to illustrate these stamps and to take on the challenge of such a sensitive and significant subject. “It is always a privilege to illustrate stamps for Royal Mail, and this project felt particularly special.” If stamps are placed in the wrong place, it could mean the parcel or letter will be delayed because Royal Mail’s sorting machines are programmed to scan that specific area. The automatic machines might also mark the item as having no postage paid, which could mean the person receiving the item will have to pay a fee for it. The recipient can visit the sorting office and look at the envelope but if they do not know who the parcel is from or do not want to pay the fee, the item will be kept for 18 days before it is returned to the sender or destroyed. There are a few other rules that Royal Mail says people should follow to avoid any delays or fees for their items. The stamp should also be placed completely flat and visible with the Queen or King’s head facing the right way up. The area around the stamp must also be kept clear, as Royal Mail uses the space for tracking codes and digital postmarks. Writing over the stamp will make it difficult for Royal Mail machines to read the tracking code. Royal Mail says: "The days of licking stamps are over. Read More "Just peel your stamp and stick it in the top right-hand corner of your letter. "You’ll need your stamp to be clearly visible, not bent over an edge and on the same face of your parcel as the address. "Many stamps contain barcodes to assist in tracking, so it’s important that the stamp is flat and easy to scan."

With firework season approaching and schools breaking up for half-term, Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service is reminding the public of the dangers posed by home fireworks and bonfires. Station Commander Scott Fretwell, community risk manager, said: "Bonfire Night is a very popular fixture in the calendar and can be plenty of fun for all of the family to enjoy. "There are, however, potential hazards to avoid, to help keep you and your family safe. "We urge anyone wanting to enjoy fireworks to attend an organised fireworks display rather than hosting your own. "There are many across the county that people can enjoy safely, which can be found on an interactive map on our website." While organised events are safest, the fire service acknowledges that many people will still choose to hold celebrations at home. Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service is urging residents to stay safe and attend an organised fireworks display (Image: Supplied) Scott said: "While most people enjoy fireworks responsibly, in the wrong hands they can cause injury and damage to property. "Fireworks are explosives and as such should be treated with respect and only used in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions and the firework safety code. "Lighting a bonfire in a garden presents significant risks to residents if they get out of hand. "Not only this, but the smoke can also aggravate neighbours with respiratory problems. "They can also get out of control very quickly, causing damage to property and sometimes serious injury." The fire service advises only buying fireworks with a CE mark, lighting them at arm’s length with a taper, and never returning to a lit firework. They also warn against giving sparklers to children under five and recommend keeping pets indoors throughout the evening. For those who do decide to light a bonfire, the service urges residents to build it well clear of buildings and fences, avoid burning hazardous items, and never leave it unattended.

It calls for the current state pension age to be reduced to 65, arguing that people aged 65 to 67 can face poor health, caring responsibilities and limited employment opportunities while waiting to qualify for their state pension. The campaign argues that forcing people to work longer can be unfair for those who are struggling with their health or unable to find suitable employment. It also suggests that allowing older workers to retire earlier could create more opportunities for younger people trying to get into work. The petition passed the 100,000-signature threshold, meaning the Petitions Committee will consider it for debate in Parliament. An update published on October 24, 2026, confirmed the milestone. However, reaching the threshold does not guarantee that a debate will take place, nor does it mean the Government has agreed to change the state pension age. In fact, earlier this month they made a statement, saying: "The Government has no plans to lower the State Pension age." They added: "State Pension age is now gradually rising from 66 to 67. "This increase began in April 2026 and will complete in March 2028. "Increases to State Pension age have been in legislation since the Pensions Act 1995. "As longevity has increased and our society aged, State Pension age rises have maintained fairness between generations and protected the public finances." The petition remains open for people to sign until March 16, 2027. Do you think the state pension age should be reduced to 65 for everyone? Tell us in the comments below...

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 7 beloved shops that have disappeared from Cambridgeshire's high streets
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From iconic department stores to beloved high street chains, many familiar shops have disappeared from Cambridgeshire in recent years. So, here are seven popular stores across the county that we have loved and lost. The Peterborough branch of Beales occupied the prominent Westgate department store building and became a major city-centre retailer. The original Beales store traded there for around nine years before the chain entered administration in 2020. A revived Beales reopened in the building in May 2021, employing around 30 staff, but the store announced its closure in October 2022 and finally shut in January 2023. The building has since been earmarked for redevelopment. For years, BHS was one of Peterborough's best-known department stores, selling clothing, homeware and electrical goods. The retailer itself was founded in 1928 and became a staple of high streets nationwide. The Peterborough branch was among hundreds affected when the company collapsed into administration in 2016. The store closed during the national shutdown of the chain, bringing an end to a familiar shopping destination for local residents. The Huntingdon branch of Woolworths was a favourite for everything from toys and music to stationery and the famous pick-and-mix sweets. Founded nationally in 1909, Woolworths became one of Britain's most recognisable high-street chains. Like all UK branches, the Huntingdon store closed during the company's collapse in late 2008 and early 2009. For many residents, its closure marked the end of an era on the town's high street. Founded in 1904 by Frank Brittain, Brittains Furnishers was one of St Neots' oldest surviving independent retailers. Originally based in Eaton Ford, the business later moved to the High Street in 1924 and became a trusted destination for furniture and home furnishings. After 120 years of trading, the family-run company announced its closure in 2023, citing online competition, rising costs and changing consumer habits. Ely's Woolworths traced its roots back to a purpose-built store opened in 1935 on Fore Street before relocating to Market Place in the early 2000s. The branch became a popular feature of city-centre shopping before closing in December 2008 as part of the chain's nationwide collapse. The prominent Market Place store has since housed other retailers, but many residents still remember it as Woolworths. The Wisbech branch of Bonmarché, located at 9-10 High Street, served shoppers for many years before closing around 2019. The premises subsequently remained vacant for several years before redevelopment plans emerged. The building itself has a long retail history dating back more than a century, having previously housed drapers and the former Bainbridges Department Store. The Peterborough branch of Debenhams was a cornerstone of the city centre for decades, attracting shoppers looking for fashion, beauty products and homewares. The retailer itself was founded in 1778, and the Peterborough store became one of the city's best-known department stores. Following the chain's collapse, Debenhams began winding down its UK operations in 2021, with stores closing nationwide as the business left the high street for good. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 9 hidden gems in Cambridgeshire you have to visit at least once
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire is packed with hidden gems that rarely make the county's tourism brochures. From ancient wetlands and secret nature reserves to forgotten archaeological sites and historic country estates, here are nine lesser-known attractions to visit. Often described as a hidden gem, Wicken Fen is the National Trust's oldest nature reserve and one of Europe's most important wetlands. Visitors can explore boardwalks winding through reedbeds, marshes and wildflower meadows while spotting dragonflies, rare birds and grazing Highland cattle. The reserve offers a glimpse into the ancient Fenland landscape that once dominated the region, making it an excellent destination for walkers, families and wildlife enthusiasts. Hidden away between Peterborough and Huntingdon, Holme Fen feels remarkably wild and remote. The reserve is home to the famous Holme Post, marking Britain's lowest land point at around 2.75 metres below sea level. Visitors can explore peaceful woodland trails, wetlands and bird hides while discovering a fascinating story of how drainage transformed the Fens. One of Britain's last remaining washlands, Nene Washes offers spectacular wildlife viewing throughout the year. Winter floods attract thousands of migratory birds, while spring and summer bring breeding cranes, godwits and marsh harriers. Birdwatchers rate it among the county's finest locations, yet it remains surprisingly under the radar with many local visitors. Covering hundreds of acres beside the River Nene, the park combines lakes, woodland, meadows and cycle routes. Families can enjoy water sports, miniature railways, walking trails and abundant wildlife. Created from former gravel workings, Paxton Pits has become one of Cambridgeshire's most important wildlife sites. Its lakes, reedbeds and woodland attract kingfishers, otters and hundreds of bird species throughout the year. Well-maintained trails and viewing hides make it accessible for families, photographers and nature lovers alike. Many visitors compare the reserve favourably with much larger national wildlife attractions while enjoying a quieter atmosphere. One of the most significant Bronze Age archaeological sites in Britain, Flag Fen remains surprisingly little known outside the region. The attraction centres on a 3,500-year-old causeway preserved beneath the peat and waterlogged soils of the Fens. Interactive exhibits, reconstructed roundhouses and fascinating artefacts help bring prehistoric Cambridgeshire to life. One of the largest habitat restoration projects in the country, Ouse Fen offers expansive wetland scenery and exceptional birdwatching opportunities. Visitors can enjoy peaceful walking trails through reedbeds and lakes while looking out for cranes, bitterns and marsh harriers. The sheer scale of the reserve creates an extraordinary sense of isolation, despite being only a short distance from Ely and nearby villages. Tucked inside Huntingdon's former grammar school, the Cromwell Museum tells the story of Oliver Cromwell and the English Civil War through a collection of nationally important artefacts. Despite its historical significance, it remains relatively overlooked compared with larger museums in Cambridge. Visitors can examine weapons, portraits and personal items linked to one of Britain's most influential and controversial historical figures. Located just outside Peterborough, Sacrewell blends history, countryside and family-friendly attractions. Highlights include a restored 19th-century watermill, rare farm animals, woodland walks and seasonal events. The setting offers a gentler and quieter alternative to larger commercial attractions while still providing plenty to keep children entertained. Its combination of heritage and outdoor space makes it particularly appealing for multi-generational visits. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than 40,000 people have signed a petition to save the BBC’s long-running home renovation series DIY SOS. The show, which first aired in 1999 and is currently fronted by Nick Knowles, is set to be “rested” in 2027 as part of the broadcaster’s latest round of cost-cutting measures. DIY SOS has earned a loyal following by transforming the homes of families facing severe illness, disability, bereavement, or building disasters, with the help of volunteers and tradespeople from local communities. The BBC’s decision has prompted a wave of public backlash. A Change.org petition calling for the show to be saved has already surpassed 40,400 signatures. The petition states: "In 2025, I had the extraordinary privilege of contributing to a show on the BBC that has made a profound impact on the lives of countless individuals. "This wasn't just another reality TV series; it was a beacon of hope for those struggling in difficult circumstances. "The show brought together a community of tradespeople who volunteered their time, skills, and resources to make miraculous transformations in people's living situations, changing lives for the better. "This program showcased raw and heartfelt stories of real people, grappling with the hardships of everyday life. "It highlighted the power of compassion and community, bringing viewers not just entertainment, but also a myriad of invaluable life lessons. "For the many families it has helped, the show has been nothing less than life-changing, offering them a chance at a fresh start and an improved future. "Unfortunately, there are discussions underway about cancelling this invaluable show. "Ending it means turning away from those in need and ignoring the good it brings. "At a time when reality often feels overwhelmingly challenging, this show stands as a reminder to all of us of the potential we have to make a difference in our communities. "We urge the BBC to reconsider any plans to cancel this essential program. "By preserving it, we continue to foster a spirit of generosity, empathy, and community support that the show so beautifully encapsulates. "Let us keep telling these important stories and making a tangible difference in people's lives." The BBC has confirmed that DIY SOS will be rested after its current series concludes. The corporation insists the programme has not been permanently cancelled, with a new spin-off show revisiting families and renovation projects from its history set to take its place. A BBC spokesperson said: "In light of the BBC’s savings challenges we have taken the decision to rest DIY SOS in 2027 and commission a new spin-off show instead from producers South Shore. "DIY SOS Rebuilt My Life will revisit successes from the show’s past and expand the brand on the BBC in a more cost-effective way next year." The BBC has also rested the annual DIY SOS Children In Need special, which typically involves a large-scale charitable project supporting young people. These decisions form part of wider efforts to save £500 million over the next three years, which have already resulted in the cancellation of other popular programmes including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, and Live At The Apollo. DIY SOS presenter Nick Knowles said he was "disappointed" by the decision but acknowledged the financial pressures facing the broadcaster. A post shared by Nick Knowles (@nickknowles) Knowles said: "You may have already seen the news that DIY SOS is being put on 'pause.' "Of course, I’m disappointed not to be filming the show next year or again in the same format we know and love. "But I do understand there’s no endless pot of money at the BBC and sometimes they have to make difficult decisions. "For 26 years it’s been an honour and a privilege to be part of DIY SOS and I’ve loved nothing more than making it. "What I always come back to is that it’s the people who are the beating heart of SOS. "It really is the best of Britain and we need to see more of it on telly." He also thanked the families, volunteers, production team, and viewers who have supported the show over the years. Knowles continued: "To the volunteers, production team, purple shirts, commissioners and everyone watching at home, we couldn’t have done this without you. "And to everyone who hasn’t seen the series yet, give it a watch. "I promise your heart will be warmed." Are you upset by the BBC's decision to "rest" DIY SOS in 2027?
