summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Senior doctors in England to strike for 2 days - what does it mean for patients?
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Senior doctors in England are to stage a two-day strike next month in a dispute over pay and pensions. The walkout will begin on Wednesday, November 25 at 6.59am, with consultants providing emergency cover only. The strike follows a British Medical Association (BMA) ballot in which 76% of participating consultants voted in favour of industrial action. Talks had taken place with the government over the past month. Consultants don’t want to strike, but after 18 months without formal negotiations, they cannot wait any longer. These strikes are planned to take place on 25 and 26 November, with Christmas Day levels of cover provided. There is still time for the Government to make progress. https://t.co/tco6pyInD8 — The BMA (@TheBMA) October 26, 2026 In a statement, the BMA said: "Our intended industrial action will take the form of ‘Christmas Day’ cover as in previous industrial action. "Consultants provide safe emergency and immediately life-saving care on Christmas day and out of hours 365 days a year, so no patients will be harmed but the Government will hear our message loud and clear. "If the Government chooses to act, by formally negotiating with us with a mandate that can lead to a credible offer across our range of demands, then industrial action can and will be stood down." Consultants – the most senior doctors in the NHS – were given a 3.5% pay increase this year. Basic pay for consultants starts at £113,500 with the most experienced paid £150,500. However, they can earn thousands of pounds in extra payments, which means average earnings are more than £150,000 a year. Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the government had been in "constructive discussions" with the BMA, so it was "disappointing" that the strike dates had been announced. She said taking strike action would be "irresponsible" and "place the health service under even greater pressure". In previous strike actions by resident doctors, patients have been warned that procedures could be cancelled, but urgent appointments should continue as normal. Patients will be contacted if their planned procedures cannot go ahead. NHS England has said in previous strike actions that hospitals should only cancel non-urgent care, such as hip and knee operations, in exceptional circumstances.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hardest primary schools to get your child a place in
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The hardest primary schools in Cambridgeshire to get your child a place in have been revealed in new data. Most schools are able to offer a place to every student who picked them as their top preference, but some don’t have enough for everyone. In 2026, the most oversubscribed primary school was Milton Road Primary School in Cambridge with 62.5 per cent of students who picked it as their first choice given a place. This was followed by Ridgefield Primary School in Cambridge which had enough places for 69.8 per cent of first preferences and Abbots Ripton Primary School near Huntingdon which had 70.8 per cent. Ridgefield had 43 first preferences for 30 places and Abbots Ripton had 24 students put it as their first preference – but only 17 places on offer. The school with the most first preferences was Milton Road Primary School, which had 60 places but 96 students picking it as their top choice. Milton Road was also the most oversubscribed school in 2025, when 113 students chose it as their first choice and only 53 per cent were successful. It was followed by Newnham Croft Primary School in Cambridge, with 56.6 per cent of students successful, and St Alban’s Catholic Primary School in Cambridge at 60 per cent. Meldreth Primary School was the most oversubscribed in 2024, when 65 per cent of 46 first preferences were offered one of the school’s 30 places. It was followed by Holywell Primary School in Needingworth, near St Ives, at 69.8 per cent and Houghton Primary School in Wyton, near Huntingdon, at 71.4 per cent. This year, 94.7 per cent of Cambridgeshire children were given a place at their first preference school – and 98.9 per cent at one of their top three preferred schools. A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said that, with just over one per cent allocated a place outside their preferences, it was the “second lowest proportion recorded in the last five years”. They said: “We’re committed to providing the best possible start in life for young people in our county and access to high quality education close to home is key. “With population centres changing over time around our growing county, the council’s Education team work hard, in partnership with schools and with careful reference to pupil forecasting figures, to try and ensure we can offer the right numbers of school places, in the right areas, when they are needed.” If your child was born between September 1, 2022, and August 31, 2023, and you live in Cambridgeshire, you will need to apply for a place in Reception for September 2027. This can be done on the county council’s website here, and the deadline for applications is January 15, 2027.

There were a few visitors nervous about entering some of the marquees, most notably the Clown City one, which was littered with terrifying clowns - as if they were not already scary enough for some people. The Stinkyface World was particularly gut-wrenching, mainly because it smelled just like poo - not for those with a delicate stomach. I won't go into too much detail on what you might find, as I don't want to spoil the surprise/horror/shock for visitors. But suffice to say if you love a bit of horror and are looking for a night of fun this Halloween, then Horror Mania at Skylark is the place to be. Tickets are on sale - although there may be limited availability for some time slots - from £29.95 to £52.95 per person. Plans for a new eight-home development in Warboys have been approved despite objections from residents and the parish council. The proposal, from applicants Mr and Mrs Robinson, involves constructing eight detached homes on land between Heath Farm and Heath Pond, north of Heath Road in Warboys. The land is currently classed as agricultural. Plans include three three-bedroom and five four-bedroom homes, 16 parking spaces, landscaping and a footpath linking the site to the village. It was granted Permission in Principle in July 2025 for between four and nine homes, establishing that the site could be developed for housing. The parish council objected because the site is located near a former sheep dip, raising concerns over land contamination and risk to human health and the environment. However, planning officers have recommended the approval of the application, arguing that the benefits of the development outweigh these concerns. They pointed out that the district has only a 3.68-year supply of housing land, against the required five-year supply, indicating an unmet housing need. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From grand art deco picture houses to busy town-centre screens, cinemas were once at the heart of communities across Cambridgeshire. While modern multiplexes have taken their place, many former venues are still remembered by residents who spent countless evenings watching films there. Here's five cinemas we have loved and lost. The Grand Cinema began life in Huntingdon's former Corn Exchange and officially opened as a cinema on 1 January 1913. It survived a devastating fire in 1954 and reopened later that same year with modern facilities and a new screen. For decades it served as a popular entertainment venue in the town. The cinema eventually closed in August 1964, after which the building was used for bingo before redevelopment. The Princess Cinema was another venue that once played a prominent role in Peterborough's recreation and leisure scene. The single floor cinema opened in 1929 and welcomed countless visitors during a time when a night at the cinema was among the most popular forms of entertainment. Odeon Theatres Ltd eventually bought the Princess Cinema in 1936 before it was leased to J.F. Emery Circuit of Manchester in 1937. It closed in March 1958 with “Son of the Hunchback” and Charlie Chaplin in “The Kid”. The Playhouse Cinema served Cambridge residents during the heyday of traditional picture houses. It became the second cinema on Mill Road in 1913 when a brand new building was created. Like many cinemas of its era, it provided affordable entertainment and a shared community experience before television became widespread. Although little remains of the building today, the Playhouse occupies a notable place in Cambridge's cultural and entertainment heritage. The Hippodrome Cinema was arguably Huntingdon's most fondly remembered picture house. Opening in 1933 with more than 800 seats and a then state-of-the-art Western Electric sound system, it became a popular destination for generations of local cinemagoers. Located close to the town centre, it remained a prominent entertainment venue for decades. Films were dropped in favour of bingo in 1971 before briefly returning, but the cinema ultimately closed and was demolished around 1977 to make way for retail development. The Exchange Cinema was once among several cinemas serving Ely residents during the peak years of cinema-going. Situated in the cathedral city, it provided local audiences with access to the latest film releases at a time when trips to the pictures were a major social event. It closed in 1963 before being demolished in 1964 and remains part of Ely's rich cultural and entertainment heritage. Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Only one in five people can pass this three-question IQ test
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Less than one in five people pass this IQ test, thought to be the shortest in the world only three questions long. The Cognitive Reflection Test has a pass rate of just 17 per cent, leaving the majority who attempt it boggled. It was originally part of a research paper published in 2005 by MIT Professor Shane Frederick, and has recently resurfaced online with many people giving it a go. As part of his research, Professor Frederick had more than 3,000 participants from a range of educational backgrounds complete the test, but even those attending top American universities such as Yale and Harvard struggled to work out all the answers. Professor Frederick said: "The three items on the CRT are ‘easy’ in the sense that their solution is easily understood when explained, yet reaching the correct answer often requires the suppression of an erroneous answer that springs ‘impulsively’ to mind." So how will you get on? 1. A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost? 2. If it takes five machines five minutes to make five widgets, how long would it take 100 machines to make 100 widgets? 3. In a lake, there is a patch of lily pads. Every day, the patch doubles in size. If it takes 48 days for the patch to cover the entire lake, how long would it take for the patch to cover half of the lake? These are the three most common answers that people guess, but they are actually incorrect: 1. 10 cents 2. 100 minutes 3. 24 days Professor Frederick said: "Anyone who reflects upon it for even a moment would recognise that the difference between $1 and 10 cents is only 90 cents, not $1 as the problem stipulates. "In this case, catching that error is tantamount to solving the problem, since nearly everyone who does not respond ‘10 cents’ does, in fact, give the correct response." The correct answers are: 1. Five cents 2. Five minutes 3. 47 days Presh Talwalkar, the author of The Hoy of Game Theory: An Introduction to Strategic Thinking, explained how to work out the correct answers for each of the three questions on his blog, Mind Your Decisions. 1. Say the ball costs X. Then the bat costs $1 more, so it is X + 1. So we have bat + ball = X + (X + 1) = 1.1 because together they cost $1.10. This means 2X + 1 = 1.1, then 2X = 0.1, so X = 0.05. This means the ball costs five cents and the bat costs $1.05 2. If it takes five machines five minutes to make five widgets, then it takes one machine five minutes to make one widget (each machine is making a widget in five minutes). If we have 100 machines working together, then each can make a widget in five minutes. So there will be 100 widgets in five minutes. 3. Every day FORWARD the patch doubles in size. So every day BACKWARDS means the patch halves in size. So on day 47 the lake is half full.

Following a storm, your policy should cover any significant damage that your house suffers as a result of high winds from the storm. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Binman tells all UK households to make food bin change urgently
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Households risk losing food waste caddies in autumn winds unless lids are clearly numbered. A refuse collector has urged residents across the UK to mark outdoor containers now before seasonal autumn gales arrive in force. Ashley, known on TikTok as The No1 Binman to his 214,600 followers, shared the advice as temperatures drop across the country. He said: "It's that time of year where the wind starts picking up and if you have a food waste bin and don't have your number on it, it could end up a million miles down the road." Householders often blame council collection crews when kerbside bins vanish, but collectors explain that empty food caddies weigh very little once emptied into lorries on collection rounds. Ashley said: "It's not the bin men's fault, it's because they don't weigh a lot." "So once you take the food out, they get put down and if they're not taken in straight away, they could end up down the road." Numbers marked clearly on the top lid allow waste collection crews to return containers directly outside the correct property after emptying. Ashley pointed out that identification stickers can be applied to food waste containers and standard general rubbish wheelie bins alike. He added: "The bin men will make sure it goes right back outside your house and then it's up to you to go and get it." The bin worker previously shared advice on marking bin lids to prevent bins from wandering across streets on collection day. In addition to outdoor containers, guidance outlines steps to maintain hygiene in kitchen caddies as central heating turns on. Kitchen containers should be emptied every two to three days during autumn to stop dampness, fruit flies and odours from developing. Caddies should always be lined with official council-approved compostable or biodegradable liners to keep bins clean and stop liquids from leaking. Hot scraps such as soup or leftover portions must also be allowed to cool completely before disposal, preventing condensation from building up inside the caddy. Households should tie a tight knot in compostable liners before dropping them into outdoor kerbside bins to keep larger containers clean. Retrieving emptied caddies as quickly as possible on collection mornings ensures containers will not blow away down the street.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Chest infection or cold? Boots pharmacist shares key signs and when to see a GP
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: As coughs, colds and flu become more common during the colder months, it can sometimes be difficult to know whether you're dealing with a common seasonal illness or a chest infection. Chest infections can develop after a cold or flu and share some of the same symptoms. However, there are certain signs people can look out for, according to a pharmacist. Boots has shared advice on spotting a possible chest infection as the retailer launches a private Chest Infection Service in more than 90 stores across the UK. Claire Nevinson, Superintendent Pharmacist at Boots, said symptoms of a chest infection can include a chesty cough producing coloured mucus, wheezing, shortness of breath and chest discomfort. Other possible symptoms include a high temperature, headaches, aching muscles and tiredness. She explained: "A chest infection is an infection of the lungs or large airways and they often follow a cold or flu, therefore symptoms can be similar. "Symptoms of a chest infection may include a chesty cough with coloured mucus, wheezing and shortness of breath, chest discomfort, a high temperature, headaches, aching muscles and tiredness." According to the Boots pharmacist, symptoms will often get better without treatment within seven to 10 days, although a cough can remain for as long as three weeks. People should seek medical advice from a GP if a cough lasts for longer than three weeks or they are coughing up blood. There are several things people can do at home to help ease symptoms. Nevinson recommends getting plenty of rest, drinking enough fluids and eating a healthy, balanced diet. Sleeping with your head raised or using extra pillows may also make breathing easier. Anyone whose symptoms persist, has had a cough for more than three weeks or is coughing up blood should seek medical attention from a GP, according to the pharmacist's advice. Some people are at greater risk of developing a serious chest infection. Nevinson said this includes babies and young children, older people, pregnant women, people who smoke, those with long-term respiratory conditions such as asthma and people with weakened immune systems. The advice comes as Boots launches a private Chest Infection Service for people aged 16 and over at more than 90 stores. Appointments last 20 minutes and involve an assessment by an independent prescribing pharmacist, who can offer advice and discuss treatment options. These could include over-the-counter medicines or, where considered appropriate, a course of antibiotics. Recommended Reading Nevinson said: "Chest infections are particularly common during the colder months and can leave people feeling unwell and unsure about the best course of action. "Our new Chest Infection Service provides customers with convenient access to advice, support and treatment right on the high street." The consultation costs £25, with prescribed medicines or over-the-counter treatments charged separately. Customers can book online through Boots and pay in store.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire's railway network was once far larger than it is today, with long-lost stations serving market towns, villages and growing industrial centres across the county. While many have since disappeared, their stories remain woven into the landscape, offering fascinating reminders of a very different age of travel. Before Peterborough became synonymous with the East Coast Main Line, the city's first railway station was Peterborough East. Opened in 1845 by the Eastern Counties Railway, it served routes towards Northampton, Rugby, March, Wisbech and Norwich. The station was known simply as Peterborough until being renamed Peterborough East in 1923. Passenger services ended in June 1966 as part of wider railway cutbacks, although the site continued handling parcels traffic until 1970. Today, little remains apart from the historic engine sheds, but the former station played a crucial role in shaping Peterborough's growth into a major railway city. Ramsey was once unusual in having two separate railway stations. Ramsey North opened in 1863 as the terminus of the Ramsey Railway branch from Holme. The line was worked by the Great Northern Railway and connected the market town with the wider national network. Renamed Ramsey North in 1923, the station struggled to attract large passenger numbers, particularly as road transport became more popular during the twentieth century. Passenger services ceased in October 1947, although freight traffic continued for many years afterwards. The station was eventually demolished and the site redeveloped, but for decades it served as a lifeline for local businesses and residents. The second of Ramsey's two stations was originally opened as Ramsey High Street in 1889 on the branch line from Somersham. Later renamed Ramsey East, it operated as the terminus of a route that linked the town with the Great Eastern Railway network. The curious existence of two unconnected railway stations in the same small town became a symbol of Victorian railway rivalry. Despite hopes that the lines would eventually be joined, the connection was never built. Passenger services ended as early as September 1930, making it one of the first stations in the area to succumb to changing travel habits. Freight traffic survived until 1956, after which the station disappeared beneath industrial development and later housing estates. Located just south of Peterborough on the Great Northern Railway main line, Yaxley and Farcet station opened in 1890 before being renamed five years later. The station served both villages and provided residents with direct access to Peterborough and destinations further afield. The station closed to passengers in April 1959, several years before the better-known Beeching cuts transformed Britain's rail network. Freight facilities lingered for a few more years before disappearing altogether. Today, little evidence survives of a station that once formed an important part of everyday life for local commuters, shoppers and travellers. Bluntisham station stood on the former St Ives to Ely branch line and served the riverside village for more than a century. Opening in the nineteenth century, it was one of several small rural stations that connected isolated Fen-edge communities with larger towns and railway junctions. Agricultural produce, livestock and passengers all passed through the station during its busiest years. The line gradually declined after the Second World War as road transport became increasingly dominant. Passenger services eventually ceased and the station was closed along with the rest of the route. Although the buildings have long since disappeared, traces of the railway corridor can still be spotted by keen-eyed walkers and railway history enthusiasts exploring the local countryside. Anthony Williams, 33, is accused of carrying out the attack on a London-bound LNER train near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on November 1 last year. The 6.25pm service from Doncaster to London King's Cross was forced to make an emergency stop at Huntingdon after British Transport Police received reports of a stabbing. Forensic investigators on the platform by the train at Huntingdon station Williams denied 10 counts of attempted murder at a hearing in July. His trial is due to begin on October 26. At a pre-trial hearing at Cambridge Crown Court on Monday, October 21, Williams pleaded guilty to 14 further charges. He pleaded guilty to ten counts of wounding with intent relating to the incident on the LNER train. Williams also pleaded guilty to two further counts of wounding with intent relating to an incident at Pontoon Dock DLR station in London in the early hours of November 1 and an incident involving a 14-year-old boy in Peterborough on October 31. He also pleaded guilty to the attempted wounding of two men, aged 22 and 28, in Peterborough on October 31. His other guilty pleas covered affray at a Peterborough barber shop, stealing knives from an Asda store in Stevenage and carrying a bladed article in several public places on October 31. Court artist sketch by Elizabeth Cook of Anthony Williams Williams also admitted possessing a knife at Pontoon Dock and on a train between Peterborough and Huntingdon, plus common assault on a Govia Thameslink train between St Pancras and Biggleswade. He further pleaded guilty to the assault occasioning actual bodily harm of a male police officer in custody on November 2. Williams denies 14 counts of attempted murder, meaning there will be a trial as the indictment is not resolved, prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC said. Of these, 10 related to the LNER train incident, three are said to have happened in Peterborough, and one is alleged at Pontoon Dock. The trial is due to begin at Cambridge Crown Court on Monday.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Career burglar' who stole war service medal and training sword jailed again
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A serial burglar has been jailed again after stealing a martial arts training sword and a Great War service medal. Jody Stones, 41, was released from prison in May 2025 but carried out more burglaries in Peterborough this year. On July 28, 2026, he broke into a property in Rivendale, Werrington, and stole a gilet and a martial arts training sword worth about £740. A blood smear on a kitchen cupboard door matched Stones, while CCTV showed him outside with the stolen sword. Two weeks later, Stones and another masked man broke into a home on Eastfield Road while the elderly resident was inside. The victim woke to find Stones standing by his bed. When challenged, Stones jumped from a first-floor balcony and fled with the victim’s wallet, bank cards, passport, cufflinks, coin and stamp collection, gold watch and grandfather’s Great War service medal. CCTV showed one of the men wearing the same clothes as Stones during the Rivendale burglary. Enquiries showed Stones had approached local collectibles dealers to sell the stolen coins. Officers recovered the stolen coins and his grandfather’s medal and returned them to the victim. Stones was arrested on August 17 when he went to Thorpe Wood Police Station to answer bail for an unrelated matter. He pleaded guilty to two burglaries and was jailed for six years and nine months at Peterborough Crown Court on October 16. He also admitted six more burglaries, three car thefts and handling stolen goods. The other man seen on CCTV with Stones has yet to be identified. Detective Constable George Corney said: "Stones is a career burglar who showed a complete disregard for the sentence he was already serving for the exact same offences. “He stole not only valuable items, but items of real sentimental value to the victims and even burgled one address while the homeowner was asleep. "I can only imagine how terrifying it must have been for him to wake up and find a masked man beside his bed. "I am glad Stones is now back behind bars."

Kaia added: "It's lovely to be able to give back to Hinchingbrooke Hospital when it has given so much to us." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: WATCH: The Cambridgeshire fire station trying to 'break the taboo of menopause'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire fire station is trying to "break the taboo of menopause" by educating firefighters about women's health. Women and Equalities Minister Bridget Phillipson visited Huntingdon Fire and Rescue Station on October 15 to mark Menopause Awareness Month. Ms Phillipson said there was still “quite a lot of ignorance” about the menopause and its effects on women, especially at work. She said: "We know that there is still far too much stigma around this and it's good we are speaking more about the health challenges and women's experiences around the menopause. "Employers leading the way are providing a culture where people can be open about the things they might be experiencing and the impact the menopause can have. "One example we have talked about here is just making sure we have period products available routinely for firefighters who might be out on jobs and can't get back to the site to get what they need." Minister for Women and Equalities Bridget Phillipson Government figures show that only about one in 10 firefighters nationally are women, far fewer than in the police force. At Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service, women make up 24 per cent of firefighters, with about a third aged 40 to 55. Huntingdon Fire Station’s menopause champion Hayley Douglas said supporting women through health challenges could help increase those numbers. Hayley said: "We're doing an awful lot as a sector to try and encourage more women to join the fire and rescue service and I think this is a really important part of that. Menopause Champion Hayley Douglas "Firefighting is a career, so people join in their early twenties for example. "We need to make sure we support them through their life cycle of hormones as well." Huntingdon Fire Station has put period protection packs in every toilet and fire engine, as well as portable toilets and tents on its engines. Huntingdon Fire Station has introduced period protection items in every fire engine The station also delivers mandatory training to everyone in the organisation about the symptoms of the menopause, how it impacts work and its effects on relationships. Hayley said: "We are a male majority organisation and a lot of the engagement during those sessions has been from our male colleagues, understanding what their partners at home are going through. "Increasing that knowledge at work is like throwing a stone and seeing all the rippled effect where people start talking about it outside of work as well. "In the service, it's given women the confidence to be able to go and speak to their line manager knowing they have had a level of input in menopause awareness. "It just makes it easier to have that conversation. "Ultimately what we are trying to do is break the taboo of menopause and make people feel like it is a safe environment to openly talk about what they are going through." October marks Menopause Awareness Month Ms Phillipson added: "Often, quite small practical changes around uniform and kit and making sure you have good toilet facilities can just make the world of difference. "From next spring, bigger employers will have to publish plans on how they are taking action to support women including in areas like the menopause. "But already we have employers like Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service who are showing what can be done." Employers with 250 or more staff can currently publish a voluntary action plan on their gender pay gap and support for employees experiencing the menopause. Subject to legislation, the plans will become mandatory from spring 2027.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: ‘Extreme danger’ posed by modified e-bikes as faulty battery implicated in fatal fire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire County Council is warning of the “extreme risk” posed by illegally modified e-bikes after a faulty battery was implicated in the deaths of two children. An ongoing inquest into the fire which claimed the lives of Gemma Germeney, 31, and her two children, aged eight and four, heard the “most probable” cause of the fire was the “failure of a charging battery pack”. Cambridgeshire County Council backed a motion calling for better awareness of the rules around e-bikes and e-scooters as modified vehicles can pose “extreme danger to the public”. Cllr Anna Bradnam, of Waterbeach, said the inquest had found that the battery had been replaced and “wired in a way that made it dangerous”. The Lib Dem councillor said: “I think we owe it to our residents to make it absolutely abundantly clear what risks they’re taking if they choose to alter the batteries. “This is not just for the people who buy them, it’s for the people working in garages who might be asked to solve an electrical problem. “Having these batteries that are very powerful and being charged in homes overnight is an extreme risk and I wouldn’t want it to happen to anybody else.” Cllr David Levien, of Trumpington, who brought forward the motion, said that modified vehicles can cause serious injuries through not just speed – but their weight too. The Lib Dem councillor said: “The high-performance models are heavy and at their top legal speed contain sufficient energy to be capable of causing serious injury or death to members of the public as well as the rider. I have seen, and no doubt others here will have seen, e-bikes being ridden in public at speeds greater than 40 miles per hour – some are even capable of 70 miles per hour.” Under current laws, e-bikes have a capped speed of 15.5mph and cannot have a maximum motor power of more than 250W – but conversion kits can be bought to change this. E-scooters are always illegal on public land unless rented from a company like Voi. The Lib Dem councillor also requested more data from hospitals on injuries and deaths so the “true nature of the danger of these vehicles can be better understood”. Cllr Geoffrey Seeff, of St Neots The Eatons, said a BBC report in 2025 found a London hospital had dealt with 150 serious injuries in six months involving both children and adults. The Lib Dem councillor said: “Because of their motors and batteries, these machines are extremely heavy and cause horrific damage in a collision or if they fall on the rider. “Numerous deaths have been reported both here and in the USA, we have tried unsuccessfully thus far to obtain the relevant statistics for Cambridgeshire and the country as a whole.” Cllr Christopher Morris, chair of the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Fire Authority, said that the vehicles are a “transformative technology”. The Lib Dem councillor said: “Regulating transformative technology is always a balancing act – we must support rapid adoption while making sure it does not run ahead of sensible risk management. “Our fire service recognises the growing risks linked to e-bike lithium ion batteries and that around three quarters of identifiable e-bike fires involve conversion kits, mismatched chargers or other post-purchase modifications. “I support this motion and the members’ bill that it references and additionally I would urge everyone involved to keep fire risk firmly in view at every stage.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The RSPCA in Cambridgeshire is overwhelmed with "multi-animal cases" and has issued an urgent plea for help. The charity is appealing for "extra-special adopters" as rescue teams struggle with rising cases of animals, sometimes more than 100, being housed at single addresses. So far this year, RSPCA frontline officers are dealing with an average 410 "multi-animal" incidents - involving 10 or more every single month - an increase on 2025 which was a record-breaking year. Ronnie, Cane corso crossbreed, aged one (Image: RSPCA) Across Cambridgeshire, there have already been a staggering 61 incidents between January and August. Many of the animals rescued from these homes have behavioural and medical needs requiring rehabilitation. Currently, at the RSPCA Block Fen Animal Centre, cats Arthur and Tizzy are looking for their forever homes, having previously lived in a multi-cat household. Dogs Ronnie, Lulu and Marlon and Posy are also waiting for adopters this Adoptober. Jo Rowland, chief executive for the RSPCA, said: "We are struggling and we urgently need help. "Our frontline officers are finding dozens, even hundreds of animals in need at single addresses. "Animals who have come from homes like this often have behavioural and medical needs, due to the environment they had been living in and need a little more care and understanding. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 9 buildings in Cambridgeshire hiding centuries of history
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From Roman burial monuments and medieval churches to grand Jacobean mansions, Cambridgeshire is home to some extraordinary historic buildings. These nine landmarks have witnessed centuries of change and continue to tell the story of the county's rich and fascinating past. Few buildings in Cambridgeshire can match the historical weight of Peterborough Cathedral. The site has been a place of worship since the 7th century, when an Anglo-Saxon monastery was founded here in 655AD. Over the centuries it grew into one of England's most important medieval abbeys and later became the striking Norman cathedral seen today. The cathedral is famous as the burial place of Katherine of Aragon, Henry VIII's first wife. Mary Queen of Scots was also buried here before her remains were moved to Westminster Abbey. Viking raids, the Dissolution of the Monasteries and the English Civil War all left their mark on the building, making it a living record of England's turbulent past. Tucked away in a suburban corner of Peterborough, Longthorpe Tower looks modest from the outside but hides one of Britain's greatest medieval treasures. Built between about 1290 and 1300 by lawyer Robert Thorpe as part of a manor house, the tower contains an collection of wall paintings dating from around 1330. These rare artworks survived because they were covered with whitewash after the Reformation and remained hidden until the 20th century. The paintings depict religious scenes, morality tales, animals, kings and everyday medieval life. Buckden Towers has witnessed nearly 900 years of history in the heart of Huntingdonshire. Originally established as a residence for the Bishops of Lincoln during the 12th century, the fortified palace became one of the most important ecclesiastical residences in England. Numerous monarchs stayed here, including Henry III, Edward I and Richard III. Perhaps its most famous resident was Katherine of Aragon, who was confined here in 1533 during Henry VIII's attempts to end their marriage. The surviving brick tower, gatehouse and moated grounds evoke both the medieval and Tudor periods. Located in the former grammar school attended by Oliver Cromwell, this building offers a direct link to one of the most controversial figures in British history. The medieval structure dates back centuries and was already well established when a young Cromwell studied there in the late 16th century. The school would have provided him with a classical education that helped shape the future Lord Protector. Over the years the building has served many different purposes, but its strongest association remains with the man who led Parliament's forces during the English Civil War. Known as the "Ship of the Fens", Ely Cathedral dominates the landscape for miles around. Construction began in 1083 after the Norman Conquest, although the site had religious significance long before that. The cathedral is renowned for its magnificent Octagon Tower, created after the original Norman crossing tower collapsed in 1322. Its architecture reflects centuries of development, from Norman stonework to Gothic grandeur. Throughout its history it has survived political upheaval, religious reform and civil conflict. Just a short walk from Ely Cathedral stands the only surviving residence of Oliver Cromwell apart from Hampton Court. Parts of the building date back to around 1215, making it one of Ely's oldest houses. Originally serving as the vicarage for nearby St Mary's Church, it became home to Cromwell and his family between 1636 and 1647. From here he managed church tithes and lived during the years leading up to the English Civil War. The timber-framed building has survived centuries of change and now operates as a museum. Behind an elegant Georgian façade in Wisbech lies a building filled with stories of wealth, philanthropy and local influence. Built in 1722, Peckover House became home to the prominent Quaker banking family whose name still resonates in Fenland history. The family used their success to support a wide range of charitable projects throughout the region. Today managed by the National Trust, the house contains richly decorated interiors that contrast with its plain exterior. The surrounding walled garden is equally remarkable, featuring rare plants, historic structures and even orange trees believed to be centuries old. This handsome Georgian townhouse on Wisbech's South Brink was built around 1740 but is best known as the birthplace of social reformer Octavia Hill in 1838. Hill later became one of the founders of the National Trust and transformed housing conditions for some of London's poorest residents. The house was home to her family during formative years in her life and reflects the prosperity of one of Wisbech's leading merchant families. Saved and restored by volunteers, the building now tells the story not only of Hill's achievements but also of the social history of Victorian Britain. Just west of Peterborough, Elton Hall has been continuously occupied by the same family for generations. Parts of the building date to the 15th century, while later additions introduced Tudor and Gothic influences. The hall has welcomed royalty, survived political upheavals and accumulated centuries of family stories. Its striking architecture reflects changing fashions across hundreds of years, creating a building that feels like a timeline of English country-house history. Surrounded by landscaped parkland, Elton Hall remains privately owned and still contains family treasures that connect modern visitors directly with the past. Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cromwell Museum unveils rare artefacts in ‘A Few of Our Favourite Things’ exhibition
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new exhibition is being held at the Cromwell Museum in Huntingdon. Titled 'A Few of Our Favourite Things', the exhibition will be showcasing selected items by the museum’s volunteers, staff, and trustees. The exhibition offers a personal glimpse into the artefacts that resonate most with those closely involved with the collection. This includes items from the museum’s stores that are not typically displayed. The museum is housed in the former grammar school where Oliver Cromwell was educated. It holds a collection of objects that relate to his life and times. Cromwell Museum 2026 exterior (Image: Cromwell Museum) Among the chosen pieces are weapons, documents, portraits, and diplomatic gifts, each revealing different aspects of Cromwell’s legacy. The exhibition will run until November 1. One of the highlights of the exhibition is the Christmas Ban Proclamation of 1647. This ordinance by Parliament attempted to suppress Christmas, Easter, and other festivities, leading to riots and widespread resistance. Although often associated with Cromwell, historical records indicate he had little direct involvement with the ban. Another notable artefact is Cromwell’s 'Mortuary' Cavalry Sword circa 1650. The finely balanced weapon is believed to have been passed down through his family and still bears the initials 'OC' on the blade. The sword shows signs of use, serving as a reminder of the close-contact combat during the Civil War. Also on display is Cromwell’s Letter of 1652, offering a rare glimpse of the private man behind the public figure. Model of the Naseby Ship (Image: The Cromwell Museum) Other exhibition highlights include original copies of the Instrument of Government and the Humble Petition and Advice, the constitutional documents that shaped the Protectorate. A unique favourite is the working model of the Naseby, Cromwell’s flagship of 1655, built by master modelmaker Fred Pearl. The museum is open from Tuesday to Sunday, 10am to 4pm. The exhibition is free to visit, with donations welcomed.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Community primary school 'coming out the other side' after devastating fire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire primary school is "coming out the other side" and finally returning to normal life after a devastating fire forced staff and pupils out of the building for a year. Fen Drayton Primary School, which has 82 pupils, was badly damaged by a fire on August 13, 2024, that started accidentally during roof work. More than 30 firefighters tackled the blaze while an ambulance and three Hazardous Area Response Team vehicles were dispatched to treat a man for "serious burns". The blaze ripped through the school's ceilings, made the school unusable and forced pupils into mobile classrooms on the playing field. The damage left the building unusable A week later, heavy storms caused further water damage because the roof was not yet watertight. Nina McQueen, who has been headteacher for six years, said: "It was the year five and six classroom that was damaged the most. "The teacher had been in a couple of days before and set her classroom up ready for September. "She had got all the stationery out and labelled all the books and everything. The blaze ripped through the school's ceilings The fire in August 2024 caused devastating damage to Fen Drayton Primary School "Everything in her room had to be disposed of, because the fire was over the corner of her room, so she lost everything: books, tables, chairs, everything that was in her room. "I think that was really hard for her." Ms McQueen said the small staff team pulled together to cope with the devastation. Headteacher Nina McQueen She said: "It was obviously very challenging; we were very upset at the time, particularly when we came in and saw the devastation in the building. The headteacher's office was damaged "There were lots of tears from staff, particularly those who were affected the most by the damage and lost personal items from their classrooms. "But everyone pulled together and everyone was really supportive - and I think the same with the children." The school stayed closed for several weeks in September 2024 while two mobile classrooms were installed on the field. All 82 pupils were taught there for a year while the school was renovated. Pupils had to learn in mobile buildings on the school field for a year Ms McQueen said she worried about how pupils would cope, but they took the disruption in their stride. Insurance did not cover all the repair costs, so local groups donated up to £2,000 to replace lost resources and support pupils during the disruption. The PTA arranged special experiences and days out for pupils during the disruption. Parents and the parish council also helped, while the village hall housed pupils before the mobile classrooms were ready. Staff and pupils returned to the renovated building in September last year, and a new extension to the school's reception area was officially opened on October 10. The pupils and staff have now returned to the newly renovated school building The school building is now usable again (Image: Newsquest) Ms McQueen said she feels that life at the school is beginning to return to normal. She said: "We are coming out the other side of it. "Last year was quite challenging, getting back in the building, moving everything back in, getting everything set up and trying to get back to normal. "But I would say that we are definitely there now." Ms McQueen said she believes the incident shows the sense of community at the school Ms McQueen said she believes that the impact of the fire showed what a strong community there is at Fen Drayton Primary School. She added: "I think we can get through anything."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Data reveals Cambs is nearly last in UK for delivering care plans on time
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire County Council has been ranked among the worst in the country for providing care plans for children with special needs within the deadline. A Freedom of Information request showed that the council is facing an active backlog of around 1,800 cases. Children who are referred for an education, health and care plan (EHCP) should receive one within 20 weeks – but last year, less than one in ten were provided within the deadline. In the 2025/26 financial year, 93.33 per cent of EHCPs were issued after the deadline – with some children facing long waits. Cambridgeshire ranked 142nd out of 148 local authorities which reported their figures nationwide. Labour councillors Alex Bulat and Bryony Goodliffe submitted the original FOI request and put the figures to Cambridgeshire County Council calling for a review. Cllr Bulat, of St Ives South and Needingworth, said: “The reality on the ground is that people don’t care about excuses. Our residents don’t care about blaming others because our case workers are being asked to manage up to 500 cases each – two and a half the regional average – and parents and children are left waiting.” Cllr Elliot Tong said he had asked the council for the longest wait time and was told this was 150 weeks – nearly three years. The independent councillor, of Abbey, said: “These are real children whose lives are affected by our choices and the fact that a child has had to wait three years to get the support that they are entitled to is absolutely abhorrent.” Council leader Lucy Nethsingha amended the motion and removed any references to the FOI figures leading to accusations of politicising it by opposition members. “Conservative group leader Ross Martin said the Liberal Democrats were “trying to blame everyone but themselves”. He said: “You’re playing politics with our children – we want to get on with delivering for them because my inbox is full of issues with ECHPs, as it is in my day job as well. This isn’t acceptable – it’s more than just the 20 week delays, it’s the delays in the refreshers. “There’s an example I’m aware of in Godmanchester where someone has been waiting for five years for an update – that’s not acceptable.” Cllr Edna Murphy, chair of the children and young people committee, agreed that wait times “aren’t where they should be” but assured councillors fixing it “is a top priority”. The Lib Dem councillor said: “We haven’t been doing nothing, we have been working incredibly hard on this for just over a year since we took control. “Although there is a lot more to do there has been significant improvement in the service in that time. “In just over a year the council is now producing three times the number of EHCPs every month than they were before. “The problem for us all is the demand for EHCPs is much greater than that and it’s grown rapidly in recent years.” Cllr Nethsingha’s amendment passed – with 28 votes for, 23 against and one abstention – but she then urged members to vote against it. She said the motion would still require the council to undergo a review, as she could not change this, and this would delay progress on improving wait times. She said: “The things that have been recommended in this motion would not help with actually declining the backlogs. “They would put an additional burden on the staff who are desperately trying to deal with these issues for children and families.” Cllr Tom Sanderson, chair of the meeting, told members they would have to vote on the motion within four minutes due to a strict two and a half hour time limit on motions. “After a number of councillors raised issues with this and asked for clarification, Cllr Sanderson said that time had run out and the motion was dropped.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Ives beat St Neots 14-7 in hard-fought local derby on narrow pitch
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: St Ives extended their winning run with a hard-fought victory over local rivals St Neots in testing conditions. The league fixture was played at St Neots, where prolonged dry weather forced the match on to a narrow pitch. The Bulls prevailed seven points to fourteen, with Henri Cole and Ben Peach scoring tries, both converted by Charlie Mandley and Dan Hawkins respectively. The main pitch had been cordoned off before kick-off, leaving both sides to adapt quickly to unfamiliar surroundings. The restricted width encouraged a direct contest, with the teams relying heavily on their forwards and struggling to remain inside the touchlines. St Neots used the wind well during the opening half, with their powerful carriers and midfield runners forcing Ives deep into their own territory. Josh Meadows produced several important ankle-level tackles, disrupting a number of promising attacks from the home side. The scoreboard remained blank after half an hour, but Ives then produced a sustained spell of possession lasting at least 25 rucks. St Neots defended stubbornly, yet their resistance finally ended when Cole stepped between two defenders and crossed beneath the posts. Ben Peach (Image: Paul Cox) Charlie Mandley converted to give the visitors a seven-point advantage at the interval. Ives hoped the wind at their backs would allow them to take control after the restart, although conditions also contributed to several misplaced passes. The visitors gained increasing authority at the set piece, with Ben Peach particularly effective in the lineout. Peach won opposition possession as well as securing accurate throws from Ives hooker Sam Marjason-Stamp. The Bulls’ pack continued to make ground and, late in the third quarter, drove towards the line before Peach forced his way over. Hawkins added the conversion to put Ives two scores ahead. St Neots responded by attacking with greater urgency, but the visitors defended resolutely, with replacement Matt Holland making a notable contribution. The hosts did pull a converted try back after a miskicked ball was carried backwards by the wind and returned unexpectedly to their winger. He ran in unopposed, but Ives held firm during the closing stages to secure victory. Director of rugby, Duncan Williams, said: “It was a really close game which we ultimately never looked like losing. “It was disappointing to only get four points but we are happy with the win and look ahead to playing second-placed Stewarts & Lloyds next week.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire residents recycled nearly 4,000 tonnes of electrical waste through household recycling centres last year. The figure, recorded between April 2025 and March 2026, highlights efforts to tackle electronic waste and promote sustainability across the county. Cllr Ros Hathorn, Chair of the Environment and Green Investment Committee at Cambridgeshire County Council, said: "We’re delighted that local residents have taken such positive action and recycled so many items of waste electrical and electronic equipment, which allows these items to be disposed of safely or recycled. "We are dedicated to supporting local people and communities to reduce waste and reuse materials, as well as supporting initiatives that help with climate change." Of the total collected, 603 tonnes were fridges and 442 tonnes were computer monitors. All items were classified as WEEE (waste electrical and electronic equipment), covering everything from large appliances like washing machines and ovens to smaller items such as kettles and toasters. The council also reminded residents that items containing batteries, such as disposable vapes, earbuds, and power banks, should be taken to recycling centres.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Calls for urgent upgrade to pipe network after ‘brutal’ summer of ‘record leaks’
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A council has called for greater collaboration with water and utility companies for an “urgent” upgrade of pipes following “record numbers of leaks”. Cambridgeshire County Council agreed to write to the government and regulators to request water companies work with councils on highway impacts, leaks and infrastructure planning at a meeting last week. Cllr Ros Hathorn said the summer’s heatwaves have been “absolutely brutal” to the pipes and moving into winter “the freeze-thaw cycle always punishes the pipes”. The Lib Dem councillor said: “There’s probably no community in the county that hasn’t experienced a trickle or a torrent of water from a burst water pipe this summer.” Cllr Hathorn, of Histon, Impington, Orchard Park and King’s Meadow, said water companies need to upgrade the system rather than patching leaks as they happen. She said: “Emergency repairs are the worst way to maintain infrastructure and that is what is happening – it’s expensive, wasteful and disruptive. “It’s clear from the number of leaks and the age of our roads that there is an urgent need for a planned upgrade of the water pipes in our road. “For far too long, we haven’t paid attention to investing in our water infrastructure.” Cllr Ian Manning, of Chesterton, said a neighbour had questioned him on why roadworks weren’t coordinated after his wife faced delays returning from work. The Lib Dem councillor said they “simply don’t have the powers” but supported the “dig once initiative” to make different companies coordinate works so they happen at the same time. He said: “If only we could have a bit of weight behind it and the power to get all these different companies to coordinate at the same time and not have to repair the roads over and over again”. Cllr Yannifer Malinowski, of Burwell, said the growth of Cambridge and surrounding areas must be accompanied with suitable infrastructure. The Lib Dem councillor said that summer saw “record numbers of leaks and extensive road closures across the county”. She said: “We need to ask whether enough is being done to address the root causes rather than always dealing with the consequences and patching up their failures.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Putting the focus on East Anglia’s community changemakers
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: There are just a few weeks remaining to submit your entries for the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027 and be in with a chance of being recognised as one of the region’s sustainability champions. Bringing together the ambitions of Insight Energy magazine and the Clean & Green campaign, these awards were created to put the spotlight on businesses, organisations and individuals who are making a difference, whether through innovation, education, green energy or environmentally friendly business practices. The entry deadline is Sunday, November 8, after which time the judging process will begin and 2027’s finalists will be shortlisted. Read on to find out more about two of the 14 categories. Sponsored by National Grid The Energy Innovation Award will recognise innovations that significantly enhance energy efficiency or reduce energy consumption. From businesses to local communities, there are countless people actively looking at their green credentials, and this award will celebrate those who are meeting their environmental commitments in a way that hasn’t been seen before. The category is open to any individual or organisation that can showcase an energy innovation that is both unique and groundbreaking. The judges will be looking for entries that demonstrate a novel and scalable approach with measurable results in reducing environmental impact, while actively engaging key stakeholders. Entrants will be expected to demonstrate how their innovation can be scaled or applied across other industries or regions, thereby maximising its impact. They will also need to show how they have actively involved energy providers, consumers or other stakeholders in their innovation. Critically, anyone entering this category must be able to evidence a reduction in energy consumption or improved energy efficiency, demonstrating measurable outcomes. An individual, group or organisation that has gone above and beyond to drive sustainability within their local community will be named Community Champion of the Year. This award recognises local heroes who have demonstrated outstanding leadership, innovation and commitment to creating meaningful environmental change while inspiring others to take action. The judges will be looking for entrants who can show a clear and positive impact on their community, whether through grassroots initiatives, community projects, education programmes, or other innovative means. Entries should provide evidence of measurable outcomes wherever possible, highlighting the real-world impact of the entrant’s work and the creative or unique approaches they have used to address environmental challenges. A key aspect of this award is the ability to engage and collaborate with others. Entrants should demonstrate how they have brought people together, encouraging participation and fostering a shared commitment to improving sustainability at a local level. If you think you or someone you know has made a lasting impact on the future of your community, now is the time to enter. Find out more about all the categories and enter at cleanandgreenawards.co.uk

Officers found a total of 17,147 indecent images of children on the phone, mainly of young or pre-pubescent boys. These included 6,080 category C images, 6,028 category B images and 5,039 category A images – the most severe. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 6 locations in Cambridgeshire with surprising royal connections
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: From Tudor queens and medieval kings to the birthplace of Richard III, Cambridgeshire is packed with locations hiding remarkable royal connections. These towns and villages have played surprising roles in some of the most dramatic chapters of British royal history. Ely’s royal connection stretches back more than 1,300 years. The city was founded around the monastery established by St Etheldreda, daughter of King Anna of East Anglia, in the seventh century. The religious settlement she created grew into one of the most important ecclesiastical centres in medieval England. Royal links continued through the centuries, with members of England’s royal families supporting the cathedral and its diocese. The city’s origins are inseparable from Anglo-Saxon royalty, making Ely one of Cambridgeshire’s oldest royal-associated settlements. Peterborough boasts one of the most remarkable royal connections anywhere in the East of England. Peterborough Cathedral is the final resting place of Catherine of Aragon, the first wife of Henry VIII and a former Queen of England. Following her death at nearby Kimbolton Castle in January 1536, she was buried in what was then Peterborough Abbey. The cathedral later also housed the remains of Mary, Queen of Scots, after her execution at Fotheringhay in 1587, before they were moved to Westminster Abbey by her son, James I. For a period, Peterborough held the graves of two of the most famous women in British royal history. The quiet village of Kimbolton is forever linked to one of the most dramatic chapters in Tudor history. Kimbolton Castle became the final home of Catherine of Aragon after Henry VIII rejected her as queen. Removed from court and increasingly isolated, she spent her last years at the castle before dying there in January 1536. Her death marked the end of a bitter royal dispute that contributed to England’s break with Rome and the English Reformation. Today the castle houses Kimbolton School, but its royal associations remain a major part of its identity. Buckden Towers was once a favoured residence of the powerful Bishops of Lincoln and hosted several monarchs. Henry VIII stayed here during the years leading up to his divorce from Catherine of Aragon, and the future queen Catherine Howard also visited the site in 1541. Most notably, Catherine of Aragon spent time at Buckden during her enforced separation from court before being transferred to Kimbolton Castle. As a result, the village became part of the chain of locations associated with one of the defining royal disputes in English history. Its surviving medieval towers provide a tangible reminder of the Tudor figures who once passed through its gates. St Ives owes much of its historic importance to King John. In 1001, the remains of St Ivo were reportedly discovered nearby, helping establish the town as an important religious centre. By the early 13th century, King John had granted St Ives one of England’s most significant fairs, transforming its fortunes and helping it develop into a thriving market town. Royal patronage brought merchants from across the country and elevated St Ives’ regional importance. While visitors today know the town for its picturesque bridge and riverside setting, its growth was closely tied to medieval royal influence. Wisbech has a lesser-known royal story linked to the turbulence of the 17th century. During the English Civil War and the years that followed, the Fens became a region of strategic importance. Local tradition and historical accounts connect the town with Charles II who renewed and enlarged Wisbech's Carter of Incorporation in 1669. Wisbech Castle itself has hosted numerous notable figures through the centuries and stands as a reminder of the town’s longstanding relationship with authority and power. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs woman, 87, scammed out of £7,000 as police launch investigation
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police have launched an investigation after an 87-year-old woman was scammed out of £7,000 in a courier fraud scheme. The Peterborough woman received a landline call on October 12 from a man claiming to be a Cambridgeshire police officer. He told her that a man had been arrested for theft and found with counterfeit money, and that £7,000 had been taken from her account but later returned. The caller said they needed her help to investigate and told her to stay on the line while he connected her to her bank. After a brief dial tone, the woman was put through to a female caller who claimed to be from the bank and confirmed the officer’s story. The fraudster told her to withdraw £7,000 for the investigation and keep the reason from bank staff. She was told to take the money home, where someone would collect it using the code word "orange 123." A man later arrived at her door, gave the code word, and took the envelope of cash. The woman later realised she had been scammed and the money was gone. A police investigation was launched, which the force confirmed on October 21 is still ongoing. In a statement to social media, Cambridgeshire Police said: "Sadly, our officers are seeing more and more of these cases of courier fraud scams and they are urging people to be vigilant and look out for vulnerable neighbours and relatives. "Remember, neither the police nor your bank will ever call and ask you to withdraw money as part of an investigation. "If in doubt, hang up and call police on 101 from another line to check before you act." More information on fraud prevention is available on the Cambridgeshire Police website.

Keegan became angry and verbally abusive, sending her a barrage of messages and threatening to take his own life. Despite the victim’s efforts to remain supportive, Keegan continued to pursue a romantic relationship and became angry when she made it clear she wanted to be nothing more than friends. When she tried to cut contact completely, he threatened to harm himself. After she blocked him on social media, Keegan created fake accounts to keep messaging her. In December 2025, the victim told Keegan to leave her alone, but he bombarded her with messages and voice notes, some abusive. He also sent pictures of himself after harming himself and again threatened to take his own life. Keegan’s behaviour escalated when he discovered where she lived and sent her a picture of himself holding rope nearby. He also contacted her family, friends and workplace, forcing colleagues to walk her to her car after work. In a police interview, Keegan admitted sending a “high volume of messages” to get “some accountability” from the victim. Jamie Keegan became angry and verbally abusive at the victim (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) On October 15, at Cambridge Crown Court, he was sentenced to two years and two months in prison after admitting stalking involving serious alarm or distress. Detective Constable Ryan Burke said: "Keegan simply refused to accept that the victim did not want a relationship with him. "She repeatedly made her wishes clear and tried to cut contact, but he continued to pursue her, creating fake accounts and contacting her friends, family and workplace. "His relentless behaviour caused her serious distress and affected her day-to-day life, including leaving her reliant on colleagues to walk her to her car after work. “This case is a reminder that if someone tells you they do not want contact, you must respect that. "Repeated unwanted contact is not romantic or persistent affection, it can amount to stalking.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Exact time clocks change in the UK this weekend and why they change
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Clocks across the UK will turn back one hour this weekend. The change takes place at 2am on Sunday, October 25, when clocks go back across the country. Moving the hands back gives an extra hour in bed for a Sunday lie-in. It also provides an hour of sunlight as November approaches and days shorten. People will not need to alter timepieces by hand in most cases. Devices connected to the internet update automatically, including smartphones, laptops, tablets and televisions. Alarm clocks, car radios and equipment not connected to the internet will require manual adjustment. The purpose of the system is to make use of daylight. Germany introduced the first clock change in 1916 during the First World War to save energy. Less electricity was needed when daylight lasted longer. Britain and European governments followed, which began British Summer Time. The system has remained in place in the UK since 1971.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Rare Royal Mint 50p coin sells for more than 400 times face value on eBay
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A rare 50p coin has fetched more than 400 times its face value after an online auction. The Kew Gardens piece drew 18 bids on eBay before being snapped up for £213.50. Released by the Royal Mint in 2009, only 210,000 copies of the coin were ever produced. The coin was introduced to celebrate the 250th anniversary of London's famous royal botanical garden. Its reverse design by Christopher Le Brun features the famous Chinese Pagoda entwined with a decorative climber, alongside the portrait of Queen Elizabeth II on the obverse. The piece has long been regarded as one of the most sought-after coins in modern British circulation. A low initial mintage combined with intense collector demand means very few examples remain in everyday circulation. The 50p piece provides a distinct heptagonal canvas for coin designers. With a diameter of 27.5mm, it is the largest British coin in circulation and offers space for commemorative artwork. Rarity serves as the primary factor driving collector demand and market prices. Low mintage figures mean fewer examples exist to buy or trade. Coin condition also plays an important role, with well-preserved specimens securing higher prices. Collectors also prize unusual design errors and striking flaws that escape the mint. Sales avenues can influence the price realised for a rare coin. Sellers often turn to competitive online bidding on eBay to test market demand. Others prefer formal valuations from professional coin dealers to establish a certified market value. Royal Mint mintage figures confirm the rarest 50p designs to enter general circulation: The 2023 Atlantic Salmon coin holds the title as the rarest 50p design in circulation. Anyone checking their loose change is urged to keep an eye out for these scarce editions.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Funding secured to continue support for frequent A&E attendees in Cambs
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than £600,000 in funding has been secured to continue a life-changing support service in Cambridgeshire. The High Impact Use (HIU) service, which helps people with complex needs reduce A&E visits, is designed for those whose frequent emergency department attendances are often linked to social, emotional, or practical challenges rather than purely medical issues. Cambridgeshire County Council has secured £609,552 for the 2027/28 financial year through a new agreement with the NHS Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Integrated Care Board (ICB). Councillor Alison Whelan, chair of the council’s communities, social mobility and inclusion committee, said: "The High Impact Use service shows what's possible when organisations work together to support residents in a more personalised and preventative way. "Many of the people supported by the service face complex challenges that cannot be resolved through healthcare interventions alone. "By helping residents access the right support at the right time, we can improve outcomes for individuals, helping them live independently and create stronger ties, while also reducing demand on our hospitals and emergency services." Launched in October 2024, the HIU service has already shown promising results. According to the ICB, health-related costs for an initial group of service users dropped from an average of £18,333 per person per year to £3,401 per person per year after receiving support. Cambridgeshire County Council is the only local authority in the country to directly host a High Impact Use service. The scheme has gained national attention, including a visit from NHS England representatives who highlighted the service as a strong example of community-led practice. It has also received an Outstanding Achievement Award from North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust. The new funding will allow the council to continue hosting the HIU Operational Team throughout the 2027/28 financial year in partnership with the ICB, local hospitals, and the East of England Ambulance Service.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Waterbeach heritage walk reveals how history is shaping the new town
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A heritage walk has brought the history of Waterbeach to life, highlighting how the past is influencing its future development. Last weekend, more than 55 people took part in the guided walk, which explored the village’s historical sites and showed how they are shaping the design and character of the new town. The route included access to areas not currently accessible to the public, which will be opened up to recreate the historic Causeway connection between Waterbeach Abbey and Denny Abbey. Jane Williamson, chair of trustees at The Farmland Museum, said: "The Heritage Walk was a wonderful community event, and I saw people I haven’t seen for ages and met some new ones too. "There’s was something really moving about going through the gate into the bit of causeway that has been inaccessible for so long. The walk explored Waterbeach’s history and its developing new town (Image: Waterbeach) "The walk along the path from the new town towards the Abbey is absolutely lovely, it’s almost like being in another world." The walk began at Waterbeach Village Green and included a visit to the Waterbeach Military Heritage Museum. It continued through Soldiers Hill, an ancient earthwork, and included a visit to Denny Abbey. Along the route, participants heard from historians and community leaders who explained how the new development is incorporating historical features into its design, including street names and transport links. Reverend Sarah Newns, pioneer minister at St John’s Church, said: "The walk showed the importance of connecting with neighbours and sharing experiences whether you have lived here a long time or are new to the area. "The history of the land is fascinating, and this walk alone showed the layers of history around us, as well as how the next chapter of the parish is being written and shaped by the new development." To find out more about Waterbeach’s heritage, visit waterbeachwb.co.uk/heritage.

Councillors have voted to refuse a controversial 199-home development plan for Ramsey despite receiving a recommendation for approval. BDW Trading Ltd submitted the proposal for land south of The Malting with landowners Susan and Robert Pickard. The scheme included up to 199 homes, 40 per cent affordable housing, children’s play areas, drainage infrastructure and related works. Developers also proposed a landscaped perimeter, a 1.1km circular walking route linked to public rights of way and green infrastructure covering around 37 per cent of the site. The site is land south of The Malting in Ramsey However, at a meeting on October 19, Huntingdonshire District Council's Development Management Committee voted to refuse the outline application, which had been recommended for approval. Planning officers said the benefits outweighed the harm, pointing to Huntingdonshire’s current shortfall in five-year housing land supply. The report said the scheme would help meet housing need and provide substantial affordable housing. Cllr Andrew Wood proposed refusing the plan against officers’ recommendation, subject to consultation with the Secretary of State. The proposal passed with nine votes in favour, none against and two abstentions. The decision followed strong opposition from residents, who submitted 228 objection letters, as well as from Ramsey Town Council, Bury Parish Council and the Middle Level Commissioners. Residents warned of more traffic, pressure on schools and healthcare services, flood risk, countryside loss, damage to wildlife and further merging of Ramsey and Bury. Ramsey Town Council said the application conflicted with the emerging Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan, which seeks to keep Ramsey and Bury separate. Sam Carling, MP for North West Cambridgeshire, told the council the development would pile more pressure on the area’s already struggling Integrated Care Board. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A 91-year-old train enthusiast has returned to the railways after regaining his mobility in Cambridgeshire. Mr Brown said: "I had given up when I came to Bramley. Staff at Bramley Court helped make the special journey possible (Image: Bramley Court Care Home) "I’d been in hospital for so long and everything was unknown." He dislocated both shoulders in a fall at his Cambridge home earlier this year and spent five months in hospital before moving to the care home in June. With support from staff and his family, he began a rehabilitation programme that included weekly physiotherapy, exercise classes, and daily walking practice. The 91-year-old enjoyed a special journey on the Poppy Line (Image: Bramley Court Care Home) Carol Morgan, head of quality at Bramley Court, said: "Peter was using a wheelchair when he came to us, but just three months later, he was walking with a frame. "He has also regained the use of his arms and he has his independence back." The trip, taken alongside his two daughters, brought back fond memories of his career on the railways. The railway trip brought back memories of Peter’s 40-year career. (Image: Bramley Court Care Home) Mr Brown began working in 1951, starting as a fireman on steam trains before moving to diesel locomotives and becoming a driver in the 1980s. He said: "I couldn’t move my shoulders or hold a cup, and I couldn’t get out of bed. "I didn’t think I’d get to where I am now including being able to walk down the train platform. Rehabilitation helped Peter regain his mobility and independence (Image: Bramley Court Care Home) "Now, when I walk, I feel so happy I could run." The care home, which provides residential, nursing, and dementia care, is currently taking part in a research study with Care England on supporting people whose mobility has reduced following hospital admission.
